articles.title: Delos Data Targets Heterogeneous AI with Data Interface - EE Times
articles.text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. – Delos Data is adding silicon to its portfolio, the startup announced at the AI Infra Summit. Delos previously announced data center orchestration software, Mosaic, and a new server architecture, Asterion, for huge scale-up domains, but is now working on Apollo, a data interface chiplet.
Apollo comes either as a 30+ Tbps I/O chiplet that sits next to an XPU, as a 10+ Tbps near-packaged optical interface, or on a 400+ Gbps card for CPUs and memory endpoints. It provides endpoints with guaranteed bandwidth and latency, handling load balancing, topology, and failure handling so the endpoint doesn’t have to do it. Delos is targeting order-of-magnitude improvements in speed, resiliency, and scale versus what endpoints can do today.
The company also announced that it has raised more than $100 million in venture capital.
New AI infrastructure will cater to either regular inference, agentic AI, or both, Delos Data CTO Dan Daly told EE Times.
“The theme we see in these emerging new types of infrastructure buildouts is a mixture of hardware,” Daly said. “The CPU folks love to talk about how the CPU is back, but scale up and scale out only connect GPUs. There is another domain needed that includes GPUs, accelerators, CPUs, memory, and storage. We’re offering a data interface that can bridge all these different types of devices, each with their own semantics, and put them in a single, flat, low-latency domain.”
For example, in prefill-decode disaggregated architectures, GPUs and dataflow accelerators have completely different approaches to memory, Daly said. GPUs place data in HBM, and all compute units can access the data via the HBM’s memory map; it’s about data objects and addresses. In a dataflow architecture, a stream of data goes through a sequence of operations—the location determines what happens to the data. The semantics of these architectures are very different and need to be bridged.
Communication semantics can also be difficult, since a CPU and a memory controller (for example) may not speak the same language; today this is handled by a switch, but it incurs latency. It would be more efficient if interconnects could be aware of the semantics of both endpoints, Daly argues, and that is what Delos’s Apollo chiplet is designed to achieve.
“There’s an opportunity here to be able to greatly simplify the switching to really maximize the value of those switches—radix, latency, low power, flexibility of media—all the things you want from a switch and less of the things you don’t…legacy things from cloud or scale-out,” Daly said. “There’s an opportunity to open up the aperture here, to enable flexibility in terms of what switches go there, and to potentially simplify the network that goes in between these devices, where it could even be optical.”
Inference platforms may use copper and/or optical links, different types of switches, and different topologies, which require detailed co-design and customization. Delos does not want to replace switches; rather, it wants to add Apollo at each endpoint to reuse existing switches of any kind in a more efficient way.
Resiliency across multiple hops (that could mean bridging multiple types of semantics) is also critical.
“A lot of these devices were not born in this new environment; they were born on the board,” Daly said. “On the board, when you access memory or Flash, it always works. So the semantics of data memory expect that reads and writes always work. So we need to build in that assumption that even if a switch fails, it should still work.”
Delos’s data interface has to be in silicon because the lowest possible latency is required, Daly said. Apollo would replace today’s I/O chiplet in the package next to a multi-die GPU or XPU, or as a packaged chip on a board in near-packaged or co-packaged optics systems. There is also demand for a form factor resembling a traditional NIC, which can temporarily help bridge endpoints—particularly CPUs, which may not need the bandwidth but would benefit from latency improvements—into a cluster without requiring the Apollo chiplet, Delos CEO Ed Doe told EE Times.
“The common attribute across these [form factors] is latency, resiliency, and ultimately, the ability to bring [everything] in scale into a single domain,” Doe said.
Delos currently has an FPGA version of the card to offer, with NPO chips to appear next year, Doe said. The chiplet version is the same tape-out as the NPO chip version, but because of XPU design cycles, the chiplet will not appear in XPU products for another couple of years, Doe said.
Delos has also combined its hardware and software into a reference architecture and offers Morpheus, a development platform that bridges customers’ pre-silicon environments and lab environments to help customers co-design system topologies based on workloads and understand the impact of changes in connectivity.
Target customers for the Apollo chiplet include AI chip companies, such as hyperscalers and frontier labs working on their own silicon, Doe said.
According to the company, Delos’s Mosaic cluster management software is already deployed in production environments using customers’ existing infrastructure. The server, Asterion, will be sampling at the end of the fourth quarter. The development platform, Morpheus, is available now.

articles.title: Prise en main des Xreal Aura : Android XR dans des lunettes, ça donne quoi ?
articles.text:
Prise en main des Xreal Aura : Android XR dans des lunettes, ça donne quoi ?
Après avoir longtemps fait parler d'elles sans se montrer, les lunettes de réalité augmentée Aura ont finalement fait leurs débuts publics à l'IFA de Berlin. Leur ambition affichée est de prouver qu'Android XR peut tenir dans une simple monture. Nous avons pu les essayer.
Depuis le lancement d'Android XR, le système d'exploitation de Google dédié à la réalité étendue cherchait encore sa paire de lunettes de référence. Samsung et Google planchent bien sur leurs propres modèles, mais ceux-ci se limitent pour l'instant à l'audio, sans aucun affichage. À l'opposé, le duo a aussi sorti aux États-Unis le casque de réalité virtuelle Galaxy XR.
C'est pile entre ces deux propositions que Xreal est venu se positionner. Dans le cadre de l'IFA qui s'est tenu il y a quelques jours à Berlin, le fabricant a présenté Aura, des lunettes conçues main dans la main avec Google et Qualcomm, et qui embarquent de vrais écrans devant les yeux. De quoi déclencher une sacrée attente autour de ce produit. Nous avons eu la possibilité de les manipuler assez longuement pour nous faire une première idée de leur potentiel.
Sur le papier, la fiche technique implique deux dalles Sony Micro-Oled affichant chacune 1920 x 1200 pixels, un taux de rafraîchissement qui grimpe jusqu'à 120 Hz, un champ de vision de 70°, une puce Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite épaulée par un coprocesseur spatial maison, le tout sous Android XR avec Gemini et le Google Play Store à bord.
Une monture et un boîtier, reliés par un câble
Mais comme beaucoup de produits concurrents, les Aura ne sont pas juste des lunettes. Ces dernières concentrent évidemment l'affichage, ainsi que des caméras, des haut-parleurs intégrés et quelques boutons de contrôle disposés sur les branches. Mais il faut aussi composer avec un boîtier externe qui héberge le processeur et la batterie de 4455 mAh. Son gabarit est comparable à celui d'une batterie externe ou d'un grand smartphone. Les deux éléments communiquent par un câble USB-C.
Ce choix de déporter la puissance de calcul et l'énergie hors de la monture allège logiquement ce que l'on porte sur le nez, mais il impose de composer en permanence avec un fil entre la poche et le visage. Chacun jugera du compromis.
Côté autonomie, Xreal annonce environ 5 à 6 h d'utilisation, un chiffre constructeur qu'il faudra bien entendu confronter à la réalité une fois le produit commercialisé.
Le fabricant nous a par ailleurs confirmé que les porteurs de lunettes de vue ne sont pas oubliés, puisque les Aura accepteront des inserts de verres correcteurs. D'ailleurs, si vous avez déjà acheté des inserts pour des Xreal One Pro, il n'y aura pas besoin de repasser à la caisse puisqu'ils seront également compatibles avec les Aura.
Dommage en revanche que le poids exact de la monture n'ait pas encore été communiqué, car c'est précisément le nerf de la guerre sur ce type de produit destiné à être porté des heures durant. Ce poids nous a paru raisonnable lors de notre essai, mais il faudra attendre de les tester pendant plusieurs heures de suite pour se faire un avis définitif.
Deux dalles micro-OLED et un large champ de vision
Le cœur de l'expérience, ce sont ces deux écrans Sony micro-Oled, un par œil, d'une définition de 1920 x 1200 pixels chacun. Le taux de rafraîchissement peut atteindre 120 Hz, de quoi assurer une fluidité confortable pour la navigation comme pour le jeu. Le champ de vision s'établit à 70°. Bien sûr, cela ne vaut pas les 110° et plus des casques tels que le Vision Pro ou les Quest 3/3S, mais il serait injuste de comparer des lunettes ouvertes telles que les Aura à ces produits.
Pour loger leurs dalles dans un format qui ressemble encore à des lunettes classiques, Xreal s'appuie sur son système optique X Prism. Le fabricant a également prévu un assombrissement électrochromique. Concrètement, les verres peuvent s'obscurcir à la demande, simplement en pressant l'un des boutons physiques de la monture. Cela permet de basculer d'un affichage en surimpression du monde réel vers une expérience plus immersive, coupée de l'environnement, avec plusieurs degrés d'assombrissement à la clé. Une souplesse bienvenue, tant les usages d'un tel appareil oscillent entre consultation rapide en mobilité et session de visionnage prolongée.
Dans l'ensemble, nous avons été assez agréablement surpris par le rendu. Attention, il ne faut pas s'attendre à retrouver la même qualité que sur des casques ou lunettes VR telles que les Apple Vision Pro et autres Meta VR Glasses, mais les couleurs, la netteté et la luminosité de l'image des Aura se sont montrées assez satisfaisantes lors de cet essai. Signalons tout de même que nous les avons portées en intérieur, avec une luminosité ambiante correcte. Il faudra voir ce que cela donne dans des environnements plus compliqués.
Android XR, Gemini et le Play Store à bord
Sous le capot, la plateforme Snapdragon Reality Elite de Qualcomm fait tourner Android XR, et Xreal y a ajouté son propre coprocesseur spatial, baptisé X1S. Cette combinaison donne accès au Google Play Store, ce qui rassure d'emblée sur le catalogue applicatif. Il faut tout de même garder en tête que le nombre d'applis vraiment adaptées à un usage en réalité augmentée semble encore assez famélique. Nous vous en dirons plus à ce sujet lors du test en bonne et due forme de ces Aura.
Pour piloter l'ensemble, plusieurs méthodes cohabitent. Parlons d'abord du boîtier externe, qui fait aussi office de contrôleur avec l'intégration d'un pavé tactile sur sa surface. Ensuite, ce sont les mains qui peuvent aussi contrôler l'interface. Les lunettes gèrent en effet parfaitement le suivi spatial 6DoF (positionnement dans l'espace) ainsi que le tracking optique des mains et des gestes sans manette. Les gestes pour naviguer dans Android XR sont quasiment identiques à ceux de visionOS d'Apple, avec des gestes de pincement, de double pincement, de déplacement ou de glissement.
Enfin, le contrôle vocal complète le tableau grâce à Gemini. L'assistant de Google occupe d'ailleurs une place centrale dans la proposition. Il a accès à ce que voient les yeux de l'utilisateur, ce qui permet des fonctions comme Circle to Search appliqué au monde réel. Vous croisez un objet, un texte, une affiche, et Gemini peut s'en saisir directement. Vous l'aurez compris, l'Aura se veut autant un écran portable qu'un assistant visuel permanent.
Un écran externe pour à peu près tout
Enfin, l'un des points les plus intéressants de la proposition tient à nos yeux à la possibilité de transformer ces Aura en véritable écran externe pour un Mac, un PC sous Windows, une console de jeu, un smartphone, etc. Le boîtier devrait accepter n'importe quel appareil par USB-C DisplayPort. De fait, l'Aura ne se limite pas à son propre écosystème Android XR et peut servir de moniteur d'appoint universel, un argument de poids pour qui voyage souvent.
Détail qui a son importance, le contenu affiché depuis un appareil externe reste accessible à Gemini. L'assistant peut donc analyser ce qui transite par le DisplayPort, exactement comme il observe le monde réel à travers les lunettes.
Disponibilité et prix
Le lancement est programmé pour l'automne 2026, vraisemblablement autour du mois de novembre. Côté tarif, Xreal évoque un prix inférieur à 1500 $, soit environ 1300 € au cours actuel, sans qu'un prix pour le marché français ait encore été officialisé.

articles.title: Google Messages déploie la mise à jour qu'on attendait tous
articles.text:
Après une phase de test, l’application Google Messages commence à déployer son nouveau design pour les conversations. Cette refonte change la manière dont vous allez interagir avec chaque message, notamment en simplifiant l’accès aux options les plus courantes et en corrigeant l’un des principaux défauts de l’ancienne interface qui reléguait la majorité des actions dans un sous-menu pas très pratique.
Une interface flottante pour un accès direct aux actions
Un appui long sur une bulle de texte ou une image fait désormais apparaître un menu flottant. Chaque action est directement accompagnée d’une icône placée juste en face pour permettre de les repérer rapidement sans avoir à forcément lire le texte qui les accompagne. On y retrouve les raccourcis habituels comme la réponse, le transfert, l’ajout d’une étoile pour mettre en favoris, la suppression, la sélection multiple, l’affichage des informations, l’enregistrement des photos, ou encore l’option de remix pour les images.
La ligne dédiée aux émojis et aux créations de photomojis reste quant à elle à la même place. Lorsque vous sélectionnez le tout dernier message d’une discussion, l’application ajuste l’affichage en centrant légèrement l’élément grâce à une animation dynamique accompagnée d’un retour haptique. On note également que le fond d’écran se floute légèrement pour détacher visuellement le menu actif.
Vous allez enfin pouvoir copier du texte précisément
Au-delà de l’interface, le plus grand changement technique est sans doute celui de l’outil pour copier le texte. Jusqu’à présent, l’application ne permettait de copier que l’intégralité d’un message, ce qui obligeait à supprimer les mots ou les phrases que vous ne vouliez pas après les avoir collés ailleurs. Cela semble archaïque, mais c’était pourtant bien le comportement de Google Messages lorsque vous faisiez un copier-coller de texte. Il est donc désormais possible de sélectionner précisément un extrait pour surligner uniquement la portion souhaitée.
Sur le même sujet : Google Messages va avoir droit à une refonte de son moteur de recherche
Cette mise à jour arrive avec la version stable 20260910_03_RC02 de l’application. Elle est déployée côté serveur, vous n’avez donc pas besoin de la mettre à jour manuellement. Un peu de patience donc avant de voir ces nouveautés arriver sur votre smartphone Android.

articles.title: Algo perturbador está pasando en la industria de los juguetes: crece a toda velocidad gracias a... los adultos sin hijos
articles.text:
Hace poco visité a unos amigos de veintipico años y me quedé con un detalle curioso: en el salón de su casa tenían una sola planta y no era ninguna de las que llevamos décadas viendo en los hogares de nuestros padres. Lo que asomaba de la estantería era una planta Lego. Un juguete, vamos. Quizás parezca una anécdota, pero conecta con una tendencia detectada hace poco por Circana: los adultos se están convirtiendo en un pilar clave de la industria. Y no porque busquen regalos para niños. Visitan Toy "R" Us o Juguettos pensando en ellos mismos.
Ya hay quien habla del (milmillonario) negocio 'kidult'.
¿Qué es eso de "kidult"? La suma de kids (niños) y adults (adultos). Suena a oxímoron, pero lleva años convirtiéndose en una palabra clave para la industria juguetera de todo el mundo, un sector que hasta hace no tanto tenía claro dónde estaba su negocio: los padres, abuelos y tíos eran quienes compraban, pero su cliente final eran en realidad los pequeños de la casa. Ya no. Los niños siguen en la ecuación, por supuesto, pero cada vez es más común encontrarse con adultos que compran para sí mismos movidos por la nostalgia o el coleccionismo.
¿Tan importantes son? Sí. Y para entenderlo viene bien echar un vistazo a un informe publicado en agosto por la consultora Circana. Tras explorar la industria juguetera de EEUU, sus analistas se encontraron con un dato curioso: los adultos se están convirtiendo en el motor del sector. Y (repetimos) no porque compren para niños. Todo indica que acuden a las jugueterías pensando en sus propios deseos y gustos. Ahora mismo en EEUU más de la mitad (55%) de las ventas de juguetes las protagonizan hogares compuestos únicamente por adultos.
No solo eso. Su porcentaje de compras creció un 16% durante el primer semestre, lo que supera ligeramente a los hogares en los que sí vive algún niño pequeño. "A nivel demográfico, el crecimiento de la industria del juguete sigue impulsado cada vez más por los consumidores de mayor edad", concluyen en Circana.
¿Para quién son esos juegos? Podríamos pensar que se venden más juguetes en hogares compuestos solo por adultos porque, sencillamente, con la caída de la natalidad hay menos hogares con niños. Es decir, compran abuelos y tíos; pero no para ellos, sino pensando en regalos para sus nietos o sobrinos pequeños.
Circana aclara que eso no es así del todo. Al analizar "las ventas para adultos mayores de 18 años" se encontró con que crecían un 25%, lo que las convierte en el gran motor del sector. De hecho, ese aumento es solo ocho puntos inferior al registrado por los adolescentes, el grupo que más crece. Entre enero y junio, los jóvenes de entre 12 y 17 años aumentaron su peso un 33%. "Juntos, adolescentes y adultos generaron casi el 60% de las ganancias incrementales en dólares".
¿Ocurre solo en EEUU? No. La tendencia es mucho más amplia, como reconocía hace unas semanas a EFE Borja López-Niclós, fundador de 'We Are Family'. En una crónica dedicada al negocio kidult, la agencia detalla que esa tendencia genera ya un mercado de 1.200 millones de euros anuales en nuestro país, una cifra que podría quedarse pequeña en no mucho tiempo.
Si las previsiones de López-Niclós dan en el clavo, el sector crecerá a un ritmo anual de entre el 4 y 6% de aquí a 2030, cuando rozará los 1.500 millones. A nivel global los kidults mueven ya unos 90.000 millones de dólares. Y las previsiones son halagüeñas: se espera que a finales de esta década ronden los 110.000.
¿Juegan los adultos? La realidad es más complicada. Los juguetes están concebidos para jugar, pero su uso se ha ido volviendo más complejo con el paso del tiempo, ganando matices. Un ejemplo claro lo deja la planta Lego que decora el salón de mis amigos. Los adultos no solo compramos para 'jugar'. De hecho esa es quizás la razón menos importante. Lo hacemos por coleccionismo, por amor a una saga o universo (y eso abarca desde Marbel o Star Wars a FIFA), por pura nostalgia... y porque ser mayor y comprar juguetes ha dejado de ser tabú.
"Estamos viendo que funcionan cada vez más como un pasatiempo, ecosistemas de fans y experiencias sociales, en lugar de productos infantiles tradicionales", explica Kristen McLean, directiva del área de análisis de clientes de Circana. "Esto está ampliando la base de consumidores y creando nuevas oportunidades para fabricantes y minoristas que saben cómo conectar con coleccionistas, aficionados, quienes hacen regalos y quienes compran para sí mismos".
¿Influye la nostalgia? Sí. Lo contaba bien en 2023 Elisabeth Buchwald, reportea de la CNN, en un artículo sobre kidults en el que confesaba su afición por los Zoo Pals, platos de papel con caras de animales. No es que el producto le guste por su estética y utilidad, lo que realmente le lleva a comprarlos siendo ya una adulta es que conectan con sus recuerdos de cuando era niña.
No es algo fuera de lo común. De hecho la nostalgia es una palanca económica tan potente que ha hecho que la industria de las chucherías apueste cada vez más por los clientes de 30, 40 o 50 años que quieren volver a probar los dulces de su infancia. Los parques de atracciones también han detectado ese nicho de negocio.
¿Por qué es importante? Por varias razones. La principal es que tanto en EEUU como España cada vez hay menos niños, lo que obliga a la industria del juguete a buscar nuevos perfiles de cliente si no quiere condenarse. Si en 2000 los niños menores de cinco años representaban eoco más del 9% de la población total de nuestro país, en 2022 su peso había descendido a un 8,52%.
El pinchazo de la natalidad (además de cambios de hábitos) explica que en los últimos años firmas como Imaginarium, Poly, Famosa y Toy "R" Us hayan pasado por dificultades. Esta última cadena ha anunciado sin embargo que en Navidades abrirá 120 tiendas en EEUU, animada en parte por el empuje de las compras por y para adultos. Totalmente comprensible si tenemos en cuenta (y esta es otra de las claves) que los millenials presentan una ventaja extra como consumidores: su poder adquisitivo, sobre todo si hablamos de profesionales jóvenes sin hijos.

articles.title: Amazon's delivery drones are annoying an entire Texas neighborhood, and there's nothing they can do about it
articles.text:
The big picture: Amazon's drone delivery service is running in Richardson, Texas, but some residents living near the facility say the service has brought steady noise, privacy concerns and limited options for recourse. The dispute offers an early look at the local backlash Amazon could face as it pushes Prime Air into hundreds of additional US communities.
The drones launch from an Amazon distribution center and deliver packages across a 7.5-mile service area. The company says customers can order tens of thousands of items for delivery in as little as 30 minutes. Packages can weigh up to five pounds, and delivery is free on some orders or costs up to $4.99.
Richardson approved the operation last December. Drones can fly between 7 am and 8 pm. Amazon has told residents that its outbound aircraft generally fly about 225 feet above the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration allows them to fly as high as 400 feet.
The program is part of Amazon's wider effort to expand Prime Air. The company said last month that it plans to offer drone delivery in 500 towns and cities by the end of the year. Walmart and other companies also operate delivery drones in parts of the country.
For some residents near the Richardson facility, the main issue is the noise. They say drones pass over their homes throughout the day and can be heard indoors.
"We hear them zoom, zoom, zoom, back and forth from morning until past dinnertime," Nikki Anderson, who lives near an active flight route, told The New York Times. She said the noise is especially noticeable on weekends.
Amazon says complaints about noise represent a small share of customer feedback. Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokeswoman, said the response to the service has been "overwhelmingly positive" and that fewer than 1% of inquiries this year have involved noise. She said the sound is similar to a window fan on low and quieter than a passing car during delivery.
Residents say that description does not match their experience. Some have compared the drones to flying lawn mowers. Others say the frequency of the flights, rather than a single drone, is what makes the service difficult to live with.
Kristi Graham complained to Amazon about drones flying over her backyard, where her family swims and cooks outdoors. She said Amazon changed the route, but the drones then began flying in front of her house. Graham has joined other residents who are trying to raise concerns in cities where Amazon may expand.
Amazon said it has adjusted operations in response to feedback. The company has not said how many route changes it has made in Richardson.
The dispute has also exposed the limits of local control. Richardson can regulate zoning and the location of Amazon's facility, but it does not control the airspace above the city. The FAA approved Amazon's operations and in July determined that commercial delivery drones such as those used by Amazon would not have a "significant impact" on the environment.
Residents have asked Richardson to limit drone operating hours or impose other restrictions. The city has not added further time limits since approving the program.
Scott Bratcher, president of a Homeowners association in one of the affected areas, said the neighborhood has become a major flight route.
"What's happening in Richardson is about to happen all over the country, and people are finally going to believe us that having all these drones flying around is actually a big, big problem," Bratcher said.
Privacy is another concern. Amazon's drones use cameras and sensors to navigate, and some residents question what the devices record while flying over homes and yards. Amazon says images are stored on encrypted drives and are available only to authorized employees. According to the company, the images are used for safety and customer service.
Stephanie Puri, a video game industry researcher, has started tracking drones over her home. She said she counted 52 on what she considered a slow day. Puri said she is uneasy about Amazon's handling of data gathered during flights.
"Amazon hasn't always been the most transparent with how they use and reuse data," she said.
The service has also produced videos of drones dropping packages in the wrong places, including a pool. Other videos have shown crashes and drones stranded in public areas. Amazon says it is continuing to improve the program.

articles.title: Okta turns Dex AI agent into customer-zero proving ground- SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Okta turns Dex AI agent into a customer-zero proving ground
The Dex AI agent is helping Okta Inc. streamline employee support. It also serves as a testbed for the identity controls the company offers customers.
After surpassing last year’s goal of saving 250,000 employee hours, Okta raised this year’s target to 1 million. The expanded effort helps the company prioritize technology investments, according to Jenna Cline (pictured), senior vice president of technology, data and intelligence at Okta.
“This year we said, ‘Let’s go big.’ About a month for every employee would be 1 million hours. That includes a lot of AI this year [and] some automation as well, because we still have a lot of deterministic workflows that we put into our systems,” she said. “But the combination of all those things is how we came up with the 1 million hours.”
Cline spoke with theCUBE Research’s Krista Case and co-host Rebecca Knight at Okta’s Oktane event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Dex’s orchestration model, productivity goals and identity controls for agents. (* Disclosure below.)
Dex AI agent routes work to specialized agents
Okta wanted to avoid creating a “swivel chair” problem as individual business teams introduced their own agents. Dex gives employees a common interface without requiring the company to build one agent capable of handling every task, according to Cline.
“Dex can call upon the right sub-agent. That agent is scoped to only work on certain things, so it’s very secure and it’s very efficient because it does one thing really well,” she said. “But Dex can do that for other agents; it can do that for the expense team [and] it can do that for our IT help desk.”
Okta applies its own identity technology to Dex, registering the agent in Universal Directory and deploying capabilities from Okta for AI Agents. Using the Dex AI agent as a testbed gives the company an enterprise environment in which to evaluate emerging features before they become generally available, according to Cline.
“We got to work with the product team,” she said. “They took feedback from what we were trying to do in order to make our product stronger.”

articles.title: Aproveite: Galaxy Watch 8 LTE fica 61% mais barato por até 10x sem juros • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Aproveite: Galaxy Watch 8 LTE fica 61% mais barato por até 10x sem juros
Galaxy Watch 8 LTE (40 mm) com sensores avançados para a prática de esportes recebe desconto de 61% no Pix com cupom em até 10x sem juros no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy Watch 8 LTE de 40 mm está saindo por R$ 1.281 no Pix em até 10x sem juros com cupom VIPNOMELI no Mercado Livre. O smartwatch da Samsung com sensores para esportes recebe desconto de 61% sobre o preço original de R$ 3.299, e fica ainda melhor por poder comprá-lo no prazo e no precinho.
O Galaxy Watch 8 é equipado com uma tela Super AMOLED de 1,34″ com brilho forte de até 3.000 nits, capaz de reproduzir cores excelentes enquanto garante a visibilidade em qualquer ambiente. O vidro Cristal de Safira protege o display contra quedas e pancadas.
O sensor BioActive e os demais auxiliares suportam várias atividades esportivas, com modos dedicados para caminhada, corrida e ciclismo. O relógio ainda traz funções de qualidade de vida, como eletrocardiograma (ECG), medidores do sono e estresse, da saúde da mulher e da oxigenação do sangue.
O relógio da Samsung ainda pode auxiliar em situações de risco: graças ao 4G/LTE e no caso de uma emergência médica, ele pode disparar alertas para contatos específicos e realizar chamadas para números como 190 (polícia) e 192 (ambulância), sem depender de um celular.
O Galaxy Watch 8 conta com o chip Exynos W1000, 2 GB de RAM e 32 GB de espaço interno, um kit que permite ao wearable instalar e rodar apps localmente com bom desempenho. Sua bateria de 435 mAh resiste até 40 horas de uso segundo a fabricante, e suporta carregamento sem fio de 10 W.
Seu corpo de alumínio Armor de 40 mm conta com as certificações IP68 e militar MIL-STD-810H, que juntas conferem proteção em cenários extremos como altas temperaturas, além de poder ser usado em esportes aquáticos, graças à certificação de até 5 ATM.
O Galaxy Watch 8 LTE de 40 mm (apenas R$ 1.199 no Pix) roda Wear OS 6, é compatível com todas as soluções do Google e suporta GPS multibanda e pagamentos via NFC. Com todas essas características, ele acaba sendo um dos melhores smartwatches do mercado atualmente.

articles.title: Cómo reservar EA Sports FC 27 para consola y PC
articles.text:
A escasas horas del lanzamiento global de EA Sports FC 27, programado para este 25 de septiembre de 2026, los usuarios de consolas y ordenadores tienen las últimas oportunidades para reservar el título y acceder a los beneficios exclusivos de prelanzamiento. Electronic Arts ofrece dos ediciones con contenidos y modalidades de acceso diferentes.
El proceso de compra digital sigue pasos similares en las principales plataformas. La reserva permite iniciar la descarga antes del lanzamiento y, en el caso de la Edición Ultimate, acceder de inmediato a los servidores.
PUBLICIDAD
Los usuarios de PC pueden adquirir el juego a través de EA App, Steam o Epic Games Store. En consolas, la compra se realiza desde las tiendas digitales de PlayStation, Xbox y Nintendo.
Cómo reservar el juego en cada plataforma
Para PlayStation (PS5 y PS4)
- Enciende la consola e ingresa a PlayStation Store desde el menú principal.
- Utiliza la herramienta de búsqueda, identificada con el ícono de una lupa, y escribe “EA Sports FC 27”.
- Selecciona la edición deseada: Estándar o Ultimate. La tienda de Sony suele ofrecer versiones compatibles con PS4 y PS5.
- Haz clic en “Reservar”, elige el método de pago vinculado a tu cuenta de PlayStation Network y confirma la transacción. La predescarga se iniciará automáticamente.
Para Xbox Series X|S y Xbox One
- Desde el panel principal, accede a Microsoft Store.
- Navega hasta la sección “Próximos lanzamientos” o utiliza el buscador superior e introduce el nombre del juego.
- Elige la versión correspondiente. Al igual que en PlayStation, las ediciones suelen incluir el sistema Dual Entitlement para funcionar en ambas generaciones de consolas.
- Selecciona “Reservar”, procesa el pago y permite que el sistema inicie la instalación del paquete de datos base.
Para PC
- EA App: la plataforma de Electronic Arts permite iniciar sesión, buscar el juego en la pestaña “Explorar”, seleccionar la edición y procesar el pago. Los suscriptores de EA Play Pro tienen incluida la Edición Ultimate sin costo adicional.
- Steam: busca el título en la tienda digital de Valve, añádelo al carrito y completa la compra. El juego requerirá la vinculación en segundo plano con una cuenta de EA.
- Epic Games Store: busca el juego en el catálogo, realiza el pago y descarga el ejecutable.
Para Nintendo Switch
- Ingresa a Nintendo eShop desde el menú principal de la consola híbrida.
- Busca “EA Sports FC 27”. Esta versión suele tener especificaciones técnicas distintas, adaptadas al hardware de Nintendo.
- Selecciona “Proceder a la compra” y descarga el software en la memoria interna o en una tarjeta microSD.
Ediciones y acceso anticipado
Al realizar la reserva, Electronic Arts ofrece dos ediciones con beneficios específicos.
- Edición Estándar: habilita el acceso al juego a partir de la medianoche del 25 de septiembre. Incluye el juego base, un artículo de jugador estrella en calidad de préstamo para Ultimate Team durante un número limitado de partidos, un espacio de Evolución y bonificaciones de puntos e indumentaria inicial para los modos Carrera y Clubes.
- Edición Ultimate: incluye 4.600 FC Points, la moneda virtual del juego para adquirir sobres; un artículo de jugador “Héroe” o “Ícono” intransferible para Ultimate Team; ranuras adicionales de Evolución, y todos los beneficios de la versión estándar. También habilita el acceso temprano a los servidores.
El período de acceso anticipado para quienes reservaron la Edición Ultimate comenzó el 18 de septiembre de 2026. Desde entonces, los jugadores tuvieron siete días de acceso anticipado para conformar sus plantillas en Ultimate Team y avanzar en sus campañas antes de la apertura general de los servidores.
PUBLICIDAD
Quienes compren la Edición Ultimate en las horas previas al lanzamiento global podrán ingresar de inmediato a los servidores, sin esperar a la medianoche del 25 de septiembre.

articles.title: Qualcomm Expands Snapdragon X2 Support to Linux
articles.text:
Thursday, September 24th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Qualcomm Expands Snapdragon X2 Support to Linux
After launching the Snapdragon X2 Elite and X2 Plus series of processors for Windows-on-Arm, Qualcomm is now bringing first-class support for these SoCs to Linux as well. According to the company, the internal developer team has been working to integrate full SoC support into the Linux kernel for the Snapdragon X2 series of hardware. Currently, the developer team is focusing on supporting the X2 SoC in traditional laptop configurations rather than desktop mini PCs. Initial enablement includes support for Hexagon NPU, Adreno GPU, and, of course, the CPU cluster that underpins the entire SoC. Modern browser acceleration, graphics, I/O peripherals, display output, and AI acceleration for local inferencing have been added. The support now also includes proper power and thermal control, as well as the reliability and endurance of the SoC under load.
Qualcomm is pushing all of this hardware enablement upstream to the Linux kernel and has also collaborated with the Debian operating system to get the latest image working. Basic workloads will now run out of the box, while the company continues testing for any gaps and other areas that need focus for enablement. More peripherals are being added to work with these SoCs, and edge cases like power spikes during workloads will be addressed in the long-term enablement, as Qualcomm continues to push these changes upstream. This work in progress is expected to finish in November this year, after which Qualcomm plans to continue adding more OEMs to the Snapdragon X2 bandwagon and potentially bring these PCs with a Linux-based OS pre-installed.

articles.title: Sony patent could turn PlayStation controllers into tap-to-pay credit card terminals — NFC and Bluetooth also support phones and gift cards for instant purchases
articles.text:
Sony patent could turn PlayStation controllers into tap-to-pay credit card terminals — NFC and Bluetooth also support phones and gift cards for instant purchases
A new patent might have spilled the beans on PlayStation's future payment plans.
Paying for your new games or in-game content like new levels and skins might be about to get even easier if a newly published PlayStation patent is anything to go by. The patent, titled “Video Game Controller-Driven Information Transfer,” details a system that would allow a PlayStation controller to accept payments whenever a gamer taps it with their credit card or smartphone. It would work with gift cards, too.
The patent was first filed way back in March 2025, but it was only made public on September 17 this year before being spotted by Dexerto.
The patent includes artwork that shows how the payment system would potentially work. One example shows a TV displaying the question "Do you wish to purchase this game?" with a PS5 DualSense controller beside a smartphone. Another shows a "Gift card received!" message, confirming that we may be about to see the end of entering long strings of text just to top up a PlayStation Store balance.
PlayStation's patent also suggests that gamers could be prompted to buy a game after playing a demo at a retailer or event. The console would handle payment once a card or phone has been presented to a controller, although it's unclear if gamers would need to sign in to their PlayStation account for the purchase to be completed. The patent does allow for both NFC and Bluetooth to be used, so it's possible the PlayStation smartphone app may play a part here.
However, those hoping the patent would hint at a future PlayStation console or controller will be disappointed to learn that is very much not the case. Imagery used in the patent shows a recognizable PS5 console and DualSense controller.
There have been rumors of a PS6 launch as soon as 2027, but given the current state of play with regard to component shortages and price hikes, that's far from confirmed at this point. A delay until 2029 has also been rumored.
Just because Sony has a patent doesn't mean this idea will hit real PlayStations. Companies apply for (and are granted) patents all the time. Not everything depicted in those patents turn into shipping products or features. There are no guarantees this new payment system will ever see the light of day.

articles.title: Could this new FEVM release be the most powerful mini PC ever?
articles.text:
Could this be the most powerful mini PC ever? FEVM mini PC pairs Ryzen 9 9950X3D with 24GB RTX5090 GPU and should beat Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio in gaming
Eight heatpipes split cooling duties between the CPU and GPU
- FEVM FA80G mini PC packs a desktop Ryzen 9 9950X3D inside a 2.6-liter chassis
- The FA80G pairs AMD’s gaming-focused processor with Nvidia’s 24GB mobile flagship
- Nvidia gives the RTX 5090 Laptop GPU 150W inside this compact system
FEVM has unveiled a new compact desktop system pairing the Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor with a 24GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU.
The pairing sits inside FEVM's FA80G chassis, a compact system built around AMD's AM5 desktop platform rather than mobile silicon components.
The flagship processor contains 16 cores, reaches 5.7GHz and carries 144MB of cache through AMD’s 3D V Cache technology.
Ryzen 9 9950X3D and RTX 5090 pack serious power
FEVM allows the processor to receive up to 90W, while the accompanying RTX 5090 Laptop GPU can receive up to 150W.
Nvidia’s mobile graphics processor has 10,496 CUDA cores, 24GB of GDDR7 memory and 896GB/s memory bandwidth.
It also supports hardware ray tracing, DLSS 4 and Multi Frame Generation, giving the FA80G several features associated with current high-end PC gaming.
The desktop processor is equally important, as the 9950X3D is designed for high-performance gaming workloads rather than conventional mobile computing.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This mini PC also supports up to 128GB of DDR5 memory via two slots, while two M.2 2280 connectors support drives reaching 4TB.
FEVM separates processor and graphics cooling, assigning four heat pipes to each component across the device’s internal thermal arrangement.
The company rates full load noise at 42dB, with CPU temperatures below 85°C and GPU temperatures below 80°C.
For connectivity, this device includes HDMI 2.0, HDMI 2.1, two DisplayPort 2.0 outputs, USB-C, USB-A, an SD reader and dual 2.5GbE.
FEVM has the hardware for a serious M5 Ultra gaming comparison
In comparison to Apple’s top M5 Ultra Mac Studio, the FA80G takes a more conventional high-end PC approach to gaming hardware.
The M5 Ultra offers up to 36 CPU cores, 80 GPU cores, 512GB unified memory and 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth.
Apple also includes hardware-accelerated ray tracing, Neural Accelerators and a 32-core Neural Engine within its highest M5 Ultra configuration.
Those specs give the Mac Studio substantial graphics and compute resources for professional rendering, video production and artificial intelligence workloads.
For gaming, however, the FA80G CPU and GPU combo fits the Windows PC gaming environment more directly.
It also supports DLSS 4, ray reconstruction, frame generation and Multi Frame Generation across its RTX 50 series gaming hardware.
Apple supports advanced gaming technologies through Metal, MetalFX and its Game Porting Toolkit, including tools for bringing Windows games onto Mac.
That means the M5 Ultra is capable of modern gaming, but developers must still account for Apple’s Metal-based gaming environment.
The FEVM instead combines established Windows gaming hardware with Nvidia’s dedicated graphics stack and AMD’s gaming-focused desktop processor.
For a device specifically judged by gaming hardware, that makes the FA80G’s specification unusually aggressive for a 2.6-liter system.
The M5 Ultra remains a much larger compute platform in memory capacity and integrated resources, but the FEVM is built differently for gaming
The flagship configuration of FEVM's FA80G costs ¥22,299 (about $3,300), before adding memory and storage to the bare-bone system.

articles.title: Voir, toucher, agir... A l’IFA 2026, MOVA dévoile la nouvelle génération de robots domestiques
articles.text:
À l’IFA 2026, la robotique domestique a franchi un nouveau cap, avec des machines qui ne se contentent plus d’exécuter des tâches. Elles cherchent désormais à mieux comprendre leur environnement, et MOVA en a fait l’une des démonstrations les plus concrètes du salon.
Il y a encore quelques années, le robot domestique idéal ressemblait surtout à une machine capable de se déplacer seule et de répéter inlassablement une tâche. Aspirer le sol, tondre la pelouse, nettoyer une piscine… La promesse était déjà très séduisante.
Mais à l’IFA 2026, la robotique domestique entre progressivement dans une nouvelle phase, celle où l’intelligence artificielle ne sert plus uniquement à reconnaître un objet ou à optimiser un trajet. Elle doit désormais permettre aux machines de percevoir, de décider, et bien sûr d’agir dans le monde réel. C’est précisément ce que MOVA a cherché à illustrer à Berlin, avec 22 nouveautés mondiales et 15 technologies présentées sur un espace de plus de 1 700 m².
Des robots qui ne se contentent plus de « voir »
En 2026, la vision par caméra est devenue banale dans l’univers des robots domestiques. Reconnaître un meuble, un animal ou un obstacle permet déjà à un aspirateur robot d’adapter sa trajectoire. Mais la prochaine étape pourrait bien être… Le toucher.
C’est l’une des démonstrations les plus intéressantes de MOVA avec TactiPercept, une technologie qui ajoute une dimension tactile à la perception des robots aspirateurs. Le système repose notamment sur 128 capteurs de pression associés à une structure flexible capable de mesurer les contacts en temps réel.
L’intérêt est assez évident, et plutôt que de considérer un contact avec un meuble comme une simple collision, le robot peut déterminer ce qu’il vient de l’effleurer et adapter son comportement. Longer un mur, se dégager d’une situation délicate, éviter un choc trop franc… Tout cela constitue alors des problèmes que la machine peut potentiellement gérer avec davantage de finesse.
C’est un changement subtil, mais révélateur, avec un robot qui n’est plus uniquement équipé de capteurs pour cartographier son environnement, mais qui commence à interagir avec lui.
Quand la tondeuse robotique gagne… Un bras
La démonstration la plus spectaculaire était sans doute celle d’AstraX, la tondeuse robot de MOVA équipée d’un bras robotisé multifonction. Sur le papier, l’idée peut sembler presque excessive. Une tondeuse est censée tondre… Mais que va-t-elle faire d’un « bras » ?
Dans les faits, grâce à sa vision et à différents embouts, le robot AstraX peut théoriquement déplacer un objet qui bloque son passage, arroser une zone ou encore saisir certains fruits situés à faible hauteur. Le bras devient en quelque sorte une extension physique de l’intelligence embarquée, avec un robot qui vient identifier une situation, choisir une action et tenter de la résoudre avant de poursuivre sa tâche.
Il reste évidemment une différence entre une démonstration réalisée sur un salon et un produit capable de fonctionner quotidiennement dans un véritable jardin. MOVA n’a d’ailleurs pas communiqué de prix ni de date de commercialisation pour AstraX. Mais l’intérêt de cette présentation est de donner une idée assez claire (et pour le moins ambitieuse) de la direction prise par le secteur.
Du robot spécialisé vers le robot capable d’agir
Cette logique apparaît encore plus clairement avec Knot 80, une main robotique dotée de 11 degrés de liberté, présentée à l’IFA pour illustrer les recherches de MOVA autour de la manipulation et de l’IA incarnée. Parmi les fonctionnalités, la machine est capable d’adapter sa force de préhension et de manipuler différents objets grâce notamment à une perception spatiale en 3D.
Une démonstration technologique qui vise à montrer les différentes briques technologiques qui devront être maîtrisées avant d’en arriver peut-être un jour à disposer chez soi d’un robot autonome qui se chargera d’absolument tout à notre place.
L’IA générative a appris à produire du texte, des images, des vidéos, de la musique… La prochaine bataille se joue peut-être dans le monde physique, avec pour objectif de faire comprendre à une machine ce qu’elle voit, ce qu’elle touche et quelle action elle doit effectuer ensuite.
La robotique domestique cherche aussi à mieux gérer ses limites
Toutes les innovations présentées par MOVA ne relèvent cependant pas de la robotique « spectaculaire ». Une grande partie du travail porte sur des problèmes beaucoup plus terre à terre, mais qui conditionnent directement l’autonomie des machines.
Dans le jardin, par exemple, la question des bordures reste un véritable défi pour les tondeuses autonomes. MOVA a présenté sa technologie UltraTrim 3.0, avec un disque capable de rapprocher la coupe des bordures à 0 cm, ainsi qu’UltraTrim 4.0, qui ajoute un mécanisme monté sur un bras adaptatif afin de mieux suivre les irrégularités et les obstacles.
Dans la maison, cette recherche de couverture maximale était déjà visible sur le V70 Ultra Complete et son système MaxiReachX, avec une serpillière capable de s’étendre de 16 cm et une brosse latérale de 12 cm. De manière générale, le robot cherche ainsi à éradiquer définitivement l’un des défauts historiques de la catégorie, ces quelques centimètres de poussière que les machines autonomes laissent obstinément derrière elles. Vous voyez de quoi on parle.
Après l’IFA, une question demeure : quand ces robots deviendront-ils vraiment autonomes ?
C’est finalement le principal enseignement de cette édition 2026. La robotique domestique ne semble plus seulement chercher à rendre les appareils plus puissants ou plus rapides, mais elle cherche à les rendre plus conscients de leur environnement.
MOVA en donne une lecture particulièrement visible, via le toucher avec TactiPercept, la manipulation avec Knot 80, l’action physique avec AstraX, mais aussi l’amélioration de technologies déjà plus matures pour les robots aspirateurs et autres tondeuses qui font partie de notre quotidien.
Tout n’est évidemment pas prêt à envahir nos maisons. Certaines technologies resteront probablement longtemps au stade de démonstration, tandis que d’autres pourraient rapidement se retrouver dans des produits commercialisés. Mais le mouvement est lancé. Pour MOVA, le robot domestique de demain ne devra plus seulement savoir où aller, mais il devra comprendre également ce qui se passe autour de lui et savoir quoi faire ensuite.
Pour découvrir les innovations et les produits présentés par MOVA, rendez-vous sur le site officiel de MOVA.

articles.title: Nouvelle fuite de données à l'État : les IBAN de 143 000 Français compromis
articles.text:
Encore une fuite de données dans l’administration française. Il y a quelques jours, un pirate s’est en effet mis à revendiquer le vol des coordonnées bancaires de plus de 143 000 Français sur un forum fréquenté par les cybercriminels. Toutes les victimes ont perçu une aide financière par l’intermédiaire de l’Agence de services et de paiement (ASP), l’établissement public chargé de verser des aides publiques pour le compte de l’État et de l’Union européenne.
 🔴 ALERTE — L’Agence de services et de paiement, organisme public de l’État, confirme une fuite de données.
Plus de 143 000 personnes seraient concernées, selon nos informations. Noms, adresses, IBAN/BIC, numéros de bénéficiaire et montants versés figurent dans des avis de… pic.twitter.com/cijvOjmcq7
— Seb (@seblatombe) September 24, 2026
À lire aussi : 2e fuite de données chez Revolut – les informations de certains clients ont encore été piratées
Le Coup de pouce énergie au cœur de la fuite
Dans son annonce, le pirate assure avoir mis la main sur des avis de paiement complets. Parmi les données revendiquées, on trouve le nom et le prénom des bénéficiaires, l’adresse postale, le numéro de bénéficiaire, les coordonnées bancaires (IBAN et BIC) et le montant exact de l’aide perçue. Toutes ces informations sont une véritable mine d’or pour les truands qui voudraient orchestrer des arnaques de phishing.
Tous les bénéficiaires piratés ont touché une aide de la part du programme « Coup de pouce énergie ». Il s’agit d’une aide de 250 euros, qui a été versée entre juillet et octobre 2023 à environ 160 000 foyers modestes d’Île-de-France. Le programme était réservé aux ménages aux revenus les plus faibles, qui touchent moins de 14 802 euros par an et par personne. De facto, ce sont des personnes peu fortunées qui risquent de se retrouver dans le viseur des cybercriminels.
L’Agence de services et de paiement n’a pas tardé à confirmer la fuite. L’organisme a officiellement reconnu la fuite de données dans un avertissement envoyé aux personnes concernées. L’alerte évoque un incident survenu sur le « portail associé au dispositif d’aide », qui a été détecté le 28 août 2026. L’incident a « été immédiatement pris en charge et toutes les corrections nécessaires ont été apportées », assure l’agence.
 « Le compte compromis utilisé pour exfiltrer les documents a été bloqué. La vulnérabilité à l’origine de cet incident a été identifiée et corrigée. Des analyses techniques approfondies ont été menées », déclare l’agence.
Sans surprise, l’administration française a prévenu la Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés de l’attaque, conformément à la loi. Ce n’est pas la première fois que l’administration se fait piller. Il s’agit d’ailleurs de la deuxième fuite de données en cinq mois. En avril dernier, l’agence avait déjà été victime d’une intrusion informatique. Un pirate s’était servi d’un compte utilisateur compromis pour dérober des numéros de Sécurité sociale et des IBAN.
À lire aussi : Plus de 700 000 IBAN piratés – une seconde mutuelle victime d’une fuite massive de données en France
Gare aux prélèvements frauduleux
Avec un nom, une adresse et un IBAN, un escroc a largement de quoi faire des dégâts. Il peut notamment créer un mandat de prélèvement SEPA frauduleux au nom de la victime et ponctionner son compte. Comme l’a démontré 01net à l’époque du piratage de Free il y a deux ans, il est bien possible de réaliser des prélèvements non autorisés sur un compte bancaire avec un seul IBAN. Un IBAN permet en effet déjà d’émettre de faux ordres de prélèvement SEPA.
Il peut aussi appeler les bénéficiaires en se faisant passer pour une administration, et tenter d’extorquer de l’argent. Si vous avez touché de l’argent dans le cadre du Coup de pouce énergie, méfiez-vous des appels, des SMS ou des mails qui évoquent cette aide ou vos coordonnées bancaires. Surveillez aussi de près votre compte bancaire. En cas de prélèvement frauduleux, vous avez 13 mois pour contester l’opération et réclamer un remboursement à votre banque.
L’incident à l’Agence de services et de paiement vient s’ajouter à la longue liste des fuites qui ont frappé les administrations françaises en 2026. Cette année, les pirates se sont en effet attaqués à l’ANTS, à Parcoursup, au fichier bancaire FICOBA du fisc, avec 1,2 million de comptes compromis, et aux impôts. Selon le 3ᵉ baromètre de Cybermalveillance, près d’un Français sur deux (45%) a appris cette année que ses données personnelles avaient fuité, contre seulement 30% en 2025.

articles.title: Roborock aterriza en España con cuatro nuevos modelos para resolver las asignaturas pendientes: desniveles y alfombras mojadas
articles.text:
El sector de la limpieza inteligente sigue apretando el acelerador en España. Tras su presentación en IFA, Roborock despliega su nueva hornada de dispositivos con un claro objetivo técnico: atajar los grandes inconvenientes que arrastran los robots tradicionales. Por un lado, la incapacidad de superar escalones o umbrales marcados entre habitaciones y, por otro, el clásico problema de mojar las alfombras al fregar el suelo.
roborock Saros 20 Neo Robot Aspirador y Fregasuelos, Succión 36000 Pa
Serie Saros 20: potencia y chasis capaz de superar desniveles de casi 9 cm
La nueva propuesta está encabezada por la serie Saros 20, donde destacan el Saros 20 Flow Complete (1.299 euros) y el Saros 20 Neo (999 euros, aunque ahora está en oferta por 849 euros). Ambos modelos rompen esquemas en el apartado de tracción física mediante el chasis elevable AdaptiLift 3.0, capaz de superar desniveles y resaltes de hasta 8,8 cm sin quedarse atrapados.
Además, la versión Flow rebaja su perfil hasta los 8,98 cm de altura equipando una mopa de rodillo SpiraFlow 2.0 que se autolimpia en la base a 100 °C. Por su parte, el modelo Neo ajusta aún más su chasis (7,95 cm) para colarse bajo casi cualquier mueble bajo. Ambos cuentan con la certificación ECARF, clave para personas alérgicas al polvo o al pelo de mascota.
roborock Saros 20 Flow Complete Robot Aspirador Succión Extrema de 36000 Pa, Negro
roborock Saros 20 Neo Robot Aspirador y Fregasuelos, Succión 36000 Pa
Qrevo 2 Pro y F25 Pro Turbo: adiós a las alfombras mojadas y máxima versatilidad

articles.title: Neo4j makes knowledge graphs shared context for AI agents- SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Neo4j makes the case for knowledge graphs as shared context for AI agents
Knowledge graphs can give enterprise agents a shared understanding of how data, business rules and processes fit together. However, that context becomes harder to maintain when each new agent carries its own version of what the business knows.
Organizations have become more proficient at building agents, but their results still vary widely. The difference often lies in how enterprise knowledge is presented, according to Jesús Barrasa (pictured), field chief technology officer of Gen AI at Neo4j Inc.
“You have to give agents not only access to your data, but also to your meaning, to your enterprise knowledge,” he said. “That’s unfortunately not always well captured … [or] well represented.”
Barrasa spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at the GraphSummit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how a shared knowledge layer could help agents use enterprise context, explain their answers and reuse knowledge across tasks. (* Disclosure below.)
Why knowledge graphs need a shared layer
As organizations expand their use of agents, they face a familiar problem: Work done for one application does not necessarily carry over to the next. Barrasa sees a parallel with earlier reporting systems that produced conflicting results.
“They identify a single problem, and they build the knowledge that the agent requires in the agent itself in the form of prompts, in the form of skills,” he said. “But then what happens? They build agent number two. They’re going to do exactly the same thing. So, we’re repeating the errors that we made seven years ago when we were building reports in different platforms and getting inconsistent results.”
A knowledge layer is a governed representation of an organization’s data assets, concepts, policies and processes, according to Barrasa. It can also help people examine how an agent reached an answer — a growing concern as agents move from conversation to action.
“This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency that we were talking about before, it gives you the explainability,” he said. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”
Building knowledge graphs across use cases
Knowledge graphs can connect data to the business concepts and relationships agents need to interpret it. Organizations can develop that context across multiple applications instead of attempting an enterprise-wide model at the outset, according to Barrasa.
“You want to start with one use case. And when you build use case two, you have to try to align it to number one,” he said. “That’s how you build the knowledge layer. You build it incrementally. It’s ‘identify use case, realize value and then build from there.’ The construction of the ontology is something that [large language models] can accelerate significantly.”
A shared knowledge layer may require a broader measure of return on investment than the results of any one agent. Organizations should also assess what changes as they build more agents, according to Barrasa.
“You want to measure how the construction of Agent 2 and Agent 3 and Agent 4 goes down as you go, because you’re building knowledge in the layer,” he said. “Another [metric] is … a negative metric: What’s the cost of drift? What happens when two agents return diverging results or act in different ways? What’s the cost of reconciling these results?”

articles.title: Sony patents PlayStation controller that could accept tap-to-pay from phones and credit cards
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Imagine buying something from the PlayStation Store but instead of entering your financial details into a form, you swipe a card or phone over the controller. That's the vision Sony explained in a newly discovered patent, and it might be a feature of the PlayStation 6.
The patent, discovered by Dexerto, was published on September 17, 2026, but filed back in March 2025. Titled "Video Game Controller-Driven Information Transfer," it essentially describes a controller with NFC capabilities.
The diagrams illustrate how the system would work. One shows a user tapping their phone on the controller to pay for a game. Another shows a gift card being swiped across the device to add $25 to an account, which would mean no more painstakingly typing in long strings of text.
The actual process works by bringing a phone near the controller, with the phone detected through NFC, Bluetooth, or physical contact. The controller then emits a light, sound, or vibration as confirmation. The user receives a receipt, and the phone sends payment information to the controller, which forwards it to the console to handle a payment-related request.
There are other uses for the technology beyond making payments. The description mentions using the connection to transfer player IDs or allow guests to quickly join multiplayer games. There are also references to sending screenshots, recordings, and other content from the console to a phone through the controller.
Another section describes a game demo being shown at a store or gaming expo. The screen asks if the player wants to purchase the title, at which point they can put their phone next to the controller and have it added to their library, ready to download when they get home. As the description mentions the use of both NFC and Bluetooth, this process could involve the PlayStation mobile app.
We've seen plenty of patents that never become real features or products, so there's no guarantee this will ever make it beyond the concept stage. The controller in the images looks like a PS5 DualSense, but it's hard to imagine that Sony would start selling NFC-equipped controllers so close to the end of the console's life cycle.
Whether these controllers become part of the PlayStation 6 remains to be seen. It would be an interesting addition, but consumers would likely worry about security issues – and Sony's reputation is at an all-time low right now.
This is the second Sony patent we've heard about recently. The company filed another in 2025 that would allow AI to silently vibe-code fixes for your PlayStation and other devices.

articles.title: I tested the Samsung Galaxy S26 FE — and it’s hard to know who this phone is for
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Galaxy S26 FE achieves its basic goal of offering a large Galaxy S experience for a discounted price. However, a price hike has reduced the potential value of going for this phone instead of a full-fat Galaxy S26, even if key elements like battery life and performance are still impressive for what you pay.
Pros
- +Premium design in fun new colors
- +Display still flagship-worthy
- +Surprisingly good gaming performance
- +Strong battery life
Cons
- -Price has increased
- -AI tools coming to older Samsungs soon
- -Telephoto and ultrawide cameras lag behind
Why you can trust TechRadar
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE: Two-minute review
Picking the Samsung Galaxy S26 FE to be your next phone would be a good decision. But whether it’s the best decision is the chewier question.
As has been the case for the past several years, Samsung has launched one final version of its Galaxy S flagship phones just before summer is out (in the US and UK, at least). This “Fan Edition” device aims to provide a more streamlined experience, focused on camera capabilities and AI, at a more approachable price.
However, Samsung has this all backwards. The Galaxy S26 FE’s cameras range from OK to weak, and the AI tools will soon be available on older models. Plus, the price hike this year makes the phone a little less of a bargain.
Arguably, the real reasons you’ll want a Galaxy S26 FE are its big screen, fast charging, strong battery life, and surprisingly good gaming performance. But then, if those are your priorities, you may still be better off looking elsewhere.
Confused yet? Hopefully the rest of my Galaxy S26 FE review will clear things up.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Price and availability
- Starts at $699 /£699 / AU$1,149
The Galaxy S26 FE first went on sale on September 4, 2026. It costs $699 / £699 / AU$1,149 for the standard version, which is $50 / £50 / AU$50 more than the Galaxy S25 FE cost when it launched.
As a result, it means there’s a $200 / £180 / AU$400 difference between this phone and the cheapest full-fat Samsung Galaxy S26, or a $400 / £400 / AU$700 gap if you compare it to the similarly-sized Galaxy S26 Plus. However, those Galaxy S26 models have twice as much storage as the S26 FE by default, which makes direct comparison a little complicated.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Also, keep in mind that you get six free months of Google AI Pro (worth about $120 / £114 / AU$200 at current subscription prices) with the purchase of the S26 FE. It’s an offer worth taking advantage of for the 5TB of cloud storage capacity alone, let alone the extra Gemini powers.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE pricing
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | US price | UK price | AU price | 
| 128GB | $699 | £699 | AU$1,149 | 
| 256GB | $799 | £799 | AU$1,299 | 
| 512GB | Not available | £949 | AU$1,599 | 
- Value score: 3.5 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Specs
Before we continue, here’s a rundown of the Galaxy S26 FE’s hardware.
| Dimensions: | 161.6 x 76.9 x 7.4mm | 
| Weight: | 193g | 
| Display: | 6.7-inch FHD+ Dynamic AMOLED 2X | 
| Resolution: | 1080 x 2340 | 
| Refresh rate: | 60/120Hz | 
| Peak brightness: | 1,900 nits | 
| CPU: | Exynos 2500 | 
| RAM: | 8GB | 
| Storage: | 128GB / 256GB / 512GB | 
| OS: | Android 17 with One UI 9, 7 years of updates | 
| Cameras: | 50MP wide (f/1.8), 12MP ultra-wide (f/2.2), 8MP 3x telephoto (f/2.4) | 
| Selfie Camera: | 12MP front camera (f/2.2) | 
| Battery: | 4,900mAh | 
| Charging: | 45W wired, 15W wireless | 
| Colors: | Blueberry, Graphite, Pistachio | 
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Design
- No major updates from previous model other than new colors
- Worthy of the Galaxy S name in terms of looks and durability
Looks-wise, there are no major body changes between the Galaxy S26 FE and the S25 FE — not that Samsung really needed to make any.
You still have three camera lenses embedded directly into the back of the phone, then flat rails with rounded corners around the sides, leading to a big display with a single centered selfie camera on the front.
Unless you’re able to tell the S26 FE apart from a regular S26 by the color of the handset, the big telltales that you’re holding an FE are the shiny back panel, instead of a matte texture, and the larger chin bezel under the display.
Speaking of colors, Samsung’s three offerings are Graphite, Blueberry and Pistachio (pictured). The gray option will satisfy anyone who isn’t fussed about the color of their phone, or who knows they’ll be using a case to add some style to their new handset, but I do like both the blue and pale green options for the balance they strike between boldness and subtlety.
Like the other Galaxy S26 models, the S26 FE is rated IP68 for water/dust-resistance, which we expect from any flagship phone launching today. However, it uses Gorilla Glass Victus Plus on both sides to protect against scratches and smashes, which is a generation behind what you get on the S26 or S26 Plus.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Display
- Big and colorful, but lower-spec resolution and brightness
- Larger bezels than other Galaxy S phones
The 6.7-inch AMOLED display of the Galaxy S26 FE matches the size of the Galaxy S26 Plus’ display, but that’s where the similarities end. The FE’s panel only reaches an FHD resolution, rather than the Plus’ more detailed QHD, and peaks at 1,900 nits of brightness according to Samsung’s testing, rather than the 2,600-nit rating of the other S26 models.
Even though the S26 FE can’t deliver as much brightness or as many pixels as Samsung’s top-tier displays, the detail and the colors of the FE’s panel are still strong, and the screen remains fairly legible even out in what remains of the summer sun.
The bezels around the Galaxy S26 FE’s display are thicker than they are on the Galaxy S26 Plus or other premium Samsung phones, which is an understandable limitation given the FE’s lower price. It doesn’t interfere with whatever you want to watch on the screen, but it’s a difference you’ll notice if you have used other recent Galaxy S phones.
- Display score: 3.5 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Software
- Samsung’s latest OS comes pre-installed
- Seven more generations of updates have been promised
The Galaxy S26 FE comes pre-installed with OneUI 9, Samsung’s take on Android 17. That actually puts it ahead of the other Galaxy S26 models, which currently can only access OneUI 9 as a beta version.
OneUI 9 gives the FE a lot of tools to play with. My FanCam — the video subject tracking tool which just debuted on the much more expensive Galaxy Z Fold 8/ Galaxy Flip 8 series — is here and works just as capably. That’s joined by other AI-powered editing features like Photo Assist and Audio Eraser.
Meanwhile, for productivity, you have Now Brief and its new custom cards option to give you even more personalized updates all in one place, more supported apps for Now Nudge, plus expanded cross-app functions and Gemini.
Perhaps most importantly for the Galaxy S26 FE, it comes with Samsung’s full seven generations of Android and seven years of security updates promise. That’s the same as other Galaxy S models, and one additional year over what the cheaper Galaxy A57 gets, which is crucial for the value proposition of the S26 FE.
- Software score: 4 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Cameras
- Minor upgrades but identical sensors to previous model
- The main and selfie cameras are good, but the ultra-wide and telephoto cameras lag behind
The Galaxy S26 FE’s camera loadout has a 50MP main rear lens as its centerpiece. You also have 12MP ultra-wide and 8MP 3x telephoto cameras on the back, as well as a 12MP selfie camera embedded in the display. This is the same basic setup as the Galaxy S25 FE, and also what you'll find on the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Plus, except that the more expensive phones get a higher-resolution 10MP zoom camera instead.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original

View Original
Our first example is a main camera shot of some brightly colored buildings in London’s Soho neighborhood. It’s a tricky one for any camera to balance due to the shaded shopfronts on the left side and the sky and brightly lit building in the center and right side. The Galaxy S26 FE still has some detail to offer in the shadowed brickwork, but Samsung’s strength in bright colors is on full display on the other half of this particular image.
Keeping with the main camera but looking out at the London Eye at night, we see another strong attempt from the Galaxy S26 FE. There’s some softness in the details, but the balance of colors between the lights and the night sky still makes for an appealing shot.
Looking across a sun-scorched park with the ultra-wide camera, we see a shot with plenty of scenery in it, with little to no distortion at the edges. The brightness and colors could use work, though, as even accounting for the patchy grass and overcast sky, things look overly drab.
The two shots of the church bell tower, one at 2x magnification using the S26 FE’s main camera and the other using the 3x telephoto camera, reveal how best to zoom in with this phone’s particular cameras. The in-sensor 2x zoom still keeps the subtleties of the colors and markings within the brickwork and foliage of the shot, thanks to the 50MP main sensor having plenty of pixels to spare even when zoomed in. However, while the telephoto camera has greater reach, the resulting image is darker and flatter, as you might expect from the lower-resolution sensor. It’s more of a trade-off than I’d like to see on a flagship phone’s zoom camera.
I’m normally a fan of Samsung selfies, but I’m not sure I like how the highlights are exposed in this particular shot. Samsung’s excellent portrait algorithm has applied the perfect level of bokeh to this image, however, cutting around my head, and especially my glasses, accurately and applying a gentle blur to the leaves behind.
Having gone through these samples, you’ll see that the Galaxy S26 FE’s photography potential is reasonable, at least for what are arguably the two most important cameras. For future generations of S FE, though, Samsung could do with upping its game if it wants to continue claiming this is a flagship product.
- Camera score: 3 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Performance
- The Exynos 2500 chip is a good performer, especially for graphics
- 8GB of RAM is limiting for a premium phone in 2026
Here’s an area where I was pleasantly surprised by the Galaxy S26 FE. Samsung’s own Exynos 2500 chipset sits inside the S26 FE, rather than the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip that basically all the other top Samsungs of 2026 are using. But that hasn’t stopped the S26 FE from turning in some decent scores.
As the table below reveals, the Exynos 2500 lags behind slightly in CPU single-core results, but is on par with or ahead of the pack on the rest of the tests. It’s a long way out in front on the Solar Bay benchmark, no doubt thanks to the Exynos’ GPU, which is well-suited to the ray-tracing graphics that this test focuses on.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE benchmark scores
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Samsung Galaxy S26 FE | 
| Geekbench 6 single-core | 2,361 | 
| Geekbench 6 multi-core | 7,831 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test best | 5,116 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test low | 3,456 | 
| 3DMark Solar Bay | 10,526 | 
Bearing only 8GB of RAM compared to the 12GB in other premium Samsung phones, the Galaxy S26 FE does struggle with multitasking or intensive apps. While you can still game on this phone happily, it’s not a handset you’ll want to do anything more practical on than standard browsing and messaging.
- Performance score: 4 / 5
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Battery
- The same battery/charging hardware as the more expensive S26 Plus
- Battery life day-to-day is good, while charging is plenty fast enough
Samsung offers the same 4,900mAh battery capacity in the Galaxy S26 FE as it does in the Galaxy S26 Plus. However, according to Samsung’s official battery estimates, the S26 FE doesn’t offer the same battery life, managing 29 hours of video playback compared to the S26 Plus’ 31 hours or the S26’s 30 hours.
For me, I used about 40% of the phone’s battery during a typical day’s use. This included some work, some photography, and some social media scrolling and video watching. The Galaxy S26 FE could definitely survive two days of regular use before needing to charge, as you would hope from a phone with this size of battery.
The Galaxy S26 FE is still equipped for 45W wired charging and 15W wireless charging. That’s the same wired speed as the S26 Plus and Ultra, but the wireless charging is slower, since the FE is not Qi2 compatible.
Using a 45W charger, Samsung estimates a 69% refill for the S26 FE in half an hour. In my own test, I found the S26 FE managed to fill to 43% in 15 minutes and to 100% in 58 minutes. Considering the battery life this phone can manage, a complete refuel in under an hour and getting over two-fifths full in a quarter-hour isn’t bad at all, even if faster options are out there.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Should you buy the Samsung Galaxy S26 FE?
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE scorecard
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | The cheapest Galaxy S26 model, although not by much post-price hike. | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | Looks like any other Galaxy S26, except with some fun, unique colors and slightly less durable materials. | 4/5 | 
| Display | Big and colorful, but lacking detail. | 3.5/5 | 
| Software | Samsung’s best features come pre-installed, but will soon be available on older phones too. | 4/5 | 
| Camera | The main and selfie cameras produce strong photos, but the phone’s let down by its ultra-wide and telephoto lenses. | 3/5 | 
| Performance | A below average RAM capacity is understandable for the price, and the phone still plays games really well. | 4/5 | 
| Battery | Less efficient than other S26 models, but still long-lasting and fairly fast-charging. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if…
You want the big premium Samsung experience for the smallest possible price
The Galaxy S26 FE is the cheapest Galaxy S26, and joint second largest. If you want a big display and long battery life from Samsung for less, then this is the model for you.
Exclusive software and AI features don’t interest you
You do get some excellent tools and toys to play with within One UI 9, but since this update will come to older Samsungs soon enough, this isn’t a phone to buy for this reason alone.
Your performance needs are about average
If you like to play games on your phone, or know you’ll spend long days away from a charger, the S26 FE will suit you well. It doesn’t offer the very best in either power or battery life, but arguably it’s a case of diminishing returns if you spend any more than this.
Don’t buy it if…
You care about photography
Taking snaps with the main and selfie cameras on the S26 FE is easy and results in great photos. But if you want more detail or know you like taking ultra-wide or zoom shots, there are many other phones that will suit you better.
You want the best long-term value
While the S26 FE is cheaper to buy right now, we’d recommend looking at one of Samsung’s more expensive S26 models, or those of another Android brand, if you’re hoping to get as many happy years out of your new phone as possible. 
If you’re willing to spend even a few dollars/pounds more
The Galaxy S26 FE sits just below the starting price of typical flagship phones. That means you could save yourself 100 bucks or so, or you can spend the extra and unlock the next tier of hardware and features that could provide far more value to you.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: Also consider
Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus
It’s quite a bit more expensive, but as an investment, it may be worth spending the extra money over the Galaxy S26 FE’s price to secure a phone that outperforms it on every important metric.
Read our full Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus review
Samsung Galaxy S26
Costing only two hundred bucks more than the S26 FE, the standard S26 gives you the premium Samsung experience at the best possible price, even if the display is quite a bit smaller.

Specific tests included running Geekbench 6 CPU benchmarks and 3DMark graphics benchmarks, a charging speed test using a compatible third-party charger, the taking of hundreds of photos across all of the S26 FE’s cameras to test image quality, and the careful monitoring of battery drain during use to figure out how reasonable the manufacturer’s battery life promises are.
