articles.title: SpaceX has stopped taking Falcon 9 bookings past 2028, betting everything on Starship
articles.text:
Looking ahead: SpaceX appears to be preparing for a future without Falcon 9, even though the rocket remains one of the most important launch systems in service. The company is reportedly no longer accepting Falcon 9 launch reservations beyond 2028. That suggests a plan to shift customers to Starship, the much larger rocket SpaceX is developing for high-volume satellite launches, deep-space missions, and NASA's lunar program.
Meanwhile, Falcon 9 is still doing much of the work in the commercial launch market. In 2025, it launched 165 times, successfully delivered every payload to orbit, and had one unsuccessful booster recovery. The rocket accounted for nearly half of all launches worldwide.
Falcon 9 changed the economics of launch through reusable boosters and a rapid launch cadence. It also made rideshare missions more common, allowing several satellite companies to place spacecraft on the same launch. That has been especially important for startups and smaller operators that cannot afford a dedicated mission.
If SpaceX stops offering Falcon 9 after 2028, those customers will need other options. Other launch providers could pick up some of the demand, but none currently launches at Falcon 9's pace. The industry has already raised concerns about a shortage of rockets and launch capacity as demand for satellite deployments grows.
Musk has said SpaceX will shift its engineering and manufacturing resources away from Falcon and toward Starship once the newer vehicle is flying often enough to justify the move. He said the company would make the shift only after Starship can fly dependably several times a week. The goal would then be to increase Starship's flight rate to several launches a day, eventually allowing SpaceX to phase down Falcon operations.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) August 22, 2026
That leaves an obvious question: Can Starship meet that standard by 2028?
The company is treating Starship as the vehicle that can eventually replace Falcon 9 and handle missions that Falcon cannot. Starship is designed to carry much larger payloads and eventually fly missions to the Moon and beyond. But the system has not yet reached orbit. Its newest prototype began flying this year, and its first orbital attempt is scheduled for Sept. 28.
Falcon 9 also performs missions that Starship cannot simply take over. It currently carries cargo and astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA. Starship's upper stage is too large to dock with the station, so retiring Falcon 9 could create a problem if the ISS operates beyond 2028. The station may receive an extension through 2032.
That could leave NASA relying more heavily on Russia's Soyuz spacecraft or Boeing's Starliner, if Starliner resolves the issues that have limited its use. Neither would be a direct replacement for Falcon 9's current role.
NASA's Artemis program may help explain why 2028 has become such an important date for SpaceX. The agency's plan calls for astronauts to launch aboard Orion on the Space Launch System. A separate Starship vehicle would be refueled in orbit through 15 launches, travel to lunar orbit, and take two astronauts to the Moon's surface.
That lunar landing is scheduled for 2028. SpaceX needs Starship to be ready if it is to meet that commitment. NASA has also reopened the lunar-lander competition, with Blue Origin as the only other candidate mentioned in the provided material.
SpaceX could change course and continue Falcon 9 flights longer than planned. For now, though, its booking policy suggests that the company is betting Starship will be ready to take over within two years.

articles.title: Claude descobre novo sistema de enzimas • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Claude descobre novo sistema de enzimas
Inteligência artificial da Anthropic foi usada para analisar aproximadamente 200 mil enzimas com 950 agentes em 21 horas.
Um novo sistema de enzimas de transcrição reversa foi descoberto utilizando o Claude, inteligência artificial da Anthropic. Ainda não se sabe a função exata desse grupo de moléculas, mas chama atenção a semelhança ao mecanismo CRISPR, tecnologia que permite realizar modificações genéticas em trechos específicos do DNA. A empresa anunciou a novidade nesta quarta-feira (23/09), destacando seu primeiro passo no ramo de pesquisas biológicas com IA.
As transcriptases reversas associadas a arranjos (da sigla ART, em inglês), foram encontradas após a análise de mais de 200 mil enzimas. Para dar conta do montante, foram empregados 950 agentes do Claude em uma leitura que durou mais de 21 horas. Segundo a Anthropic, atividades do tipo podem economizar semanas ou até meses de pesquisa.
Junto ao novo sistema, a Anthropic também aproveitou para confirmar a fundação de um laboratório voltado para estudos biológicoas utilizando IA. O local, que fica na região de São Francisco, na Califórnia, foi instalado sem muito alarde, conforme noticiou a Reuters.
Segundo a Anthropic, bastou um único prompt para que o Claude começasse o trabalho. A equipe pediu à IA que analisasse uma base de dados com sequências de DNA para encontrar “novos exemplos de transcriptases reversas”. O próprio modelo ficou encarregado de mobilizar agentes, julgar seus resultados e identificar os melhores candidatos.
Ao todo, foram 950 agentes, 21 horas de processamento e cerca de 210 milhões de tokens utilizados. A partir disso, a IA encontrou um padrão de repetições de DNA relacionado a um sistema incomum de transcriptases reversas. Os cientistas então analisaram as sequências e entenderam que se tratava de um sistema de enzimas encontrado em bacteriófagos, vírus que destroem células bacterianas.
O ART funciona de forma semelhante ao CRISPR, método utilizado em biotecnologia para editar trechos de DNA de maneira bastante específica. Por meio da técnica, cientistas têm buscado tratamentos para doenças autoimunes, câncer, entre outros exemplos. Também é dessa forma que são feitas modificações genéticas em plantas e animais para melhores resultados na agricultura. Dessa forma, o ART pode vir a ser uma nova alternativa de ferramenta biotecnológica para estudos do tipo.
A descoberta do ART foi levada pela Anthropic ao pesquisador Feng Zhang, professor do MIT e um dos pioneiros na técnica CRISPR. Segundo ele, esse é um “exemplo animador de como agentes de IA podem contribuir para descobertas biológicas”. O cientista também disse desejar que o trabalho inspire outros biólogos a explorarem o uso de IA como apoio para suas pesquisas.
No início de setembro, a Anthropic revelou ter “bloqueado” uma possível produção de arma biológica após suspender o Claude em alguns cenários considerados perigosos. Um dos casos citados envolveu o vírus Chikungunya, arbovirose bastante comum no Brasil.
Segundo a empresa, os cientistas buscavam possíveis mutações que reforçassem o patógeno, provavelmente pensando no desenvolvimento de vacinas para a doença. Como houve tentativa de burlar uma salvaguarda do Claude durante as buscas com a IA, a empresa classificou o caso como perigoso e bloqueou o uso da IA.
As preocupações da Anthropic acerca das capacidades do Claude em trabalhos científicos são apontadas há algum tempo. Ao anúnciar o modelo Mythos, revelado como “muitoa avançado” à época, a empresa revelou que atrasaria seu lançamento para desenvolver mecanismos de segurança suficientes para buscas envolvendo assuntos biológicos.
Atualmente, um dos exemplos de salvaguarda é o downgrade do modelo utilizado para entregar respostas menos aprofundadas em consultas do tipo. Vale ressaltar que, no caso da descoberta das enzimas ART, a Anthropic não revelou qual modelo de IA foi utilizado. Ainda assim, é provável que seja uma versão sem tantas travas de segurança como as que estão disponíveis publicamente.

articles.title: F-Droid gets its biggest update in a decade with new UI and smoother app installs
articles.text:
Virtually every Android device comes with the Play Store preloaded, but there are other ways to get apps. F-Droid bills itself as a community-driven source for free and open source Android apps, but its official app store has gone 10 years without a major update. That’s finally changing: After a multiyear effort, the team has just announced F-Droid 2.0 is rolling out.
The new F-Droid client was redesigned from scratch in Kotlin Compose, which is the standard for modern Android apps. This makes the store much more responsive, and there’s optional support for Android’s Material theming. The interface has also been cleaned up considerably, making the most important functions easier to access and hiding some others in overflow menus.
While the new F-Droid looks nicer, the update was largely about making it easier to find and install apps. When F-Droid first appeared, there wasn’t much to see, but now it has thousands of open source apps. Unlike the Play Store, F-Droid doesn’t track your taps and installs to push ads and suggestions—it helps you find things and gets out of the way.
F-Droid now includes a huge number of categories, drilling down to specialized niches like firewalls, password managers, and VPNs. You can see all these groups in the search tab. There are also higher-level categories listed on the main Discover page. When searching for apps, F-Droid will now be able to return results based on app descriptions rather than just names.
When you find an app, F-Droid 2.0 will make the installation process easier. Google has long put up roadblocks for sideloaded apps, citing the security implications. This is also the rationale behind its upcoming developer verification system. For now at least, apps will be easier to install from F-Droid thanks to the use of Google’s pre-approval API. Instead of downloading an APK, opening it, and confirming the scary sideloading pop-up, you’ll just be able to verify that you want to install an app before the download. So you tap “Install” in F-Droid, and then tap “Install” again in a system pop-up. That’s one more click than the Play Store, but it’s still an improvement.

articles.title: Matthew McConaughey confiesa que quiere volver a 'True Detective' con Woody Harrelson: "Lo echo de menos"
articles.text:
Lo que parecía imposible cada vez está más cerca. Matthew McConaughey acaba de reconocer públicamente que le gustaría volver a True Detective junto a Woody Harrelson. Ambos actores, amigos desde hace muchos años, protagonizaron la primera temporada de la exitosa serie allá por 2014. Desde entonces, los fan han pedido insistentemente su regreso, pero hasta ahora no ha estado ni cerca de suceder.
Sin embargo, todo podría cambiar próximamente. Porque ahora Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson estrenan una nueva serie, Brothers, de Apple TV. Con motivo de su lanzamiento, en Hipertextual hemos podido compartir con ellos un encuentro con la prensa. Y ha sido ahí cuando el primero ha confesado su deseo de volver a trabajar codo con codo en True Detective al responder a la pregunta sobre qué próximo proyecto les gustaría hacer juntos.
"Tío, si Nic Pizzolatto escribiera otra temporada de True Detective, yo estaría dispuesto a hacerlo", confiesa Matthew McConaughey, ante la sorpresa de Woody Harrelson. "¿De verdad?", le responde él. "Sí, ¿y tú? En realidad no quieres tocarlo", se anticipa McConaughey, sabedor de las reticencias de su amigo a regresar a la serie. "Sí, bueno, tengo la mente abierta. Quiero decir, creo que la primera temporada salió muy bien y por eso quiero volver para una sexta temporada", reconoce Harrelson.
¿Volverán Matthew McConaughey y Woody Harrelson a True Detective?
"Es que lo echo un poco de menos", insiste McConaughey. "No quiero volver a ver la cara de Rust Cole nunca más. Jamás", bromea entonces Harrelson. Recordemos que, como han contado en multitud de ocasiones, Matthew McConaughey llevó a cabo un proceso bastante extremo para preparar su personaje de True Detective, no saliéndose del papel en ningún momento, ni siquiera fuera de cámaras.
"Ves, por eso True Detective seguía siendo una comedia, precisamente por eso", se ríe McConaughey. "Por tu culpa, Marty, que eras muy pesado", le sigue Harrelson, también entre risas. "Siempre me decías: «¿Podrías callarte de una vez? Sea lo que sea lo que se te pase por la cabeza, no abras la boca y se lo sueltes a todo el mundo»", rememora el primero con evidente nostalgia.
"Sí. Es verdad. Había comedia en ello precisamente por eso. Antes de que empezáramos a rodar, le dije: «Tío, creo que necesitamos más chistes; es decir, la gente va a querer reírse antes de que empecemos la serie». Y él me miró como diciendo: «Oh, qué idiota». Me dijo: «¿Sabes qué? Habrá humor. Simplemente surgirá. Será humor situacional». Y así es. Hay humor ahí", sentencia Woody Harrelson sobre cómo True Detective, pese a su tono oscuro y adulto, contenía trazas de humor.

articles.title: Steam und Switch: Dieses Aufbauspiel ist wholesome - und perfekt für den Feierabend
articles.text:
Steam und Switch: Dieses Aufbauspiel ist wholesome – und perfekt für den Feierabend
In Videospielen geht es oft um Vernichtung: gigantische Waffen und verheerende Schlachten, die brennende Erde zurücklassen. Aber das Zurückgebliebene, der Schutt und die Asche, spielt nur selten eine Rolle. Terra Nil von Free Lives für Steam auf PC, iOS, Android und Nintendo Switch stellt genau diese menschlichen Spuren in den Mittelpunkt. Denn in diesem Spiel ist die Erde am Ende.
Ökosysteme sind kollabiert, der Boden trocken und unfruchtbar. Tiere und Pflanzen haben keine Lebensgrundlage mehr. Und Menschen sowieso nicht. Was könnte da helfen? Ein Superheld, der alles wieder in Ordnung bringt? Magie, die das Leben zurückholt? Nein, in Terra Nil ist Greentech die Rettung. Und inzwischen mit einem neuen Heatwave-Update versehen worden.
Aufbau ohne Menschen
Das Spiel gehört zu einem Genre, das in Deutschland besonders beliebt ist: Es ist ein Aufbauspiel. Doch anders als in Anno 1800 oder Die Siedler geht es eben nicht darum, eine florierende Stadt aufzubauen, um irgendwann mit einem industriellen Imperium zu enden. Vielmehr soll der Mensch hier gar keine Rolle spielen.
Terra Nil funktioniert grundlegend so: Die Spieler beginnen auf einem ausgestorbenen Planeten. Also bauen sie Bewässerungsanlagen oder Windturbinen, um mit Strom und Wasser den Boden wieder fruchtbar zu machen. Im Laufe des Spiels kommen viele andere Gebäude hinzu. Entgiftungsanlagen, die Flüsse reinigen, oder solarbetriebene Gewächshäuser, die die Pflanzen zurückbringen.
Dabei ist es wichtig, wo diese Gebäude und Anlagen platziert werden, denn sie haben unterschiedliche Auswirkungen auf ihre direkte Umgebung. So lassen bestimmte Forstanlagen etwa einen Wald in ihren Parametern wachsen. Dafür braucht es aber den passenden Boden, damit Bäume Wurzeln schlagen können. Ebenso gilt es, die verschiedenen Objekte passend miteinander zu kombinieren, um mehr Punkte zu bekommen. Eine Bewässerungsanlage in der Nähe eines Gewächshauses ergibt logischen Sinn und wird vom Spiel entsprechend belohnt.
Terra Nil bietet vier verschiedene Biome, die unterschiedliche Taktiken erfordern. Von tropischen bis zu arktischen Ökosystemen sollen alle wieder aufblühen – -inklusive der -Tiere, die hier einst lebten. Ein virtuelles Kompendium im Spiel -erklärt die verschiedenen Aufgaben, die die Spieler er-ledigen müssen. Ebenso werden die Geräte und ihre Funktionsweisen beschrieben – und auch zu den Tieren und ihre Eigenschaften gibt es Informationen.
Der Fokus auf die Natur und wie sie zu retten ist, steht hier also ständig im Fokus. Damit ist das Spiel auch ein Kommentar auf unsere immer wärmer werdende Erde und darauf, wie der Mensch dazu beigetragen hat.
„Wholesomes“ Spielvergnügen
Insgesamt will Terra Nil aber „wholesome“ sein, also bei den -Spielern ein wohlig-warmes Gefühl auslösen. Die -Spielmechaniken sind entschleunigt und können geradezu entspannend sein. Die Soundkulisse unterstützt die friedvolle Atmosphäre und die Optik des Spiels zeigt in vielen kleinen Details eine langsam wieder gesundende Erde.
Das Thema – der Klimawandel und was man gegen ihn tun kann – wird selten in Videospielen aufgegriffen. Zumal das Medium selbst mit seinem hohen Stromverbrauch und der -Hardware, die viele Ressourcen frisst, nicht unbedingt zu einer gesunden ökologischen Bilanz beiträgt. Das kann man bei einer kleinen Runde Terra Nil nach Feierabend – das Spiel ist in etwa sechs Stunden durchgespielt – aber vielleicht mal kurz vergessen.
Und sich stattdessen wenigstens virtuell darum kümmern, dass unsere Erde wieder lebenswert wird. Der Clou ist übrigens, dass zum Schluss alles wieder abgebaut werden muss, Terra Nil endet im Recycling. All die so nützlichen Gebäude und Anlagen werden wieder in ihre Einzelteile zerlegt und abtransportiert. Und das ist in Terra Nil das Happy End: Greentech, die überflüssig wird. Weil die Natur es jetzt allein schafft.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 24.08.2025 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Und wer die Mobile Version kostenlos spielen möchte hat Glück, wenn man Zugriff auf ein aktives Netflix Abo hat(zumindest bei Android bin ich mir sicher, denke aber iOS sollte da auch drin sein).
Das Spiel klingt klasse.
Aber: Bitte seid nicht so voreingenommen. Es ist auf dem PC kein exklusives Steam-Spiel.
Man kann dieses Spiel auch über GOG beziehen. Vielleicht auch über andere Stores.
Ich hacke darauf herum, da man im Gegensatz zu Steam bei GOG noch in der Lage ist, eine Spielkopie richtig zu erwerben und nicht nur ein eingeschränktes Nutzungsrecht bekommt. Steam erlaubt das Spielen nur, wenn sie die Lizenz überprüfen konnten und Steam bestimmt, welche Version man spielen darf.
Bitte beschränkt euch in Zukunft nicht nur auf Steam oder schreibt PC-Spiel anstelle Steam-Spiel.

articles.title: Meet Feather, the startup building the 'Android of robotics' for developers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there is one thing robotics founders and investors agree on, it’s that the “ChatGPT moment” where a general-purpose robot can seamlessly adapt to any environment has not arrived. Opinions vary on whether the breakthrough is just around the corner or a decade away.
Feather Robotics, a humanoid startup founded last year, is developing a robot for either timeline. Unlike Tesla or Figure, which are tackling the lofty mission of building both the body and a foundational “brain” that isn’t yet widely deployed, Feather provides the hardware and software toolkit for developers to tackle real-world tasks now.
“You can’t buy a Tesla robot today and develop on top of it,” Feather co-founder Hoa Mai told TechCrunch. “We realized that this is not how most companies became successful. Hardware players like Nvidia or Apple started with a product that worked and was deployable, and then they added complexity over time.”
In 2025, after his previous humanoid startup was sold to 1X, Mai (pictured above, left) teamed up with Parsa Bakhtiari (pictured above, right), a former Tesla Model 3 engineer who at one point reported directly to Elon Musk, to build what the duo hopes will become the Android of robotics.
That vision was attractive to Gradient Ventures, which backed Feather at its inception, leading the startup’s previously announced $7.6 million pre-seed round.
Since then, Feather has rolled out a modular robotic system that allows developers to customize the hardware for different use cases, such as adjusting arm lengths. The startup has already begun selling to customers, surpassing $1 million in revenue.
Although Feather is not disclosing its customers, it said that its robots are working as cooks in restaurants and cleaning up science labs. On the software side, the hardware can run models from any leading robotics AI provider, including Nvidia, Skild, or Physical Intelligence.
“We’ve been selling small quantities of these robots, and now that we resolved like almost all the issues over the last year of field testing, we’re getting ready for a big product launch,” Mai said.
According to Darian Shirazi, general partner at Gradient, Feather doesn’t have direct competitors in the U.S. He breaks down the current hardware robotics landscape into three categories: startups like Sunday building domestic household robots, heavyweights like Figure and Tesla aiming for general-purpose machines, and Feather, which, he believes, is the only U.S. startup developing a modular humanoid platform.
Mai admits that Feather took a page from Chinese robotics companies like Unitree. But with new foreign-made models restricted from entering the U.S. market, Feather is now uniquely positioned as a homegrown option of its kind.
Feather’s other advantage is its price. The robot costs $30,000, which is about half the price Unitree’s H2 Edu.
Shirazi believes the market size at that price could be very large. “You would hire a laborer for $50,000 to $60,000 a year, you’d have to train [them]. They’d have to have HR. They’d have to have all these different support mechanisms,” he said. “You can now buy a Feather robot to do that.”
Feather is also operating extremely efficiently, having spent only a fraction of its pre-seed funding, according to Shirazi.
The startup’s big bet, of course, is that the value in robotics will come from an ecosystem developed around the hardware.
“If we think about the market size today for physical AI companies, it’s very small,” Mai said. “But if you think about how many physical AI application companies will probably exist in five years, we expect it to be in the thousands.”
Feather hopes to be the platform that powers all of them.

articles.title: Application Modernization Services: What They Are and How to Choose a Partner - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Most companies do not set out to run old software. It happens slowly. A platform that worked well in 2012 keeps doing its job. A few integrations get bolted on.
The original developers move on. Then one day the finance team realizes that half the IT budget goes to keeping that system alive. This is the moment application modernization services start to matter.
Modernization brings aging software in line with current technology, security standards and business needs. It does this without throwing away the value already built into the system. Done well, it lowers costs and speeds up release cycles. It also removes the risk that one retiring engineer takes critical knowledge out the door. Done poorly, it turns into an expensive rewrite that misses deadlines. The difference usually comes down to strategy and the partner you choose.
Why Modernization Has Moved Up the Priority List
The financial case is hard to ignore. Gartner has found that companies which neglect technical debt spend far more on maintenance than peers who deal with it early. Much of the typical IT budget goes to keeping old systems running rather than building anything new. Every dollar locked into old code is a dollar not spent on features customers want.
The market reflects this pressure. Spending on modernization keeps climbing. Analysts project growth from roughly $19 billion in 2025 toward $22 billion in 2026, at a compound annual rate in the mid-teens. Companies are not buying modernization because it is fashionable. They buy it because the alternative keeps getting more expensive.
Three forces tend to push a project from “someday” to “now”:
- Skills are drying up. Finding developers who want to maintain a fifteen-year-old codebase gets harder every year. The few who can do it command a premium.
- Security and compliance keep tightening. Old systems often cannot meet current rules for GDPR, HIPAA or SOC 2 without major rework.
- The business wants speed. Customers expect frequent updates and quick fixes. Monolithic legacy systems struggle to deliver them.
The Main Approaches to Modernization
There is no single way to modernize. A good provider will not push one method on every problem. The common strategies are often called the “Rs,” and each suits a different situation.
Rehosting moves an application to new infrastructure with little code change. It is the fastest option. It works well when the goal is to leave a data center quickly.
Replatforming shifts the app to a new platform with targeted tweaks. It captures some cloud benefits without a full redesign.
Refactoring cleans up the existing code while keeping the outside behavior the same. This pays down technical debt and makes future changes easier.
Rearchitecting redesigns the structure. It often breaks a monolith into services so teams can deploy and scale parts on their own.
Rebuilding rewrites the application from scratch but keeps the original specifications. It fits when the old code is beyond saving but the requirements still hold.
Replacing retires the app for a commercial product. Retaining keeps a system as it is when it still delivers value. Knowing when to leave something alone is part of good judgment.
A capable team mixes these approaches across a portfolio. One system might get rehosted to buy time. A customer-facing apps might be rearchitected for the long term.
What Good Application Modernization Services Include
The label covers a wide range of work. When you evaluate providers, look past the marketing and check what the engagement includes.
A thorough assessment comes first. The team should audit your architecture, map dependencies, identify risks and tie its advice to your business goals. This produces a clear roadmap, not a vague promise to “make things better.” The best application modernization services build their work around this kind of phased assessment, connecting every technical decision to a business outcome before any code is touched.
Beyond the assessment, expect these to be part of a complete offering:
- Cloud migration to AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, with the architecture matched to your workload.
- Security and compliance upgrades built into the work, not added afterward.
- DevSecOps and CI/CD pipelines so releases become routine instead of risky.
- Performance tuning to fix the slow queries and bottlenecks that age into systems.
- UX and interface improvements where the design has fallen behind.
- Ongoing maintenance with clear response times, because modernization is a cycle.
AI tooling has become a real differentiator here. Modern teams use it to map dependencies during assessment, generate migration scripts during development and watch for anomalies during maintenance. This shortens timelines and lowers the chance of disruption when a system goes live.
How to Choose the Right Partner
Choosing a modernization partner is more like hiring a long-term collaborator than buying a product. The work often runs many months. The choices made early shape what happens for years. A few criteria separate strong candidates from the rest.
Look for outcome accountability
The best providers talk about business results, not just technology. Ask how they measure success. A team that commits to timelines and reports on metrics like on-time delivery and client retention is showing you how it works. McKinsey’s research is sobering here. In a study of more than 5,400 IT projects, large efforts ran far over budget and delivered much less value than predicted. Accountability keeps your project out of that statistic.
Check for relevant industry experience
Modernizing a banking platform is not the same as modernizing a retail catalog. Rules, data sensitivity and uptime needs vary a lot. A partner who has worked in your sector already understands the constraints. They will not learn them on your budget.
Demand transparency
You want a provider who shows progress in weeks, not quarters. You also want one who tells you when something is harder than expected. Hidden problems do not stay hidden in software. They surface late, when they cost the most to fix.
Confirm the engagement model fits
Some companies need engineers embedded in their own teams. Others want a dedicated team to take full ownership. Still others want a fixed-scope project with a clear end date. A flexible provider offers staff augmentation, managed delivery, project-based work and consulting. Then it helps you pick rather than forcing you into one box.
Avoiding the Common Failure Modes
Modernization projects fail in predictable ways. Knowing them helps you steer clear.
The first trap is the “big bang” rewrite. A team tries to replace everything at once. These projects tend to run long, drift from their goals and arrive too late to matter. Phased delivery, where value ships continuously, is far safer.
The second trap is lift-and-shift thinking. An old app is moved to the cloud unchanged and the team expects savings that never come. Research shows that only a small share of cloud transformations reach their full value. The reason is usually that teams skip the harder work of redesigning for the new environment. Moving to the cloud is not the same as modernizing for it. The savings live in the redesign.
The third trap is treating modernization as purely technical. A new architecture that nobody on your team understands becomes its own legacy problem. Good partners transfer knowledge as they go. They leave your people able to maintain and extend what was built.
A fourth trap is underinvesting in testing. Legacy systems collect undocumented behavior over the years. These are small quirks that the business quietly depends on. Skip thorough testing and these hidden requirements break in production, often weeks after launch. Strong test coverage protects you from inheriting bugs you cannot trace.
Where AI Has Changed the Work
It is worth pausing on how much AI has reshaped this work, because it affects timelines and risk. The slowest part of working on an old system is simply understanding it. Which parts depend on which? What breaks if you change a module? Where does the risk hide? AI tools now read legacy codebases, map those dependencies and suggest refactoring strategies that a human can accept or reject.
During the build, AI helps with code generation and migration scripting. This cuts the repetitive labor of porting logic from an old platform to a new one. During maintenance, it supports anomaly detection and vulnerability scanning. It catches problems earlier than periodic manual review. None of this removes the need for skilled engineers. They still make the calls that matter. AI just frees them to spend time on judgment rather than grunt work.
The takeaway for a buyer is simple. Ask how a partner uses these tools. A provider that has built AI into assessment, development and maintenance will likely deliver faster and with fewer surprises.
What a Realistic App Modernization Project Looks Like
A full modernization usually runs six to twelve months, though scope drives the range. It starts with a few weeks of assessment that produces a roadmap and a clear view of risk. Development then proceeds in phases. The highest-risk or highest-value systems often come first, so benefits show up early.
Throughout, you should see working software, not just status reports. A modernized payment flow that handles real transactions tells you more than a slide claiming the project is “70 percent complete.” After the main work, the engagement shifts into a maintenance rhythm. Security patches, performance tuning and small improvements keep the system healthy.
The cost savings tend to compound. Teams that modernize well often report much faster release cycles and big cuts in infrastructure and maintenance spend. That frees budget and attention for actual product work.
A Short Pre-Project Checklist
Before you sign anything, run through a few simple checks. They take an afternoon and save months of grief.
- Know your worst system. Which application causes the most pain or risk? Start there.
- Set a baseline. Write down today’s maintenance cost, release speed and uptime. You will want the comparison later.
- List your constraints. Note the rules you must meet, such as GDPR, HIPAA or SOC 2.
- Decide your model. Do you need extra hands, a full team or just a plan? That shapes who you call.
- Pick your metrics. Agree on how you will judge success before the work starts.
This short list keeps the conversation grounded. You walk into vendor meetings with facts instead of vague frustration. You can also tell quickly whether a provider listens to your situation or just pitches their standard package. The best ones will ask many of these same questions back to you.
The Bottom Line
Application modernization services solve a problem nearly every established company faces. The software still works, but it costs too much, moves too slowly and gets riskier each year. The work is not glamorous. The payoff is real when it is done with a clear strategy and an accountable partner.
The right approach starts with honest assessment. It matches the method to each system rather than forcing one pattern everywhere. And it keeps your team involved so the knowledge stays in-house. Choose app modernization services from a partner who talks about outcomes, shows progress quickly and has done this in your industry before. Get those things right and modernization stops being a cost center. It becomes the thing that lets your business move at the speed it needs.

articles.title: Un robot cuadrúpedo completó una maratón en 4 horas sin recargar su batería
articles.text:
Un robot cuadrúpedo desarrollado en Corea del Sur logró completar una maratón de 42 kilómetros con una sola carga de batería. RAIBO 2 terminó la 22 edición de la Maratón de Sangju en 4 horas, 19 minutos y 52 segundos, corriendo junto a participantes humanos y sin necesidad de detenerse para recargar su batería.
Sin embargo, el tiempo empleado no es el principal resultado de la prueba. Los investigadores del Instituto Avanzado de Ciencia y Tecnología de Corea (KAIST), responsables del desarrollo, destacan la eficiencia energética alcanzada por la máquina. Según sus autores, RAIBO 2 puede ofrecer una autonomía por carga aproximadamente tres veces superior a la de otros robots cuadrúpedos existentes.
PUBLICIDAD
La demostración busca responder a uno de los principales problemas que todavía limitan el uso de robots con patas: su capacidad para desplazarse durante largos periodos sin depender de una fuente de energía.
Un robot diseñado para consumir menos energía
Los robots cuadrúpedos necesitan utilizar energía constantemente para mantener su cuerpo estable mientras caminan. Cada una de sus patas incorpora articulaciones y motores que deben coordinarse para sostener el peso de la máquina y generar movimiento.
Este funcionamiento supone un desafío mayor que el de los robots con ruedas, especialmente cuando se pretende recorrer grandes distancias. Las pérdidas de energía producidas durante cada paso terminan reduciendo la autonomía disponible.
PUBLICIDAD
El equipo de KAIST diseñó RAIBO 2 precisamente para reducir esas pérdidas. El robot incorpora patas más ligeras, circuitos de control de los motores optimizados y estrategias de movimiento mejoradas mediante aprendizaje automático.
Los resultados de este trabajo fueron publicados en la revista científica Nature, donde los investigadores presentan el sistema como una alternativa para mejorar la eficiencia de los robots capaces de desplazarse mediante patas.
Completó la maratón a 2,64 metros por segundo
Durante la competición, RAIBO 2 mantuvo una velocidad media de 2,64 metros por segundo y tuvo que enfrentarse a un recorrido que no era completamente sencillo para una máquina de este tipo.
El trazado de la Maratón de Sangju presentaba un desnivel acumulado de 286 metros y también incluía tramos de terreno resbaladizo. A pesar de estas condiciones, el robot logró completar los 42 kilómetros y llegar a la línea de meta con una única carga.
PUBLICIDAD
Al finalizar la carrera, había utilizado aproximadamente 1.280 vatios-hora de energía. Los investigadores calcularon además un coste de transporte de 0,25, una medida que relaciona la energía necesaria para desplazarse con el peso del robot.
Según los autores del estudio, esta cifra es inferior al valor de referencia humano de 0,37. Sus cálculos indican que RAIBO 2 podría haber recorrido aproximadamente otros 25 kilómetros antes de agotar por completo su batería.
Una mayor autonomía para rescates y exploración
La importancia de la prueba no se limita a que un robot haya completado una carrera de larga distancia. Para los investigadores, el objetivo es demostrar que una mayor eficiencia puede permitir que los robots cuadrúpedos funcionen durante más tiempo en situaciones reales.
PUBLICIDAD
Estas máquinas pueden desplazarse por superficies irregulares y lugares donde los vehículos con ruedas encuentran dificultades. Por esa razón, una autonomía más prolongada podría resultar útil en operaciones de rescate, exploración de zonas montañosas y trabajos en lugares afectados por desastres.
En una emergencia, por ejemplo, un robot que pueda recorrer una distancia mayor antes de necesitar una recarga tendría más margen para inspeccionar un área o transportar información sin depender constantemente de una estación de energía.
RAIBO 2 demuestra así que la evolución de los robots con patas no depende únicamente de conseguir movimientos más rápidos o complejos. Reducir la energía necesaria para cada desplazamiento también puede ser determinante para ampliar sus posibilidades de uso fuera de los laboratorios.

articles.title: Opera muscle son VPN gratuit pour mieux protéger votre vie privée sur les Wi-Fi publics
articles.text:
Le VPN gratuit intégré à Opera gagne une nouvelle option sur ordinateur. Une fois activée, elle déclenche automatiquement la connexion au VPN lorsque le navigateur détecte un réseau Wi-Fi public.
Un VPN automatique, mais limité au trafic d’Opera
Une fois l’option activée, Opera détecte les connexions à des réseaux Wi-Fi publics et établit automatiquement le tunnel VPN. Le navigateur peut ensuite couper la connexion lorsque l’appareil retrouve un réseau privé.
Le service conserve les caractéristiques du VPN gratuit proposé par Opera depuis 2016. Il ne demande ni abonnement ni création de compte et ne fixe pas de quota de données. Opera affirme également ne pas conserver de journaux d’activité liés au VPN, une politique qui a fait l’objet d’un audit indépendant mené par Deloitte en 2024.
On en profitera pour rappeler que, contrairement à un VPN installé au niveau du système, celui d’Opera ne prend en charge que le trafic qui transite par le navigateur. Les échanges provenant d’un autre navigateur, d’un client mail, d’une messagerie ou de toute autre application continuent donc à utiliser directement la connexion de l’appareil.
Un tunnel VPN est une connexion chiffrée entre votre appareil et un serveur VPN, qui encapsule vos données pour les rendre illisibles à un tiers présent sur le même réseau Wi‑Fi. Sur un point d’accès public, cela limite notamment les risques d’écoute (sniffing) ou de manipulation du trafic par un attaquant local. En pratique, le Wi‑Fi du café ne voit plus le contenu des échanges, seulement qu’une connexion chiffrée vers le serveur VPN est établie. En revanche, le VPN ne rend pas anonyme “par défaut” : le site visité peut toujours vous identifier via vos comptes, cookies ou l’empreinte du navigateur. Enfin, il ne corrige pas une connexion déjà compromise par un malware sur la machine.
Un VPN intégré au navigateur ne chiffre que les flux réseau qui passent par ce navigateur (pages web, requêtes, téléchargements lancés depuis lui). À l’inverse, un VPN système (au niveau de l’OS) route et chiffre l’ensemble du trafic de l’appareil, y compris les autres navigateurs, clients mail, messageries et mises à jour. La différence vient de l’architecture : le VPN navigateur fonctionne comme un proxy/VPN applicatif, tandis que le VPN système agit sur la pile réseau de l’appareil. Conséquence directe : activer le VPN d’un navigateur ne protège pas les données envoyées par les autres applications. Pour une protection globale sur Wi‑Fi public, c’est le VPN système qui couvre le périmètre le plus large.
Une politique « no‑logs » signifie que le fournisseur affirme ne pas enregistrer l’historique de navigation, les requêtes DNS, les adresses IP sources ou des horodatages permettant de relier un utilisateur à une activité. Dans les faits, certains services conservent malgré tout des données techniques minimales (par exemple pour la stabilité, l’anti-abus ou la capacité), ce qui rend la portée exacte du « no‑logs » dépendante de la définition retenue. Un audit indépendant peut examiner l’infrastructure, la configuration et les procédures internes pour vérifier l’alignement entre la politique annoncée et les pratiques observées à un instant donné. Il ne garantit pas à lui seul qu’aucune donnée ne sera jamais collectée dans le futur, ni qu’un partenaire technique n’en collecte pas en amont. Pour juger la robustesse du « no‑logs », il faut aussi regarder la transparence sur les types de données exclus, la durée de conservation et le cadre légal applicable.

articles.title: OpenAI’s agent had a routine task. It breached a government portal.
articles.text:
OpenAI’s agent had a routine task. It breached a government portal.
An OpenAI agent researching public medicine spending bypassed security blocks and gained unauthorized access to public and non-public files on an Australian government Medicare statistics portal, the government there disclosed Thursday. The agent, which OpenAI said was running during an internal evaluation in June, also wrote files to an internal server, according to the complaint.
Transluce, an independent nonprofit AI research lab, analyzed public request logs from the URL scanning service urlquery.net and found autonomous agents attempting SQL injection, cross-site scripting, command injection, and path traversal against the University of New Mexico’s digital library, the public data platform Data USA, and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW). The agents tried to retrieve ordinary information, including a historical photograph, University of Iowa data, and local pharmaceutical data in Victoria, and the offensive behavior appeared only after normal retrieval methods failed.
Transluce ties the Data USA and AIHW activity to an agent swarm that it says OpenAI previously confirmed originated from the company, based on shared targets, tactics and timing.
A day after Transluce published its findings on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed that an OpenAI agent researching public medicine spending bypassed blocks on a Services Australia Medicare statistics portal in June and gained unauthorized access to public and non-public files. OpenAI, which said the agent was running during an internal evaluation, notified the Australian government on September 10. According to Albanese, the agent also wrote files to an internal server.
The incidents have not been publicly confirmed as the same activity. However, OpenAI told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that much of what Transluce documented overlaps with cases in its ongoing review of misaligned model activity.
Transluce ties the Data USA and AIHW activity to an agent swarm that it says OpenAI previously confirmed originated from the company, based on shared targets, tactics and timing.
Probing public data providers
On May 25 and 26, agents trying to retrieve a photograph from the University of New Mexico’s Valmora collection ran into repeated failures. They responded with seven vulnerability probes against the service. The probes included an attempt to execute a system command, a path traversal request targeting /etc/passwd, and a SQL injection string containing UNION SELECT; they also arrived alongside a burst of 80 requests aimed at the image, although none appear to have succeeded.
Two days later, agents gathering University of Iowa data from Data USA hit errors caused by a malformed query parameter and followed those errors with 12 vulnerability probes against the API, covering SQL injection, reflected XSS, server-side template injection, path traversal, and command injection.
Cloudflare blocks, staging server workaround
The AIHW case on June 20 and 21 followed a very similar pattern. While trying to download pharmaceutical spending data from an AIHW Tableau dashboard, the agents ran into Cloudflare’s bot protections. One of them responded within minutes by testing the dashboard with a reflected XSS payload, although Cloudflare stopped it before it reached the application.
Transluce found no evidence that the probe succeeded, and AIHW says there is no evidence that non-public information was accessed. The agent ultimately found the same public dataset on AIHW’s pre-production server at pp.aihw.gov.au, and retrieved it through more than 100 scans.
The agent ultimately found the same public dataset on AIHW’s pre-production server at pp.aihw.gov.au, and retrieved it through more than 100 scans.
Agents build their own toolchains
The earliest clear sequence Transluce documented dates to March 6, when an agent tried to pull drug-enforcement statistics from the API of Thailand’s Office of the Narcotics Control Board. A direct request returned no page content, and adding a JSON format parameter changed nothing, so the agent routed the page through r.jina.ai three times and got text back with the Thai province names garbled.
Then, it wrote a custom Base64-encoded script and submitted it through urlquery.net, effectively using the service’s remote scanning browser to run its own client-side JavaScript against the data. That script ran into the same parsing problem, and a later attempt through Jina triggered a redirect to localhost that got the entire API blocked by Jina for an hour.
Beginning in mid-April, Transluce found the same technique across thousands of agent requests on urlquery.net, and on June 14 agents used the service’s browser to create a disposable email inbox and then tried to register a urlquery.net account with it. Registered users can make their scans private, which means the public records Transluce analyzed may understate how much of this activity actually took place.
An agent with web access isn’t limited to the software its developer gave it because remote browsers, proxies, URL scanners, and other public services can fill in the gaps, which gives the agent ways to make requests or run code that its own environment doesn’t provide.
Egress controls for AI agents
Instructions won’t be enough if the agent can still send whatever it wants over the network. For narrowly defined jobs, outbound traffic can be limited to approved hosts, a closed-by-default approach also used for securing AI agent sandboxes. Research agents may need to reach more of the web, so the focus shifts to controlling where they can connect.
Guidance for GKE Agent Sandbox recommends isolated runtimes with default-deny network policies that open only the endpoints an agent needs. Public proxies, URL scanners, and disposable email services can stay blocked unless the job requires them.
Developers can also limit what an agent can send. So, instead of handing it a networking tool that accepts any URL or request body, an API integration can restrict requests to specific fields and formats. The runtime can then catch path traversal attempts, SQL injection strings, and executable markup before anything is sent. OpenAI takes a related isolation approach in its Agents SDK sandboxes, and the company’s Responses API tech lead has said large enterprise deployments often call for agents that are isolated from the network entirely.
Repeated failures can also be a reason to pause a run, especially when an agent keeps hitting client errors, anti-bot challenges, or unexpected redirects and begins trying increasingly aggressive ways to get around them, as Transluce documented in several of these cases.
Keeping the original task, tool calls, and server responses in the same trace gives operators a better chance of catching that behavior change when a retrieval job starts generating encoded scripts, visiting staging domains, or sending exploit payloads, rather than discovering it later in someone else’s security logs.

articles.title: Beyond Good & Evil 2 est toujours en vie et intègre un scénariste d'Assassin's Creed Shadow
articles.text:
Nous revoilà avec un article sur Beyond Good & Evil 2, alors que le jeu ne s’est toujours pas montré à nouveau. Mais alors, pourquoi parler de l’arlésienne d’Ubisoft, encore une fois ? Parce que son parcours nous fascine autant que l’incroyable volonté d’Ubisoft de continuer à croire en son projet. Visiblement, l’histoire continue : le jeu est toujours en chantier, et un scénariste d’Ubisoft Bordeaux y prête main-forte depuis quelques mois.
Cela fait maintenant 18 ans que Beyond Good & Evil 2 s’est montré pour la première fois. Attendez, je vous le mets en lettres : dix-huit ans. C’était en mai 2008, avec un premier teaser. Le jeu a ensuite été officiellement annoncé en 2017, avant de refaire une dernière apparition en 2018.
Alors qu’on oublie à chaque fois que son développement se poursuit, une nouvelle vient nous rappeler que, si, Beyond Good & Evil 2 est bel et bien vivant. C’est ce 22 septembre 2026, sur Bluesky, que Rik Godwin, scénariste et directeur narratif associé chez Ubisoft Bordeaux, a confirmé avoir rejoint le projet il y a maintenant quelques mois, en tant que consultant et en soutien de l’équipe. Il parle lui-même d’une « drôle de non annonce » : « Depuis quelques mois, je travaille sur Beyond Good & Evil 2 dans un rôle de soutien et de consultant. J’ai le droit de le dire, j’ai vérifié. »
Beyond Good & Evil 2 donne des signes de vie
Si son nom ne vous dit rien, sachez que Rik Godwin a travaillé sur plusieurs titres développés et édités par Ubisoft, notamment Assassin’s Creed Shadows, sur lequel il a travaillé comme scénariste. Toujours chez Ubisoft, il a travaillé sur Last Rites, la mission gratuite ajoutée à Ghost Recon Wildlands en 2026 pour les 25 ans de la série. En dehors d’Ubisoft, il a aussi écrit pour d’autres studios.
Une annonce discrète, au détour d’un post sur un réseau social, et nous voilà déjà à rêver à nouveau du prochain Beyond Good & Evil. Ubisoft n’a plus rien montré du jeu depuis 2018, mais ce simple message de Rik Godwin suffit à nous rappeler que, quelque part, dans les entrailles d’Ubisoft, le jeu est toujours en chantier. Merci, et à dans six mois pour une nouvelle mise à jour du développement d’un jeu que, malgré tout, on attend encore beaucoup.

articles.title: From Bihar to SEMICON India: How Shweta Suman is building Swadeza for the world
articles.text:
From Bihar to SEMICON India: How Shweta Suman is building Swadeza for the world
From Bihar to SEMICON India 2026, Swadeza is building AI-native semiconductor engineering tools designed for secure, on-premises deployment.
Swadeza began with a simple question. What would "Made in India" really look like if globally relevant technology were built from places people rarely associate with deeptech?
That question became a company. Today, Swadeza is being built from Bihar with ambitions that go well beyond its geography. It also reflects a larger shift in India's technology landscape, about where the country's next generation of technology companies can come from, and who gets to build them.
A journey in the opposite direction
Founder Shweta Suman's path has been anything but linear. She went to school in Oman, studied engineering at BIT Mesra, returned to Oman, and eventually moved back to Bihar after marriage. Rather than look elsewhere for opportunity, she chose to build here.
That choice matters in the context of the state. Bihar is often discussed in terms of migration, with talent and opportunity leaving. Suman's journey runs the other way: coming back, building a technology company, entering India's startup ecosystem, and eventually seeing Swadeza on one of the country's most visible semiconductor stages.
One company, three businesses
Swadeza operates across semiconductor technology, IT consulting and development, and 360° digital marketing. Its deeptech work is increasingly focused on AI-native semiconductor engineering.
On the software side, it builds platforms for government and public-sector teams. The company describes itself as women-led, and says its engineers average 11 years of experience across fabless semiconductors, consumer platforms and government deployments.
It also built an automated AI verification system for government recruitment for the Government of Bihar, which it says cut turnaround from several months to weeks.
The problem FORGE is targeting
Before a chip goes to fabrication, engineers must prove the design behaves exactly as specified. That verification work is among the most time-consuming stages of chip development, and errors caught after tape-out are expensive.
Swadeza's argument is that general-purpose AI assistants struggle at this scale. As a design grows, the assistant's prompt fills with unrelated and conflicting fragments, and answer quality drops. Its semiconductor platform, FORGE, instead keeps the chip in a cited map, sends a language model only what a given question touches, and converts what it learns into deterministic models, so each run is meant to finish faster and cost less than the last.
Four products across the chip lifecycle
FORGE is designed to bring AI-native workflows across the chip lifecycle, from verification and physical design to post-silicon validation and standard cells.
DV-FORGE handles verification. It reads a chip's reference manual into a map and generates the verification plan, coverage model and UVM testbench from it. The company says DV-FORGE has been used on OpenTitan-class SoCs, signing off OpenTitan Earlgrey, a taped-out root-of-trust chip, in 30 days, and finding seven bugs across roughly 40 IP blocks and 2,581 registers. Its derivative, Darjeeling, was signed off in 21 days, with most of that time spent in regression. Swadeza also claims 80% fewer tokens than an AI assistant, and says it has run the pipeline on reference manuals from NXP, STMicroelectronics, Renesas and Infineon.
PD-FORGE is being developed for physical-design closure, tracing signoff violations back to the stage that caused them. It links reports from every stage, run and tool to the same nets, across 26 Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens and open-source back-ends, and is in closed testing ahead of a Q4 2026 production release.
PS-FORGE, for post-silicon validation and debug, and SC-FORGE, which aims to produce provably optimal standard cells, are both still in development.
FORGE is deployed on-premises. In an industry where chip designs are among a company's most sensitive IP, keeping data inside customer environments removes a major barrier to adopting AI tools.
Swadeza says it is building with professors from BIT Patna and with Signitude, a fabless semiconductor company.
Bihar on the semiconductor stage
At SEMICON India 2026, Swadeza showcased its semiconductor technology alongside some of the industry's most recognised names. The event was also FORGE's first public demonstration, at startup pod 6.
The fifth edition of SEMICON India ran from 17 to 19 September under the theme "Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem". It came two months after the Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, a ₹1,27,500 crore second phase of India's chip mission.
Swadeza was subsequently included in Forbes India's photo coverage of the event, in the same visual showcase as IBM and Tata Electronics.
For a company that chose to build from Bihar, that moment carried significance far beyond publicity. It placed a Bihar-built product in the same frame as global semiconductor leaders.
A state trying to enter the chip economy
Bihar is making its own push into the sector. The state cabinet approved its Semiconductor Policy 2026 earlier this year, seeking fabrication units, display fabs and chip design facilities, and a Bihar Semiconductor Mission has been set up to oversee implementation.
Most of that policy targets manufacturing investment. Swadeza represents a different kind of participation: design tooling built locally and aimed at chip teams anywhere.
Building from India, for the world
Swadeza's broader vision is to build from India for a global market. The near-term tests are clear: moving PD-FORGE into production, and turning conversations from SEMICON into on-premises deployments with paying chip teams.
If it gets there, Swadeza will be a proof point that India's deeptech companies do not need to start in the usual hubs, and that the next wave of builders may come from places the ecosystem has overlooked.

articles.title: Nouveau déluge de failles Chrome : Google corrige plus de 100 vulnérabilités, dont 11 brèches critiques
articles.text:
Google vient de lancer le déploiement de Chrome 154 sur Windows, macOS et Linux. L’éditeur colmate d’un seul coup 108 vulnérabilités. C’est nettement plus qu’à l’accoutumée. On reste néanmoins loin des 400 failles corrigées en juillet dernier.
11 failles critiques de Chrome
Parmi les 108 failles, on trouve 11 vulnérabilités critiques. Le niveau « critique » est le plus haut degré de gravité chez Google. Ce niveau désigne les failles qui permettent à un pirate de prendre le contrôle de l’ordinateur, simplement en poussant l’internaute à visiter une page web piégée. Plusieurs des brèches critiques concernent ANGLE, le composant graphique de Chrome qui traduit les commandes d’affichage pour les adapter aux différentes cartes graphiques. On recense plusieurs problèmes de mémoire. Un bug du même acabit touche WebGL, la technologie qui affiche des graphismes 3D dans le navigateur.
D’autres failles critiques visent le composant GPU, chargé de dialoguer avec la carte graphique. Google a colmaté deux vulnérabilités de type « écriture hors limites », capables d’aboutir à la corruption de la mémoire de l’ordinateur. Google a aussi corrigé plusieurs bugs estampillés « use-after-free ». Ces failles découlent de l’utilisation d’une zone mémoire qui n’est plus libre par le programme. Ce type de faille est très prisé des pirates. Dans certaines conditions, elles permettent de manipuler la mémoire du navigateur pour y exécuter du code malveillant sans la moindre autorisation.
Des failles graves dans V8
Au-delà des failles critiques, Chrome 154 comble 25 vulnérabilités de gravité « élevée ». On y trouve une douzaine de bugs relatifs à la mémoire et plusieurs bugs dans V8, le moteur qui exécute le code JavaScript des sites web. Deux des failles de V8 ont été signalées par l’équipe de sécurité d’OpenAI, qui s’est servie de l’IA pour analyser le code de Chrome.
À lire aussi : Google colmate plus de 40 nouvelles failles Chrome, installez la mise à jour sans tarder
Sur les 108 failles corrigées, 32 ont été découvertes par des chercheurs extérieurs à Google. La firme a donc versé 18 000 dollars de primes aux chercheurs. Les autres brèches ont été débusquées en interne, grâce à des outils automatisés.
Bonne nouvelle, Google assure n’avoir constaté aucune preuve que des pirates ont exploité les failles pour lancer des cyberattaques. Par précaution, la firme américaine garde tout de même secret certains détails techniques, tant que la majorité des internautes n’a pas installé la mise à jour. Quoi qu’il en soit, on vous invite à mettre à jour votre navigateur sans tarder. Ouvrez le menu de Chrome, rendez-vous dans « Aide », puis dans « À propos de Google Chrome ». La mise à jour se télécharge alors toute seule et s’applique après un redémarrage du navigateur.

articles.title: Rydox marketplace admin pleads guilty, faces 22 years in prison
articles.text:
A Kosovar national has pleaded guilty to operating Rydox, a large illegal online marketplace that sold stolen personal information, login credentials, credit card details, and cybercrime tools.
Kosovo law enforcement and Albania's Special Anti-Corruption Body (SPAK) arrested 28-year-old Ardit Kutleshi and two other Rydox administrators (Jetmir Kutleshi and Shpend Sokoli) in December 2024.
The arrests were part of a joint international law enforcement operation that also shut down the Rydox marketplace, seized the Rydox[.]cc domain, and seized its servers in Kuala Lumpur with the help of the Royal Malaysian Police.
Ardit Kutleshi was extradited from Kosovo to the United States in 2025, when he was charged with crimes related to their Rydox admin role, including conspiracy to commit identity theft, aggravated identity theft, two counts of identity theft, access device fraud, and money laundering.
"Rydox put cybercriminal tools and sensitive data up for sale, including the stolen identities and logins of thousands of people," said Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division. "The FBI and its foreign partners shut the marketplace down, and now the man who created it and ran it pleaded guilty."
According to court documents, between February 2016 and Rydox's shutdown in 2024, marketplace sellers were involved in over 7,600 sales of login credentials, credit card information, and stolen personal information (including Social Security numbers, names, and addresses) of thousands of U.S. citizens.
Rydox also offered over 321,000 other "cybercrime products" for sale to more than 18,000 users, including various devices, software tools, and materials for committing cybercrimes.
Rydox users had to deposit cryptocurrency into their accounts before making a purchase via Bitcoin ("BTC"), Monero, Ripple, Ethereum, Litecoin, Perfect Money, Tron, or Verge payments that were deposited into a Rydox-controlled cryptocurrency wallet and could be used to buy illicit products, services, tools, and programs from Rydox sellers.
The marketplace also charged registered users a one-time fee (that fluctuated between $200 and $500) to become authorized sellers, who received 60% of the sale proceeds, while the marketplace retained 40% from every sale.
Kutleshi has pleaded guilty to aggravated identity theft and money laundering conspiracy and is scheduled to be sentenced on February 9, 2027.
He now faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for money laundering and a minimum penalty of two years in prison for the aggravated identity theft count.
Since the start of the year, the owner of the Incognito dark web drugs market was sentenced to 30 years in prison in February, while a California man who sold fentanyl and methamphetamine on the Nemesis dark web marketplace was sentenced to more than 26 years in federal prison.

articles.title: Ce qu'un ex-dirigeant de Stellantis a découvert en passant chez le géant chinois BYD
articles.text:
Dans les anciens locaux où Wang Chuanfu, fondateur de BYD, a assemblé ses premières batteries il y a plus de trente ans pour des téléphones mobiles, nous avons pu échanger pendant une trentaine de minutes avec Alfredo Altavilla, conseiller spécial de BYD pour l’Europe. Ancien bras droit de Sergio Marchionne chez Fiat Chrysler (FCA), dont il a dirigé les activités Europe, Afrique et Moyen-Orient jusqu’en 2018, l’Italien connaît parfaitement l’industrie automobile européenne.
Son arrivée chez BYD lui a pourtant réservé quelques surprises. Culture technologique, vitesse de développement ou encore organisation interne : son regard offre un éclairage rare sur ce qui distingue aujourd’hui le constructeur chinois des groupes automobiles traditionnels.
Nous faisons partie d’un petit groupe de journalistes européens invités à Shenzhen pour interroger Alfredo Altavilla. Depuis plusieurs jours, BYD nous a ouvert les portes de son univers : musée, siège historique, démonstrations technologiques, usine, conférence sur sa nouvelle puce… Cet entretien apporte un autre point de vue. Là où les responsables chinois détaillent les technologies et les ambitions du groupe, l’ancien dirigeant de Fiat Chrysler livre un regard plus extérieur sur ce qui l’a réellement surpris en découvrant BYD de l’intérieur.
Alfredo Altavilla a rejoint BYD fin août 2024 comme conseiller spécial pour l’Europe, après avoir notamment présidé la compagnie aérienne ITA Airways. Sa mission : aider à structurer l’organisation et la distribution du groupe sur le continent, au moment où BYD y installe ses premières usines de voitures, en Hongrie puis en Turquie.
Le but de cet entretien ? Comprendre ce qui fait aujourd’hui la singularité de BYD alors que le groupe est devenu l’un des acteurs majeurs de l’automobile mondiale. À écouter Altavilla, la première erreur consiste justement à voir BYD comme un constructeur automobile classique.
« BYD ne se voit pas comme un constructeur automobile »
Après plusieurs décennies passées dans l’industrie automobile européenne, Alfredo Altavilla explique que le premier choc culturel en arrivant chez BYD en 2024 concerne la manière dont l’entreprise se définit elle-même. « Très souvent, les dirigeants de BYD ne parlent pas de leur entreprise comme d’un constructeur automobile, mais comme d’une entreprise technologique », explique-t-il. Pour lui, cette différence de perception est fondamentale et c’est ce qui distingue l’entreprise de la concurrence. « Ce que BYD vend avant tout, c’est un engagement technologique », poursuit-il.
Une approche qui transparaît d’ailleurs dans le discours du groupe. Altavilla raconte qu’en interrogeant Wang Chuanfu sur la mission de BYD, le fondateur ne répond pas en termes de parts de marché, ni de chiffre d’affaires ou de rentabilité. « Notre mission est de faire baisser la température de la planète d’un degré », résume-t-il.
Un message que nous avons effectivement retrouvé à plusieurs reprises lors de nos visites dans les différents sites du groupe à Shenzhen. Pour l’ancien dirigeant européen, cette vision explique aussi une partie des différences observées chez BYD, à commencer par le fonctionnement même de l’entreprise.
Le « BYD Way » : être exigeant et aller vite
Lorsqu’on lui demande ce qui l’a le plus marqué en rejoignant le groupe chinois, Altavilla cite une expression utilisée en interne : le « BYD Way ». Derrière ce qui ressemble à un slogan, il décrit une méthode bien réelle, qui repose sur deux piliers : une exigence élevée et une exécution très rapide.
« Le BYD Way signifie la capacité à être incroyablement exigeant et incroyablement rapide dans le développement de solutions », explique-t-il. Cette rapidité ne se limite pas au développement d’un nouveau véhicule. Elle concerne également les améliorations apportées en continu aux produits existants.
L’ancien dirigeant raconte ainsi qu’une grande partie de ses déplacements en Chine consiste à essayer les véhicules du groupe. À l’issue de chaque session, une liste de modifications est établie avec les équipes techniques. « Je reviens plus tard et je teste les changements. Ces équipes à Shenzhen sont capables de réaliser en très peu de temps des évolutions qui prendraient plusieurs mois chez de nombreux constructeurs historiques », affirme-t-il.
Derrière cette réactivité, Altavilla décrit une véritable machine industrielle où les équipes d’ingénierie, de qualité et de production semblent fonctionner quasiment en continu. Les allers-retours entre les essais, les demandes d’amélioration et leur mise en œuvre lui paraissent sans commune mesure avec ce qu’il a connu durant plusieurs décennies dans l’automobile européenne.
Au-delà des 120 000 ingénieurs, l’intégration des équipes
Lorsqu’on évoque BYD, un chiffre revient régulièrement : celui de ses quelque 120 000 ingénieurs. Pour Alfredo Altavilla, ce nombre n’explique pourtant pas à lui seul les performances du groupe. « 120 000 ingénieurs, c’est impressionnant. Mais cela ne signifie rien si ce qui est développé en recherche et développement ne trouve pas sa traduction dans la production », estime-t-il. Il dit avoir surtout été frappé par le niveau d’intégration entre les équipes de recherche et développement, les services qualité et la production.
« La machine de Shenzhen est incroyablement bien intégrée », résume-t-il. Autrement dit, l’innovation ne reste pas bloquée dans les laboratoires. Les équipes chargées du développement des technologies et celles responsables de leur industrialisation travaillent de manière suffisamment étroite pour accélérer la mise en œuvre des évolutions.
Si Altavilla insiste autant sur cette intégration entre les équipes, c’est aussi parce qu’il estime qu’elle devra être reproduite en partie en Europe. BYD a d’ailleurs annoncé en mai 2025 l’installation de son siège européen et d’un centre de recherche et développement à Budapest, en Hongrie, appelés à grandir dans les prochaines années. Mais selon lui, retrouver le même niveau de réactivité que celui observé aujourd’hui à Shenzhen constituera l’un des grands défis de l’expansion européenne du groupe.
L’échéance est proche : l’usine BYD de Szeged, en Hongrie, doit démarrer sa production au quatrième trimestre 2026, avant un second site en Turquie. En produisant sur place, BYD veut échapper aux droits de douane que l’Union européenne applique aux voitures électriques importées de Chine, un point qui pèse directement sur ses prix de vente en Europe.
Une transformation qui dépasse BYD
Au fil de l’échange, Altavilla dépasse d’ailleurs le seul cas de BYD pour évoquer l’évolution de l’ensemble du secteur automobile. Selon lui, l’industrie mondiale entre dans une phase de consolidation majeure qui laissera inévitablement des perdants sur le bord de la route. Entre électrification, logiciels et montée en puissance des constructeurs chinois, les années à venir pourraient profondément rebattre les cartes du secteur. « Nous sommes au début d’un processus de consolidation qui fera de nombreuses victimes », estime-t-il.
BYD n’échappe pas lui-même à cette recomposition. Ses ventes sont passées de 427 000 voitures en 2020 à 4,27 millions en 2024. Elles n’ont ensuite progressé que de 7,7 % en 2025, puis ont reculé de 20 % sur les cinq premiers mois de 2026. Le groupe prépare une réorganisation de sa R&D, pour donner plus de poids aux équipes de chaque marque face au centre d’ingénierie central. La machine décrite par Altavilla doit donc, elle aussi, s’adapter.
Le discours d’Altavilla reflète aussi le changement d’équilibre observé depuis plusieurs années entre la Chine et les constructeurs historiques. Pour l’ancien dirigeant de Fiat Chrysler, la question ne se limite plus à l’électrification. Elle concerne désormais la vitesse d’innovation, les logiciels, les systèmes intelligents et la capacité des entreprises à transformer rapidement une idée en produit.
Des constructeurs historiques comme Renault ont d’ailleurs essayé de reproduire cette méthode avec la nouvelle Twingo : une grande partie de son développement a été menée à Shanghai, dans le centre ACDC du groupe, avec des partenaires chinois comme Launch Design pour le haut de la carrosserie. La citadine a ainsi été conçue en 21 mois, près de deux fois plus vite qu’un projet équivalent en Europe, ce qui a aussi permis de contenir les coûts.
Sur tous ces sujets, il dit avoir découvert chez BYD une approche différente de celle qu’il a connue pendant plusieurs décennies dans l’automobile européenne. Au fil de-l’entretien, Altavilla parle d’ailleurs assez peu des voitures elles mêmes : il revient surtout sur les méthodes de travail, la vitesse d’exécution et l’organisation interne du groupe, qu’il faudra en partie reproduire en Europe, l’un des grands défis de BYD sur le continent selon lui.
