articles.title: New Jersey fines data center $1.1M after drone pics expose 62 gas generators
articles.text:
This week, New Jersey ordered the operator of one of the East Coast’s largest planned data centers to pay a $1.1 million fine for secretly installing and operating gas generators in violation of the state’s Air Pollution Control Act.
DataOne got hit with the fine after an investigation by The Guardian and Floodlight News in August shared thermal drone footage showing that 45 of the 62 gas generators were operating. None of the generators had permits required for generators with 37-kilowatt capacity or higher, despite running at 1,982-kw capacities more than 50 times higher than the state limit.
States track gas generators like DataOne uses because they emit “carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and other combustion-related pollutants,” officials from New Jersey’s Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) noted. Those pollutants can worsen asthma, trigger heart attacks, and cause early deaths.
Calling out the enforcement action as “by far the largest ever taken against a data center in New Jersey,” DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak vowed that data centers would not be “constructed or operated with impunity in this state.”
However, while historic, the state’s solution doesn’t immediately relieve residents’ concerns. DataOne was given 45 days to apply for the permits or else cease operations, but they can continue operating the gas engines while seeking permits. Nichole Gardner, a co-chair of a local environmental nonprofit Sustain SJ, told Ars that “we believe it is insufficient, both in dollar amount and enforcement. The DataOne site should be made to discontinue operations during the 45-day period until the proper permits are issued.”
In a statement to The New York Times, the company seemed unfazed by the fine.
“We will apply for the air permits for the temporary generators,” a DataOne spokesperson said, while noting that DataOne “disagreed” with the fine. Eventually, the polluting gas generators will supposedly be phased out, as the data center is “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells,” the spokesperson noted.

articles.title: Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
articles.text:
It’s right there in the name: “Insta360” makes 360-degree cameras, ones that film every angle simultaneously so you can shoot first and frame later. It didn’t invent the idea, but Insta360 has become so synonymous with 360 cameras that it dominates the category with 73 percent of worldwide marketshare. It’s preparing to ship so many cameras, it just spent $298 million — more than GoPro’s entire valuation — on memory chips alone.
Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
The Chinese brand has 73 percent of the worldwide 360 camera market. What’s next?
Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
The Chinese brand has 73 percent of the worldwide 360 camera market. What’s next?
But as Insta360 sells its 10 millionth camera and opens its first flagship US store in New York City’s Times Square, it’s thinking bigger than two hemispherical lenses on a stick. It’s looking to challenge Canon, Sony, Nikon, and Fujifilm by becoming a “top imaging camera company” or “even a tech company,” cofounder Max Richter tells me — and it’s experimentally building its own mirrorless cameras and smart glasses to get there.
Insta360, also known as Shadow Stone or Arashi Vision in its native China, isn’t targeting Meta’s AI glasses or DSLR-wielding professional photographers just yet. Nor is it trying to replace the smartphone camera in your pocket.
“We don’t try to fight against the rise of the smartphone in photography and content creation,” says Richter. “We see that there’s an opportunity between smartphone users and professional cameras — a growing trend that people want to express themselves,” he adds.
He tells me that if Insta360 were to sell a pair of smart glasses, “we wouldn’t necessarily compete with companies on smart intelligent features.” It’d be about helping people conveniently capture high-quality images, not about an AI assistant on your face. And while that doesn’t sidestep the “pervert glasses” problem, there might be room for Insta360 to go about it differently, with headgear that’s obviously a camera instead of covertly spying.
Though Insta360’s smart glasses ambitions haven’t been widely reported — I could only find one brief mention — founder JK Liu previously confirmed that two mirrorless cameras are already in development. One will have a shape that “you have never thought of before,” Liu told MyNavi News in August. (Liu reportedly became a billionaire when Insta360 went public last year.)
“When you think about mirrorless, for us it would really go into making it more convenient and making a camera that is really suited for a new generation of content creators, not necessarily what’s already out there on the market,” Richter tells The Verge.
If Insta360 does expand into those camera categories, they’ll just be the tip of the spear. The company has already been pushing into many other categories dominated by its Chinese rival DJI, including DJI-challenging drones, gimbals and gimbaled baby steadycams, and modular action cameras.
While Insta360 might be the 360-camera market leader with 73 percent share, it’s a distant number 2 in other categories that DJI serves. IDC estimates that Insta360 has 20 percent of the worldwide handheld smart camera market compared to DJI’s 73 percent overall. Still, Insta360 is making significant headway: In Q2 2026, it had 43 percent of the detachable action camera market, 17 percent of non-detachable GoPro style action cameras, and its brand-new Luna Ultra already has 6 percent marketshare in gimbaled cameras.
GoPro itself, meanwhile, is a distant number 3 in IDC data, with just 3 percent of the smart camera market in Q2 2026, after shipments fell by half to just 200,000 cameras in the quarter.
It’s not unthinkable that Insta360 could help challenge traditional cameras. The traditional market leader, Canon, shipped 4.5 million digital cameras last year according to Nikkei data. DJI shipped 4.3 million cameras last quarter alone, according to IDC.
Insta360’s founders have explained that their grand vision is to become the robot cameraman for the world — not necessarily an actual humanoid robot, but rather an expectation that these devices can do more and more of the capture and motion and editing themselves, automatically understanding your intent using built-in AI tech.
The company’s latest Insta360 X6 is another small step in this direction: It comes with an onboard AI model and enough processing to automatically create a highlight reel from your footage while the camera is plugged in and charging, and it’s got a 2.0 version of a previous “InstaFrame” feature that can track and frame the person you select and automatically produce a video.
Insta360’s also launching a new feature for the X6 that can create 3D Gaussian splats with one tap in the company’s smartphone app, for free. It takes an hour or two for cloud servers to process the video, and users will only get four free splats per month, says Insta360 spokesperson Caroline Chen, but early results look neat.
It’s not at all clear whether the United States will embrace Insta360 the way Insta360 has embraced the US. While Apple, Best Buy, and Costco all stock the company’s products, that could change if the US government decides to enact a foreign camera ban — or if it simply decides that Insta360 is a drone company, like DJI, and pushes back on its cameras, too.
Insta360 already distanced itself from its drone brand Antigravity in the lead-up to the US drone ban, which will theoretically prevent Antigravity from shipping any future drones into the United States. Its first drone beat the ban by weeks.
As for Insta360, “We remain on the ground,” Richter tells me. “When it comes to drones, it’s not something that Insta360 is working on,” he says, suggesting I speak to Antigravity CEO Michael Shabun instead.
Richter says he’s “quite confident” that he can continue to bring cameras to people all around the world, and that Insta360 will fully comply with any local laws, but admits “there are certain things that are out of our control.”
I ask: Would Insta360 consider hedging against future risk by manufacturing some products in the US? If the company was required to, perhaps — but there’s no current plan to do so. “We would potentially look into it, but it’s not in our plan or roadmap at this moment.” He says the US is a key market, and Insta360 plans to be there for the long haul.

articles.title: KI-Kennzeichen und Sperrung für Tantiemen: Wie der Musikstreaming-Dienst Qobuz gegen KI-Musik vorgeht
articles.text:
Kennzeichen und Sperrung für Tantiemen: Wie der Musikstreaming-Dienst Qobuz gegen KI-Musik vorgeht
In die Riege von Musikstreaming-Plattformen, die KI-generierte Musik über ein Label kennzeichnen, reiht sich nun auch der Anbieter Qobuz ein. Nach Deezer, Apple Music, Youtube Music, Tidal und jüngst Spotify führt jetzt auch der Dienst, der in Frankreich gegründet wurde, eine Markierung ein. Der sogenannte „AI-Tag“ ist bei Veröffentlichungen zu sehen, die KI-generierte Tracks enthalten. Die Kennzeichnung ist innerhalb der App oberhalb der Musiktitel, die ein:e Künstler:in veröffentlicht hat, platziert. So wolle man seinen Nutzer:innen transparent anzeigen, welche Art von Musik sie gerade hören, heißt es von Qobuz in einer Pressemitteilung.
Kennzeichnung von KI-Musik auf verschiedenen Musikstreaming-Diensten
Die Plattform hatte nach eigenen Angaben im Februar dieses Jahres seine KI-Leitlinien veröffentlicht, die KI als Hilfsmittel einordnen und die Kuration durch Menschen hervorheben. Qobuz zählt zu einer der weniger bekannten Alternativen für Spotify und richtet sich mit seinem Portfolio in Hi-Res-Audio in 24 Bit und 192 kHz an Musikhörer:innen, die auf verlustfreie Soundqualität Wert legen. Ergänzt wird das Musik-Angebot noch durch ein Magazin mit Artikeln und Interviews mit den Künstler:innen.
„Die Identifizierung KI-generierter Musik ist ein erster Schritt. Nun geht es darum, gemeinsame Standards für Transparenz und Betrugsbekämpfung in der Musikindustrie zu entwickeln. Jede Plattform trägt dabei Verantwortung, doch wirksame Lösungen können nur gemeinsam entstehen“, äußert sich Georges Fornay, der stellvertretende Geschäftsführer von Qobuz in der Pressemitteilung. Die KI-generierten Titel würden aus den Playlisten und Empfehlungen von den menschlichen Redakteur:innen ausgeschlossen. Auch „betrügerische Streams“ hat Qobuz im Blick und meint damit solche, bei denen Wiedergaben von Musiktiteln zum Beispiel durch Bots künstliche erzielt werden. Sie werden aus Tantiemenzahlungen ausgeschlossen. KI-generierte Stücke werden erst entfernt, wenn bei diesen Betrug festgestellt wird.
Wie viel Anteil KI-Musik auf den Musikplattformen hat
Insgesamt nennt Qobuz pro Tag eine Summe von fast 69.000 KI-generierte Musiktiteln, die auf der Plattform hochgeladen werden (zum Vergleich: Deezer meldete im Juni eine Zahl von rund 90.000 KI-Liedern täglich). Dies entspreche rund 40 Prozent der erhaltenen Tracks. 60 Prozent dieser KI-Songs hat Qobuz als „betrügerisch“ eingestuft. Und 0,38 Prozent aller Wiedergaben auf Qobuz entfielen auf KI-Musik. Der Musikkatalog des Anbieters umfasst nach eigenen Angaben rund 100 Millionen Songs.
Neben Qobuz haben auch andere Musikstreaming-Anbieter haben bereits Kennzeichnungen für von der KI erzeugte Tracks eingeführt. Während Deezer, Apple Music und Tidal die KI-Lieder kennzeichnen, geht Spotify einen anderen Weg und führte jüngst ein Label für „AI Personas“ ein. Der Marktführer kennzeichnet also nicht Inhalte, sondern Accounts, die KI-generiert sind. Spotify setzt bei der Vergabe des Labels auf Selbstauskunft des Erstellers sowie auf eigene Prüfverfahren. Die algorithmische Sichtbarkeit des Profils schränkt Spotify aber ebenfalls ein.
Erkennen die Hörer:innen KI-Musik?
Leicht verfügbare Musikgeneratoren wie Suno AI, Udio und Mureka, aber auch Googles Lyria Pro 3, die allesamt komplette Musikstücke durch Prompteingabe erzeugen, setzen die Musikstreaminganbieter zunehmend unter Druck. Künstler:innen prangern wegbrechende Einnahmen durch den Einzug von KI-Musik an und Hörer:innen fordern Transparenz über die Herkunft der Musik. Dabei ist das konsequente Ermitteln von KI-generierter Musik mittels Detektoren unter bestimmten Umständen zwar zuverlässig, dennoch schreitet auch hier die Entwicklung der Musikgeneratoren immer weiter voran.
Wie sehr sich KI-Musik dennoch in die Hörgewohnheiten schleicht, zeigt eine Studie der US-Großbank Morgan Stanley von Anfang 2026. Demnach hören 50 bis 60 Prozent der 18- bis 44-Jährigen in den USA wöchentlich 2,5 bis drei Stunden KI-generierte Musik. Unklar bleibt aber, ob sich die Hörenden stets bewusst sind, dass die Musik nicht von Menschen gemacht wurde.

articles.title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
articles.text:
The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
Polygraph+ will use new sensor technologies and AI to vet staff and hunt leakers. Experts say AI-enabled lie detection is “the worst of both worlds.”
The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.
According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.
Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.
But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.
It selected two companies to build prototypes: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment.
Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”
The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”
Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.
There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.
“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.
AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.
“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away. 
Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.
“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.
“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”

articles.title: 'La Bola Negra' (★★★★☆), los Javis invocan a Lorca y sueñan con hacer historia en los Oscar
articles.text:
Por fin llega a los cines la película española más esperada del año, La Bola Negra de Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi. Los cineastas responsables de éxitos como Paquita Salas, La Llamada, La Mesías o Veneno, se lanzan ahora con un auténtico drama bélico. Una superproducción que pretende hacer historia no solo en nuestro país, sino también en Hollywood y el mundo entero.
Y es que La Bola Negra tuvo su estreno original en el Festival de Cannes, quizá el más importante y prestigioso del mundo. Allí, arrasó de improvisto con la segunda ovación más larga de su historia, que duró 20 minutos ininterrumpidos; y con el premio a mejor dirección para los Javis.
Ahora, más recientemente, también ha conquistado el premio del público en el Festival de Toronto. Por supuesto, se trata de la candidata por España para el Oscar a mejor película extranjera. Pero es que las quinielas apuntan mucho más allá, hablando de ella como una de las principales candidatas para varias categorías más, incluyendo mejor película. Con la maquinaria de Netflix detrás, el cielo es el límite.
La Bola Negra narra las vidas interconectadas de tres hombres en tres épocas distintas, 1932, 1937 y 2017. Son tres existencias íntimamente ligadas por la sexualidad y el deseo de sus protagonistas, así como por su dolor y la herencia; y una de las últimas obras, inacabada, del gran poeta español Federico García Lorca, asesinado en 1936.
La Bola Negra apunta muy alto
Hay algo innegable que se sobrepone a cualquier prejuicio y opinión preestablecida contra la temática o sus directores. La Bola Negra es muy buena. Sobre todo porque es una película tremendamente ambiciosa desde su concepción. A pesar de ser española, con las limitaciones que eso suele conllevar en la magnitud de una producción, los Javis han ido con absolutamente todo.
Ya en los primeros minutos queda claro que lo que estamos viendo no va a ser solo un drama profundo y sentido (que también). Esto es una película de gran escala. Disparos, bombardeos, explosiones, destrucción por los cuatro costados... El arranque de La Bola Negra confirma que la película es grande y, sobre todo, que se sabe grande. Vestuario, decorados, atrezzo, localizaciones... Todo rema a favor de esa grandilocuencia impulsada por la propia historia y también por su extraordinario diseño de sonido y su impresionante fotografía.
A nivel de guion, La Bola Negra impacta por su sensibilidad y su constante búsqueda de la emoción intensa. Profundamente Lorquiana en fondo y forma, su carga poética y simbólica es enorme. La cinta nos habla del dolor, de la necesidad de ser y de vivir. Su mensaje es marcadamente humanista. Es un esperanzador canto a la memoria de los antepasados que vivieron escondidos en los márgenes. Empleando para ello, además, la figura de Federico García Lorca como nexo de unión de una forma especialmente bella.
La Bola Negra es, en resumen, la consagración definitiva de los Javis como directores. Ambos cineastas han recogido aquí todo lo que habían sembrado durante sus trabajos anteriores a lo largo de los años. Porque el filme demuestra una destreza asombrosa detrás de las cámaras, con secuencias que son ya historia del cine español. Emocionan y rompen por dentro desde el descaro y la ambición más puras de quien cree firmemente en lo que hace.
Por supuesto, como consecuencia de esto último hay también puntos de imperfección en la obra. Su metraje, de más de 2 horas y media, hace que por momentos se haga un poco larga. Especialmente porque el continuo sentimentalismo imbuye todas las escenas hasta el punto de saturar en secuencias que quizá requerían un ritmo más ligero, no tan denso. Hay instantes en los que La Bola Negra se emborracha de sí misma. Y cuenta con algunas subtramas que no era necesario incluir, solo recargan más y más el conjunto.
En cualquier caso, esa sensación de cierta pesadez en sus tramos más irregulares desaparece por completo al llegar a su acto final. El desenlace de La Bola Negra es extraordinario, de una potencia emotiva cinematográfica muy alta. Un cierre magnífico que compensa cualquier mal, cualquier pecado en el que la película pudiera caer antes. Déjenla unos días de reposo, gana aún más.
Guitarricadelafuente quiere conquistar Hollywood
Una de las grandes evidencias de La Bola Negra es que hay que hablar de su reparto. Y no se puede empezar por otro que por Guitarricadelafuente. Reconocido por su faceta como cantante en su particular estilo, debuta aquí como actor. Y su irrupción es bárbara, está que se sale. Su magnetismo con la cámara es innegable. La gran labor de los Javis, siempre estupendos directores de actores, ha sacado de él un intérprete total.
Lo más sorprendente de todo es que lo hace sin necesidad de mostrarse exuberante. Guitarricadelafuente parte desde un estilo mucho más naturalista. Miradas y gestos muy sutiles que denotan una profunda sensibilidad artística. Transmite vulnerabilidad, verdad y dolor como si llevara muchos años delante de las cámaras. Sin lugar a dudas, una de las interpretaciones del año. Si sumamos además la canción que ha compuesto para la película, La Nieve, hay quinielas en medios especializados de Estados Unidos que hablan ya de una posible doble nominación al Oscar para él.
Además, uno de los momentos más esperados de La Bola Negra es el anunciado "cameo" de Penélope Cruz. Es cierto que no es más que eso, un cameo, porque su aparición es muy breve. Pero en su corto tiempo en pantalla nos regala una de las mejores escenas de toda la película. Su actuación es soberbia, con una energía desbordante, una garra que zarandea toda la historia con mucha gracia. Se nota en dicha secuencia la clara influencia de Pedro Almodóvar que, como Lorca, ha inspirado a los Javis en su condición de maestro.
Hablando de papeles pequeños, también podemos hablar de una Glenn Close como sorprendente madrina del filme. Su papel también es pequeñito, pero deja buen sabor de boca. Aunque quienes destacan en el resto del reparto principal son Lola Dueñas y, sobre todo, Miguel Bernardeau. El actor de Élite sigue creciendo a pasos agigantados y en La Bola Negra está mejor que nunca. Su dupla con Guitarricadelafuente es el corazón del filme. Cada vez hay menos miedo a afirmar que puede convertirse en uno de los mejores actores de su generación.
En definitiva, La Bola Negra es una película extraordinaria, lorquiana. Los Javis demuestran que respiran cine con un proyecto de gran ambición y escala que consolida las grandes virtudes que ya se vislumbraban en sus anteriores títulos. A pesar de algunos excesos (también de herencia propia), el filme no defrauda gracias a su potente guion, su eléctrica dirección y su inspiradísimo reparto. Como consejo, no vayan al cine esperando ver la mejor película de todos los tiempos ni nada por el estilo. Moderen sus expectativas y vayan más bien con la ilusión de ver, sencillamente, una gran película. Si lo hacen, saldrán satisfechos.

articles.title: TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026: Everything you need to know | TechCrunch
articles.text:
TechCrunch Founder Summit is a full-day gathering in Boston on November 4 where founders across all stages connect with top VCs and experienced entrepreneurs to gain tactical insights on building and scaling their companies. It’s the latest in our long line of founder-centric events, which are smaller and more hands-on than Disrupt.
If an extensive lineup of speakers from Anthropic, Nvidia, OpenAI, and Benchmark is your thing, Disrupt tickets are still available here. But for the founder looking to really get in the weeds during a one-day crash course, Founder Summit is the ideal place to get a head start on your 2027 plans.
Before you dig in on the event details, you can get info on all of our tickets, which are available for a $200 discount for investors and founders, right here.
Who is TechCrunch Founder Summit for?
All founders end up wrestling with the extensive, complicated mechanics of building a company from the ground up. There’s fundraising, hiring, legal, marketing, PR, and leadership, as well as the investors needing the means to vet, invest in, and develop founders as they build out their skills.
Founder Summit is the best way to cover all of the challenging questions with community members who have been there, and lived to tell the tale, through constructive failure and massive success.
When and where is TechCrunch Founder Summit?
The event takes place on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, at the SoWa Power Station in Boston. It’s accessible via public transportation and a short walk from the Back Bay and Tufts Medical Center stops on the Orange Line, or the Broadway stop on the Red Line.
What’s on the TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda?
To deliver on that promise of equipping founders for success, this year’s agenda and speakers lean hard into fundraising, AI-native building, and leadership. Sessions include:
- The New Rules of Raising Capital: Brian Devaney, partner at Underscore, breaking down what investors look for now and where founders lose leverage without realizing it.
- The CEO Job Never Gets Easier: HubSpot co-founder and Sequoia partner Brian Halligan on how the CEO role changes at each stage of growth.
- Built for AI From Day One: 7AI co-founder and CEO Lior Div on what changes when AI is the foundation of a company rather than a bolt-on feature.
- Not Every Dollar Is Equal: Cogent Security co-founder and CEO Vineet Edupuganti on evaluating investors and cap-table trade-offs beyond valuation.
- How to Spot the ‘King of the Hill’ Company: TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong unpacking a framework for evaluating startups on economics, scalability, and timing.
- Your Company Is Who You Hire: NEA partner Melissa Taunton on early hiring decisions that shape a startup’s culture and execution.
- The Boston Founder Playbook: HqO co-founder and CEO Chase Garbarino on building a category-defining company outside Silicon Valley, having raised $200 million and scaled to 30+ countries.
- Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale: Bessemer Venture Partners‘ Kent Bennett on validating demand and avoiding scaling before the fundamentals are in place.
Didn’t this event have a different name?
Yes. Founder Summit was formerly known as Early Stage and All Stage. This year, we have the same mission, but with a new name. Keep that in mind if you want to do any more research before attending.
Is TechCrunch Founder Summit just panels, or is there more to it?
Founder Summit is far from a series of panels, though the agenda does provide a ton of valuable insights for founders and investors. In addition to all of those sessions, we also have our breakout sessions, where even more intimate panels discuss vital topics for the community to dive deeper into.
There’s also networking available via the Braindate app to help connect investors with founders, or facilitate founders with similar challenges to bring their expertise together to reach shared solutions. Or that time is the perfect opportunity for students to build out their nascent network.
Then there’s Founder Summit week, taking place November 1-7. That’s when all of our Side Events are held, expanding the opportunities for you to gather with the community. And if you’re especially eager to take part, you can apply to host your own Side Event right here.
How much does a ticket cost, and how can I get the best price?
Pricing moves in phases, with our next increase happening after October 16. Our current pricing tiers are Investor for $399, Founder for $199, and students for $149. If you buy a second ticket for a co-founder or co-worker, you’ll also get 50% off their admission. And bundles for groups for four or more offer additional discounts.
Is there a free way to attend?
Yes! We’re looking for volunteers to help staff the event, and those individuals will get a behind-the-scenes look at how the event comes together on top of their free access to programming beyond their shift. Learn more about our program, which closes to new applicants October 19, right here.
Where can I register and learn more?
You can get the full rundown of the event, with everything from up-to-date speaker information, the full agenda, logistics, and more right here. Ticket information across all three tiers is available here. And remember, our current discounts end October 16 — act now before they expire.

articles.title: SEMICON India 2026: Startup Mitra Tackles Silicon Funding Gap - EE Times
articles.text:
At SEMICON India 2026, the India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) held an early-stage silicon startup funding round under its Startup Mitra initiative, sponsored by Lam Research and Synopsys. Eleven startups were selected from a pool of 200, with Elphins Technologies taking first place, Meukron Technologies coming second, and Multi Nano Sense and CraftifAI jointly taking third. The top three received cash awards.
“We wanted to do a pitching event where the startups could raise funds,” said Akshay Agarwal, executive committee member at IESA and senior director of technology at MediaTek. He added that there was no commitment that the startups would receive funding from the VCs attending the event, but the organizers hoped the participants would be able to raise funds through connections made at the event.
From zero to one
The event targeted startups at the seed or pre-Series A stage, which the organizers described as the phase that takes a company “from zero to one.” The focus on early-stage funding comes as India’s semiconductor startups navigate the capital requirements of building products before they generate revenue.
Vishal Katariya, VP of deep science tech investing at Ankur Capital, told EE Times that the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme had helped de-risk seed rounds for many such companies.
“As a venture investor, if we are talking to a startup and we know that there is a good chance of it getting anywhere from ₹100 million [~$1.04 million] to ₹300 million [~$3.13 million] of support from the government, and if it is raising a comparatively sized seed round… there is a comfort that we receive,” Katariya said. “The risk profile of our investment is pushed down a little bit.” He added that government support in some cases matches the size of the seed round itself.
Staircase capital
However, Katariya said the funding challenge extends beyond the seed round, with India needing more Series A, Series B, and other investors willing to back pre-revenue deep-tech companies. He said investors need to account for the value created as startups move through successive stages of technology development, rather than focusing only on revenue at an early stage.
He described this approach as “staircase capital”, reflecting how a startup’s technology moves from one technology readiness level to the next, with each stage adding value.
More than 20 venture capitalists attended Startup Mitra, along with other investors from the audience. The organizers said the event aimed to connect VCs with startups and with each other. It followed IESA’s earlier Startup Connect initiative at the Vision Summit, where startups pitched to Pontiac Ventures for connections and support rather than funding.
IESA executive committee member and India managing director for TYLSemi, Sundeep Gupta, said the organizing team received more than 70 applications through incubation centers across India. The applications were evaluated on technology, team, prototype level, intellectual property, and funding already received. “The selected startups spanned manufacturing, artificial intelligence, fabless semiconductor design, electronic design automation, defense, and automotive,” he said.
Navin Bishnoi, chairperson of IESA, outlined five Ts for startups: total addressable market, technology, team, timing, and treasure. He said IESA’s startup initiatives aim to help founders address these areas by providing access to capital, markets, policy, incentives, networks, and connections, with Startup Mitra focused particularly on capital.
Ajit Manocha, president and CEO of SEMI, called on VCs to support founders who had chosen to build startups over conventional employment, describing AI as accelerating innovation and startups as capable of turning difficult ideas into businesses. He urged VCs to back startups over the long term so founders could focus on developing their ideas.
Sudeep Shivalli, regional senior director at Synopsys India, highlighted the role of technology partners in helping startups develop products. For Startup Mitra, Synopsys committed $250,000 in credits for startups to access tools, storage, and licenses.
“We decided about $250,000 as a credit to enable the startups so that they can build the next product,” Shivalli said. “Today we are enabling globally more than 200 startups in this environment. We give them technology access; we give them compute, storage. In some cases, IPs are as well, so that we accelerate the entire product cycle.”
The support could help address some of the technology development costs faced by fabless semiconductor startups. Katariya said access to EDA tools, prototyping, and tape-out support can reduce financial barriers for companies at the early stage.
The six-member jury included Aadith Ramesh, associate at Peak XV Partners; Aashish Gupta of IvyCap Ventures; Abhishek Sud of Applied Ventures; Adarsh Sekhar, director at Lam Capital and Corporate Development at Lam Research India; Aviral Pandey, principal at AktiVentures; and Sunil Cavale, investment principal at Speciale Invest.
Katariya told EE Times that the seed stage support provided by DLI has worked particularly well in the fabless space, where several beneficiaries have gone on to raise larger follow-on rounds. He cited Indian startups such as Mindgrove Technologies and NetraSemi as examples that raised $10 million or more in subsequent rounds and said Ankur Capital’s own portfolio company, Turiyam AI, had drawn continued investor interest.
Katariya described deep-tech investing as requiring a different kind of underwriting than for typical startups, since investors back product creation rather than revenue creation at the stage firms like his come in.
Funding beyond tape-out
Katariya said the funding requirement can rise again as semiconductor startups move from tape-out toward commercial and high-volume production. “Companies still need capital for engineering work and volume production after the first chip and engineering samples, with the amount depending on the type of chip and potentially reaching the scale of an Indian Series B or Series C funding round,” he said.
He added that there is not yet any specific mechanism for Indian semiconductor startups to raise this production capital, leaving them to rely primarily on conventional equity funding. “The Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) fund could provide support to deep-tech startups through loans or equity,” he said.
Katariya expects Indian fabless companies to reach meaningful revenue once they move into volume production and sign purchase orders with customers. “Once that happens, you will see a good amount of investor interest,” he said. “Whenever there is one big success story, a lot of things will follow from that.”

articles.title: Managing 3D-IC Design And IP
articles.text:
Design data management, traceability, and revision control are critical for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration.
By Keith Felton and Todd Burkholder
The trend towards multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration is here to stay. It promises faster innovation, more powerful and specialized devices, and greater design flexibility. However, realizing its potential hinges on our ability to manage the complexity that comes with it.
However, with this newfound modularity comes a significant challenge: managing the vast and intricate web of data that defines these systems. This is where robust data management and meticulous data traceability become not just beneficial, but essential. Without data management, even the most brilliant multi-chiplet design can quickly become a tangled mess, leading to costly errors, delays, and a loss of confidence in the final product.
In the first three articles of this series (published in the June, July and August editions of Semiconductor Engineering), we covered the first seven steps toward streamlining your 3D-IC design process. This article focuses on design data and design IP management, traceability, and revision control. This is a critical step for multi-chiplet heterogeneous integration, as there is so much design data and IP involved that using an incorrect version or missing an ECO can mean product failure.
Data management can be broken down to four components that will help you streamline your 3D-IC design flow:
In the world of multi-chiplet design, we often bring together various pieces of IP from different sources—from internal teams, external vendors, or even open-source initiatives. Each piece of design IP comes with its own set of design files, specifications, and usage guidelines.
When you have multiple chiplets from different sources, potentially designed with different tools and at different times, the sheer volume and diversity of this data can be overwhelming. Without a well-defined data management strategy to manage these diverse sources, the risk of introducing defects is significantly higher.
Innovator3D IC Data Management software supports robust data and design IP management to provide single moment-of-truth management of design IP data. It treats the design itself as a work-in-progress, applying a revision-controlled and access-rights managed process at every stage of design, all the way to tape out.
Fig. 1: Innovator3D IC Data Management’s centralized cockpit.
Multi-chiplet designs inherently involve a complex hierarchy. Chiplets are integrated into a larger multi-chiplet heterogeneous assembly using interposers and substrates. Managing this hierarchy effectively, especially with the inevitable design iterations, requires a powerful revision control system. When you manage your design hierarchy with revision control and history tracking, you avoid errors. Revision control is like a time machine for your designs. It allows you to track every change, revert to previous versions, and allow different teams to work on separate features or bug fixes concurrently without interfering with each other. Once a team’s work is complete and verified, their changes can be merged back into the main design.
Without this meticulous historical tracking, understanding how a design evolved, diagnosing issues, or even just knowing which version is currently “in play” becomes a monumental task. Errors can appear through miscommunication or accidental overwriting, leading to significant delays and increased costs. A well-managed design hierarchy with robust revision control is fundamental to preventing these types of errors.
In a distributed design environment, where different teams might be working on different chiplets across various locations, having a single, centralized hub for all design data is invaluable. This hub acts as the single source of truth, providing direct access to all relevant information for authorized personnel.
When engineers can quickly access information they need, cycle times are dramatically reduced. This direct access speeds up design, verification, and debugging processes, leading to faster time-to-market.
Beyond just storing data, an effective data management system provides real-time visibility into a project’s status. This capability is crucial for efficient project management, especially in the complex landscape of multi-chiplet integration.
Instant access to status tracking and analytical data empowers project managers and engineering leads to make informed decisions, proactively address issues, and ensure that the project stays on track. It transforms data from a passive record into an active tool for driving project success.
By embracing robust data management practices, including diligent management of the design and its IP sources, meticulous revision control, centralized information hubs, and comprehensive status tracking for traceability, you establish a solid foundation for success. These “unseen architects” ensure that your multi-chiplet designs are not only functional and perform well, but also are reliable, maintainable, and auditable — allowing you to build the complex, interconnected systems of tomorrow with confidence and clarity.
To learn more about how to improve your 3D-IC flow, please check out the full complement of eBooks from Siemens on streamlining 3D-IC design:
Todd Burkholder is a senior editor at Siemens DISW. For over 25 years, he has worked as editor, author, and ghost writer with internal and external customers to create print and digital content across a broad range of EDA technologies. Burkholder began his career in marketing for high-technology and other industries in 1992 after earning a Bachelor of Science at Portland State University and a Master of Science degree from the University of Arizona.

The Africa Early-Stage Investor Summit (AESIS), co-created by ABAN and VC4A, will host its 13th edition in Cape Town, South Africa, on November 25-26.

Building on this legacy, this year’s summit will bring together the ecosystem once again to advance conversations, partnerships, and investments that will shape Africa’s entrepreneurial future.
Under the theme Capital with Conviction, AESIS will bring together more than 300 angel investors, venture capital fund managers, limited partners (LPs), development finance institutions (DFIs), family offices, corporate venture capitalists, policymakers, and ecosystem builders from across Africa and around the world to examine how capital can be deployed with greater purpose, discipline, and long-term impact.
“As Africa’s investment ecosystem matures, the conversation can no longer be limited to raising more capital. The real question is how we deploy that capital with greater intention, discipline, and long-term commitment,” said Vincent Hoogduijn, CEO of VC4A.
“Capital with Conviction challenges investors to move beyond market cycles and invest in building resilient companies, stronger ecosystems, and lasting value.”

articles.title: 5 Lessons from the Grammar of Silence by R Seshasayee
articles.text:
5 Lessons from the Grammar of Silence by R Seshasayee
Discover 5 powerful lessons from The Grammar of Silence on resilience, courage, identity, and challenging social barriers.
History is often told through the stories of kings, leaders, and revolutions. Yet some of the most remarkable acts of courage happen quietly, far from the spotlight. In The Grammar of Silence: Five Centuries.
Three Women. Towards Liberation, R. Seshasayee follows the lives of three women, Dharma, Vinodhini, and Mary Amelia, as they navigate the constraints of patriarchy, caste, and social expectations across different periods of Tamil history. Through their journeys, the novel explores resilience, agency, and the enduring pursuit of freedom.
5 Thought-provoking lessons from the book
1. Silence does not always mean surrender
One of the novel's most compelling ideas is that silence can sometimes be a form of strength rather than weakness. The women in the story often face situations where open rebellion is impossible, yet they find subtle ways to challenge the systems that seek to control them. Their quiet determination becomes a tool for survival and resistance.
The book encourages readers to rethink the assumption that power only exists in loud acts of defiance. Sometimes resilience is found in persistence, patience, and refusing to give up one's sense of self.
2. Courage takes many forms
The protagonists come from different backgrounds and eras, but each demonstrates courage in her own way. Whether it is questioning restrictive traditions, seeking independence, or pursuing opportunities that society denies them, their actions show that bravery is not limited to dramatic gestures.
The novel reminds readers that courage often appears in everyday decisions: the choice to keep learning, keep hoping, and keep moving forward despite obstacles.
3. Social barriers are powerful but not permanent
Throughout the story, caste, gender, and social status shape the lives of the characters. Yet the novel also shows that these barriers, while deeply entrenched, can be challenged and overcome. The journeys of Dharma, Vinodhini, and Mary Amelia reveal the possibility of change even within restrictive systems.
This lesson remains relevant today. Progress may be slow, but history is filled with individuals who expanded opportunities for those who came after them.
4. Identity should not be defined by society alone
The women in the novel are frequently judged according to the roles society assigns them. However, each character struggles to define herself on her own terms rather than accepting the limitations others impose. Their stories highlight the importance of self-belief and personal agency.
The book suggests that true empowerment begins when people stop allowing external labels to determine their worth and potential.
5. Shared struggles can create lasting solidarity
Although the protagonists live in different centuries, their experiences are connected by common themes of perseverance and resistance. The novel emphasises the importance of solidarity among women and how one generation's struggles can inspire the next.
Readers are reminded that personal victories rarely exist in isolation. Every act of courage can create possibilities for others, building a legacy that extends far beyond a single lifetime.
Why these lessons matter
The Grammar of Silence is more than a historical novel. It is a reflection on how ordinary people confront extraordinary challenges and how change often begins with small acts of determination. Through the lives of its three protagonists, the book explores themes of resilience, identity, and liberation that continue to resonate in the modern world.
Its greatest lesson may be that even when voices are ignored or silenced, the desire for dignity, freedom, and self-expression endures across generations.

articles.title: Sweden launches campaign telling people to be ruder as scammers exploit good manners
articles.text:
Nice guys never win People today could stand to be a little less rude. Unless, that is, they're talking to scammers. Then they can use all the profanities they want. In Sweden, celebrities are promoting a national operation against fraud, one that tells the country: Dare to be rude.
Swedish police authority Polisen writes that total profits from fraud in the country amounted to 5.7 billion SEK, around $575.3 million. As is the case everywhere, the most common targets are elderly people.
To fight back against the practice, a campaign has been launched featuring four celebrities from the Nordic nation. One of them, 74-year-old Suzanne Reuter, says many people of her generation have been raised to always be polite and accommodating. But as those are traits that scammers are quick to exploit, they need to be more questioning. Reuter adds that this isn't rude; it's self-protection.
The most common types of scams against people over 60 in Sweden are telephone-based. These often start with a text message in which the scammers claim to represent an official body, such as a government agency, a company, a bank or an association. The message contains a phone number that the recipient is asked to call for help or more information.
When the person calls this number, scammers use prepared scripts to gain the person's trust while inducing stress and creating a sense of urgency to act quickly. They're sometimes told a crime is taking place and money needs to be moved from their account into another one to protect it.
The campaign urges people to feel more comfortable simply hanging up the phone if they believe anything is amiss during the call.
The same applies to fake officer scams. These involve criminals turning up at someone's door dressed as police. They then tell a story that somehow culminates in the victim needing to hand over credit cards or valuables such as gold, which the owner never sees again.
Polisen's national operations leader, Robert Öhman, said police would never ask to collect and safely store a person's items, and urged people to ignore their inclination to be polite by shutting the door at the slightest hesitation.
In addition to the personal loss suffered by victims, police warn that the stolen goods are often used to help fund other serious crimes.
In the US, adults aged 60 and over reported $7.75 billion in losses across 201,266 complaints in 2025, up 59% from 2024, according to the FBI. Investment, tech support and romance scams caused some of the largest losses, with more than 12,000 people reporting losses exceeding $100,000.
Although older adults are less likely than younger people to report losing money to fraud, they typically lose more when they do, according to the FTC. These figures only reflect reported cases, so the actual financial toll is likely higher.

articles.title: Speaker-labeled transcription with WhisperX on SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Speaker-labeled transcription with WhisperX on SageMaker AI
Any team working with spoken audio hits the same wall with generic speech-to-text. Think contact-center calls, all-hands meetings, podcasts, depositions, and broadcast media. These workloads need two things that standard transcription gets wrong. First, timestamps land at the utterance level, off by several seconds. Second, there’s no reliable answer to “who said what.” Those gaps make transcripts hard to search, caption, redact, or analyze at scale. A missing speaker label breaks compliance review, and an imprecise timestamp breaks a caption or a redaction.
WhisperX closes both gaps. It wraps OpenAI’s Whisper with batched inference, adds wav2vec2 forced alignment for precise per-word timestamps, and adds speaker diarization to label who spoke. These capabilities map directly to real workloads. Contact centers can measure talk time, check script adherence, and run sentiment analysis, while teams turn meetings into searchable notes. Media and e-learning teams generate accurate captions (in SubRip Subtitle (SRT) and Web Video Text Tracks (VTT) format) for large content libraries. Time-sensitive uses get text the moment someone speaks. In regulated fields like healthcare, legal, and finance, speaker-labeled transcripts support audits and legal discovery.
The AWS WhisperX Deep Learning Container (DLC) packages all of this into a GPU-ready image. You deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time or asynchronous endpoint without building a custom image. In this post, we show how to deploy both endpoint types and when to choose each. We also cover the production details that matter: the GPU AMI pin, scaling, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) setup, and cost controls. This post is part of a multimodal series showcasing specialized AWS DLCs. The series spans three AWS DLCs across four use cases: (1) vLLM-Omni for text-to-speech, (2) vLLM-Omni for image and video, (3) WhisperX for speech-to-text (this post), and (4) llama.cpp.
What is WhisperX, and what workloads it unlocks
Whisper is a popular open source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model family from OpenAI that transcribes spoken audio into text accurately across many languages. It focuses on high-quality transcription and produces timestamps at the phrase or segment level. WhisperX is an open source project that builds on Whisper and extends it for production workloads. It adds per-word timestamps, speaker labels, and faster transcription, three capabilities that together turn raw audio into structured, analyzable transcripts.
Why a purpose-built Deep Learning Container
The AWS WhisperX DLC is a maintained, GPU-ready image that already contains Whisper, the alignment models, and the diarization weights, with no Hugging Face token required. It follows the standard Amazon SageMaker AI serving contract, so you deploy it like any other model.
- Serving contract: The container serves on port 8080 and exposesPOST /invocations for inference andGET /ping for health checks.
- Request format: The endpoint expects multipart/form-data , with the audio as thefile part plus optional string fields such aslanguage ,diarize , andresponse_format . Amazon SageMaker AI passes theContentType header (including the multipart boundary) through to the container unchanged.
- Output formats: json ,verbose_json ,srt , andvtt , so the same endpoint feeds analytics pipelines and video editors alike.
Choosing between real-time and asynchronous endpoints
Amazon SageMaker AI supports both real-time and asynchronous endpoints, so you can serve the same WhisperX DLC through either pattern. The decision usually comes down to clip length and interactivity. For long audio, use the asynchronous endpoint: it’s the recommended path when transcription, alignment, and diarization need more time to run. Reserve the real-time endpoint for short, interactive clips that finish within the Amazon SageMaker AI 60-second response cap.
| Dimension | Real-time endpoint | Asynchronous endpoint | 
| Best for | Short, interactive clips | Long audio, high-volume batch | 
| Latency | Synchronous, must finish < 60s | Submit-and-poll. No response cap | 
| Invocation | InvokeEndpoint (inline body) | InvokeEndpointAsync (S3 reference) | 
| I/O | Body in request / response | Input + output in Amazon S3 | 
| Scaling | Add instances (one request/container) | Add instances. Can autoscale to zero | 
| Cost profile | Bills while endpoint is up | Scale-to-zero when idle saves cost | 
Solution architecture
Both patterns share the same container contract. Amazon SageMaker AI forwards each request to the WhisperX DLC on port 8080. The real-time pattern is synchronous, and the asynchronous pattern brokers input and output through Amazon S3. Instance selection (ml.g4dn.xlarge for cost, ml.g5.2xlarge for headroom) and the required GPU AMI pin apply to both, and you scale throughput by adding instances rather than concurrency. The request/response sequence for each endpoint type is shown in its walkthrough section.
Prerequisites
- An AWS account and an Amazon SageMaker AI execution role that can create_model ,create_endpoint , and (for asynchronous inference) read and write S3.
- GPU service quota for your endpoint instance type (for example, ml.g4dn.xlarge orml.g5.2xlarge ).
- The WhisperX DLC image URI from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) (for example, 763104351884.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/whisperx:3.8.6-cu128-amzn2023-sagemaker ).
- For asynchronous inference, an S3 bucket whose name contains “sagemaker.” The default AmazonSageMakerFullAccess policy grants S3 access only to such buckets.
A complete, runnable JupyterLab notebook that walks through these steps end to end is available in the AWS Samples repository. You can run it in Amazon SageMaker AI Studio against your own audio.
Walkthrough: Real-time endpoint
The real-time endpoint returns the transcript in the same synchronous call. Use it for short clips that comfortably finish within the 60-second cap. Figure 1 is a sequence diagram that traces a single real-time request end to end, from the client call through in-container transcription to the inline transcript.
Reading the sequence end to end: the client assembles a multipart/form-data body (the audio as the file part plus fields such as language, diarize, and word-level timestamp granularity) and calls InvokeEndpoint. Amazon SageMaker AI forwards the request to the container on port 8080, passing the ContentType and its multipart boundary through unchanged. Inside the container, WhisperX runs voice-activity detection and batched Whisper transcription, wav2vec2 forced alignment for per-word timestamps, and speaker diarization to label who is speaking. It then serializes the result. The runtime returns the transcript (segments, words with timestamps, and speaker labels) inline to the client, which must complete within the Amazon SageMaker AI 60-second response cap.
Create the model and endpoint config
Register the WhisperX DLC as a model, where IMAGE_URI points at the WhisperX DLC in Amazon ECR, then create an endpoint config. On every GPU variant, you must set InferenceAmiVersion to al2-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-3-1. Without this pin, the endpoint fails to start with a zero-log CannotStartContainerError. Allow a generous startup health-check timeout because the weights load lazily.
Invoke with diarization and word timestamps
Build a multipart/form-data body with the audio as the file part and fields such as language=en, diarize=true, and response_format=verbose_json. The response contains segments, per-word timestamps, and speaker labels.
The example GitHub repository uses a public-domain recording of the air traffic control (ATC) communications from US Airways Flight 1549, the 2009 “Miracle on the Hudson” emergency landing. It’s a real multi-party radio exchange with background noise, radio compression, and rapid callsign and frequency readouts. Those conditions make it a strong test of transcription accuracy, word-level timestamps, and speaker diarization. The full approximately 3-minute recording is sent to the asynchronous endpoint, and a 40-second segment to the real-time endpoint.
Running this against a 40-second segment of the source audio returns the following diarized, word-timed transcript:
Walkthrough: Asynchronous endpoint
The asynchronous endpoint removes the 60-second cap and is the recommended path for long audio. Input and output are brokered through Amazon S3, and you poll for the result. Figure 2 is a sequence diagram that traces the full asynchronous lifecycle, from the S3 upload and InvokeEndpointAsync call through container processing to the S3 output and failure paths.
Reading the sequence end to end: the client uploads the multipart body to Amazon S3 and calls InvokeEndpointAsync with the object’s InputLocation. It receives an OutputLocation and FailureLocation immediately rather than waiting for the transcript. Amazon SageMaker AI reads the input from Amazon S3 and forwards it to the container on port 8080. There, the same voice-activity detection, batched transcription, forced-alignment, and diarization pipeline runs, one request per container. On success, the container writes the transcript to the S3 output path, or an error document to the failure path. The client polls the output path for the result and checks the failure path, so a failed job surfaces an error instead of looping indefinitely. Because work is brokered through Amazon S3, this path isn’t bound by the 60-second cap and suits long audio.
Create the asynchronous endpoint config
The only structural difference from the real-time endpoint is the endpoint config: it adds an AsyncInferenceConfig with an S3 OutputPath and S3FailurePath. Set MaxConcurrentInvocationsPerInstance=1 to match the container’s single-worker limit, and keep the same InferenceAmiVersion pin. IMAGE_URI is the same WhisperX DLC used for the real-time endpoint.
The rest of the workflow is identical to the real-time walkthrough. Building the multipart/form-data request (the build_multipart helper and transcription fields) is unchanged. You submit it with invoke_endpoint_async by S3 reference instead of invoke_endpoint, then read the transcript from the OutputLocation and check the FailureLocation. Cleanup is also the same.
Submitting the full approximately 3-minute recording to the asynchronous endpoint returns the following transcript (first and last five lines shown):
Cleaning up
A GPU endpoint bills continuously until you delete it. When you are done, delete the endpoint, endpoint config, and model for both endpoints, and remove any S3 input and output artifacts you no longer need.
Best practices and production considerations
- Pin the GPU AMI – Always set InferenceAmiVersion=al2-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-3-1 on GPU variants. The default host AMI ships drivers that fail to start this CUDA 12.8 image.
- Scale by instances, not concurrency – Inference is serialized to one request per container. Set MaxConcurrentInvocationsPerInstance=1 on asynchronous endpoints and add instances or containers for throughput.
- Autoscale asynchronous endpoints to zero – For bursty batch workloads, scale the asynchronous endpoint to zero instances when idle to cut cost, and use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) completion notifications instead of tight polling.
- Right-size the GPU, and use instance pools for availability – Use ml.g4dn.xlarge (T4) for cost orml.g5.2xlarge (A10G) for headroom. To avoid insufficient-capacity errors, list up to five instance types in an Amazon SageMaker AI instance pool. It provisions the highest-priority type first and falls back automatically when capacity is unavailable.
- Secure the S3 artifacts – Turn on S3 Block Public Access, default SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS encryption, and BucketOwnerEnforced ownership on the asynchronous bucket. Scope the execution role to specific buckets and keys.
- Handle personally identifiable information (PII) responsibly – Transcripts of calls and meetings might contain sensitive data, so encrypt artifacts, restrict access, and apply redaction downstream using the word-level timestamps.
- Observe and retry – Monitor with Amazon CloudWatch, alarm on failures, and retry around the cold-start behavior described earlier. For deeper GPU and inference visibility, turn on the Amazon SageMaker AI detailed metrics and Insights dashboard on CloudWatch.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to deploy the AWS WhisperX Deep Learning Container to Amazon SageMaker AI for word-level, speaker-labeled transcription. We used a real-time endpoint for short interactive clips and an asynchronous endpoint for long, high-volume audio. We covered the production details that matter most: the required GPU AMI pin, single-request-per-container scaling, S3 bucket naming, and cost controls.
To go further, explore the WhisperX DLC deployment guide, review Amazon SageMaker AI asynchronous inference, and try the accompanying demo notebook against your own audio. You can also find the full working example in the AWS Samples GitHub repository.
Acknowledgements
The authors thank the AWS Deep Learning Containers and Amazon SageMaker AI teams for their technical review and contributions to the sample.

articles.title: Filtrado el diseño de los Galaxy Buds On, los primeros auriculares tipo clip de Samsung
articles.text:
Samsung planea lanzar nuevos auriculares con diseños que nunca antes había usado, y se han filtrado su diseño al completo. Según publica Android Headlines, el dispositivo en cuestión se lanzará al mercado bajo el nombre de Galaxy Buds On y son los primeros de la marca en adoptar un formato tipo clip.
De la mano de los Galaxy Buds On, Samsung pretende insertarse en un segmento de auriculares que ya tienen varios exponentes interesantes; entre tantos, los Huawei FreeClip 2. La cita publicación ha compartido dos imágenes del nuevo producto que parecen provenir del material de marketing oficial del fabricante coreano. Esto hace pensar que su presentación formal podría darse muy pronto.
Como todos los auriculares tipo clip, los Samsung Galaxy Buds On presentan un diseño que se compone de dos partes unidas por una banda que permite la sujeción con la oreja. Sobre las características técnicas puntuales del dispositivo todavía no hay demasiadas novedades. Aunque sí se rumoran algunas funciones interesantes a considerar.
Los Galaxy Buds On son auriculares open-ear, de modo que no se introducen en el canal auditivo. Samsung los dotaría de una tecnología de conducción de aire para dirigir el sonido hacia los oídos. Todavía no está claro si la empresa surcoreana planea dotarlos de algún tipo de cancelación activa del ruido, aunque sí se menciona la presencia de al menos un micrófono para realizar llamadas y disparar comandos de voz.
Así son los Galady Buds On, los auriculares tipo clip de Samsung
Más allá de la falta de precisiones técnicas de los Galaxy Buds On, se mencionan tres presuntas características a tener en cuenta. Por un lado, Samsung ofrecería soporte para el uso de asistentes de inteligencia artificial a través de los auriculares. No se especifica cuáles, pero es lógico pensar que la integración abarque tanto a Bixby como a Gemini.
Por otra parte, los Galaxy Buds On serían capaces de ajustar automáticamente el volumen dependiendo de las condiciones del entorno. Al ser auriculares de diseño abierto, Samsung implementaría esta función para contrarrestar un posible deterioro de la calidad de escucha cuando se usen en ambientes demasiado ruidosos.
Por último, Samsung dotaría a los Galaxy Buds On con soporte para gestos con la cabeza. Todavía no está claro si la función sería para responder o rechazar llamadas, o si también podría servir para concretar acciones sin tener que sacar el móvil del bolsillo.
Respecto del precio y la disponibilidad de estos auriculares, aún no hay novedades. Pero como ya dijimos, que las imágenes filtradas sean del material de marketing del producto hace pensar que se lanzará muy pronto. Estaremos atentos a cualquier novedad en tal sentido.

articles.title: Microsoft thinks its new Copilot ‘super app’ will be as influential as Office
articles.text:
After teasing its new Copilot “super app” last month, Microsoft is officially unveiling it today. The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents. As part of the launch, Microsoft is also rebranding Scout, the AI personal assistant it unveiled at Build earlier this year, as Autopilot.
Microsoft thinks its new Copilot ‘super app’ will be as influential as Office
The new Copilot merges AI chat, coding, and Autopilot agents.
This new Copilot app will have three tabs for Home, Code, and Autopilot, with Home combining Copilot Chat and Cowork together. It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.
“Home is where you get your bearings, keeping you grounded and moving forward: review recent activity, get suggestions on what Copilot can help with, and pick up work right where you left off,” explains Jared Spataro, chief marketing officer of AI at work at Microsoft.
The Code tab is the surprise addition to this so-called “super app,” and not one you’d typically associate with an app designed for knowledge workers. It will let anyone create an app, tracker, dashboard, or automation and share the results with colleagues as cloud-hosted internal apps. “Powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot, Code runs in a sandboxed environment and can be hosted securely within your tenant,” says Spataro.
Autopilot is a new addition to the Copilot experience, and one that Spataro describes as a “digital teammate.” Previously called Scout and available initially as a desktop app, Autopilot is the cloud equivalent that enables a personal AI assistant to keep running while you’re asleep. Like many other AI agents, Autopilot has its own cloud computer instance that can be tasked to do things like watch Teams channels, run recurring work tasks, or handle follow-ups.
The real difference against some other AI agents is that Microsoft has made Autopilot enterprise grade, appealing to businesses that rely on its Office and identity management suites. “Autopilot lives in your tenant with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace, and it’s built on Microsoft IQ so it understands how your organization actually works,” says Spataro. “It shows up where people already work — Teams, Outlook, chats, channels, and documents — so you can @mention it like a colleague, with permissions, audit, and governance behind it.”
All of this focus on enterprise security and control is a big part of Microsoft trying to sell businesses on Copilot once again. The difference this time around is that how much a business pays for Copilot will depend on what their employees are doing. Microsoft is using usage-based billing for the Cowork, Code, and Autopilot parts of this new Copilot app, so any long-running agentic capabilities or usage of models like Astra and Fable will be billed based on usage.
The regular Copilot license, known as a user subscription license, will give you Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams. Microsoft is using an auto model picker to match the model for each task, but IT admins will need to use Microsoft’s new FinOps for AI to manage AI spend and ensure any agentic usage doesn’t get out of control.
With this new Copilot app it feels like Microsoft has finally settled on a formula for its AI assistant. The company has redesigned Copilot plenty of times since its introduction as a chatbot inside Bing, and this latest three-tab design builds on the combination of its two separate consumer and commercial Copilot apps last month. That’s a long-overdue change, alongside some big AI leadership shapeups that helped finally appoint a single Copilot boss for the first time.
The new Home and Code tabs will start rolling out to Microsoft’s Frontier program for early access AI features “in the coming weeks,” and Autopilot will go into private preview later this month. Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.
It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest. This new Copilot app isn’t really designed to compete with things like Muse, and Microsoft is now calling it “the AI built for work.” It’s even comparing it to how influential Office was on productivity. “Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” says Spataro.
That might well be Microsoft’s goal, but there’s a lot more competition in this AI era than there ever was in the PC era. Microsoft has certainly fallen behind the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Meta, and it’ll be interesting to see if “the AI built for work” is enough to help it catch up.
