articles.title: Cursor acquired Firetiger. A month later, it launched a bot that tracks code changes from PR to production.
articles.text:
Cursor acquired Firetiger. A month later, it launched a bot that tracks code changes from PR to production.
We all know that producing code is easier than ever thanks to the abundance of AI coding tools and agents. The harder part undoubtedly comes after that code is written: making sure changes are safe to ship, spotting regressions in production, and figuring out what went wrong.
And that’s why Cursor is introducing Rollouts, a new agent that follows code changes into production and monitors whether they behave as intended.
The Firetiger effect
The announcement comes a little over a month after SpaceX closed its bumper $60 billion acquisition of Cursor, giving the AI coding company access to SpaceX’s vast GPU infrastructure as it develops its own models.
The day before that deal closed, however, Cursor quietly announced an acquisition of its own: it snapped up the team behind Firetiger, a three-year-old startup building AI agents that monitor software changes from pull request through deployment.
At the time, Firetiger co-founder and CEO Rustam Lalkaka argued that coding agents had dramatically reduced the effort involved in creating software changes, while doing little to reduce the risks involved in actually deploying them.
“Over the last two years, agentic coding has changed software dramatically,” Lalkaka wrote in a LinkedIn post following the deal’s announcement. “The cost of creating changes has dropped to near zero. The cost and risk of deploying them has stayed largely the same.”
Fast forward to today, and Lalkaka, now at Cursor, has unveiled the first fruits from that acquisition — including Rollouts. In a blog post published on Wednesday, Lalkaka notes that the new agent, or “bot” as the company calls it, is all about helping developers “get safe, reliable code into production faster.”
“Writing code is no longer the slow part,” Lalkaka writes. “What hasn’t sped up is everything after the PR goes up: making sure code is secure, watching the deploy, deciding whether a latency bump is real, figuring out which of eleven changes broke checkout.”
Rollouts is effectively Firetiger’s Change Monitors reborn inside Cursor, rebuilt using a tool dubbed Bot Development Kit. This kit, too, appears to be new from Cursor: an early-stage framework for building and serving Cursor bots and agents, published as the @cursor/bdk package on npm. Its documentation says developers can define agents using Markdown and TypeScript, with support for tools, skills, subagents, webhooks and scheduled runs.
Like Change Monitors before it, Rollouts starts working when a pull request opens. It examines the proposed code change, works out which systems could be affected, and produces a monitoring plan covering what the change is supposed to do, the risks it sees, the signals it intends to watch, and any holes in the available instrumentation. Developers can review and edit that plan before the code reaches production.
Once the change is deployed, Rollouts checks the resulting telemetry — including logs, metrics and traces — against that plan. Staging and production are assessed independently, with each deployment ultimately receiving one of three verdicts: verified healthy, regression detected or inconclusive.
That means a change could, for example, pass its checks in staging before Rollouts subsequently spots a problem when the same code reaches production.
If Rollouts does detect a regression, it can identify the change it suspects, alert the developer responsible and, depending on how it’s been configured, either open a revert pull request for review or hand the problem to a Cursor cloud agent to attempt a fix. There is still a human in the consequential part of that loop for now: Rollouts doesn’t merge fixes or roll back deployments by itself, though it can pause a progressive rollout.
Lalkaka notes that Rollouts is already capable of picking up problems limited to a particular endpoint or region before they trigger a broader alert, while it can also distinguish expected changes in behavior from genuine regressions.
Also “coming soon” to Rollouts, according to Cursor, is an integration with feature flags so it can directly adapt the traffic reaching a change, while support for release trains and deployment freezes is also in the works.
Enter Security Reviewer
Alongside Rollouts, Cursor is also introducing an upgraded Security Reviewer bot, which first appeared in beta back in April.
At launch, the bot could automatically inspect pull requests for security vulnerabilities, authentication regressions, privacy and data-handling risks, agent tool auto-approvals, and prompt-injection attacks, leaving findings alongside the relevant code.
As with Rollouts, the idea is that developers don’t have to remember to invoke it manually: Security Reviewer can be set to run whenever a new pull request is opened.
In its current guise, Security Reviewer analyzes pull requests in the context of the wider codebase, with a focus on exploitable issues such as injection flaws and broken authentication, and returns a severity rating, attack path and proposed fix.
“Security Review reads code the way a security engineer does,” Lalkaka writes. “Where does user input enter, where does it end up, what does it pass through on the way.”
“Security Review reads code the way a security engineer does.”
He says that things have sped up considerably, too: average review time has fallen 21%, from 4.8 minutes to 3.8, while developer acceptance of its comments has risen from roughly 45–50% to 60–70%.
Both Rollouts and Security Reviewer are available through Cursor’s Automations tab for customers on its Teams and Enterprise plans.
The Origin story
Digging into the nuts and bolts of Rollouts reveals how it might serve as a boon for Cursor as it builds out Origin, the fledgling Git-compatible code hosting platform it launched back in August.
Origin is essentially an effort to build an alternative to GitHub for an agent-heavy software development world. It remains early, with limited functionality, but Cursor has been clear that tighter integration with its own agents is supposed to become one of the main reasons to use it.
When Cursor announced the Firetiger acquisition last month, Maxime Prades on the Cursor product team noted in a blog post that the deal was part of a “broader investment in long-running, autonomous, context-aware agents for teams.”
And he pointed to Origin and Change Monitors as two examples of that investment.
“Agents that write code should also be able to tell whether it works in production,” Prades wrote. “Today, those systems are mostly separate. Cursor and Firetiger bring them closer together so an agent can ship a change, see how it behaves, and respond when something goes wrong.”
Rollouts offers an early glimpse of that. It can connect to either Origin or GitHub for source control, pull deployment events from continuous delivery systems, and use signals from Datadog and other telemetry providers. If it spots a regression, it can then pass the problem back to a Cursor cloud agent to investigate or attempt a fix.
Origin potentially gives Cursor a native home for more of that loop: its cloud agents can already create branches, commit and push code, and open pull requests against Origin repositories. Rollouts then adds information about what happened after.
That could become increasingly important as more companies take aim at GitHub’s central role in software development. Zed, for example, put Delta into public beta last week, with its own ideas about how source control should change for teams working heavily with agents.
Cursor also faces competition further downstream. Datadog’s Bits Release, launched in preview in June, similarly follows changes from pull request into production and checks telemetry for regressions. Harness has long offered automated deployment verification and rollback based on logs and metrics, while LaunchDarkly’s Guarded Rollouts can monitor feature releases for regressions and automatically reverse them.
What Cursor can potentially bring to the table is proximity: the coding agent, repository, pull request, security checks, and production feedback can all sit much closer together. Rollouts doesn’t require Origin — GitHub remains supported — but owning the forge gives Cursor more room to integrate those pieces over time. And that may prove more compelling than simply recreating GitHub’s existing feature set.

articles.title: The GPU Madness Has Come to This: 9070 XT vs. 5060 Ti 16GB
articles.text:
Good news, guys. I've saved up my dollarydoos and I'm finally ready to buy a new graphics card for playing all my favorite video games. So let's go shopping, shall we?
I've got around $1,200 to spend here in Australia, roughly $850 USD, though ideally we'd like to spend a little less. Let's aim for a mid-range GeForce GPU because we've heard over on Reddit that GeForce is better than Radeon, so that's probably correct. Clearly, we're off to a very sensible start.
The GeForce RTX 5060 Ti seems like what we're after, the 16GB model of course, because we might eventually play something other than Fortnite. You never know.
Wow, what's going on here? The last time we checked, admittedly earlier in the year, the 5060 Ti 16GB was priced around $750. Now they're starting at $1,050 and are mostly out of stock.
In fact, PC Case Gear has just a single model available, a PNY card for $1,049. Yikes. Bugger that, let's try Mwave. Here we go, $769. Nice. Wait, it's out of stock. Okay, $1,000, also out of stock. $1,049, finally one that's available, and it's another PNY model. Then there's the Asus Dual at $1,129. Man, it's rough out here.
Okay, so we know those Radeon GPUs aren't meant to be as good, but we're getting desperate, so let's take a look. Based on what we're seeing at local retailers, a GPU called the Radeon RX 9070 XT appears to be the direct competitor to the 5060 Ti 16GB. They're a little more expensive, but pricing is surprisingly similar, starting at $1,149 with plenty of models around $1,249. Hopefully it's not much slower than the GeForce GPU.
Just to make sure this isn't some bizarre Australian pricing anomaly, we also checked Newegg. There, the 5060 Ti 16GB starts at around $780, which means the 9070 XT is actually cheaper, with Radeon models starting at roughly $740. Both GPUs come with 16GB of VRAM, so we clearly need to see how they compare.
For that, we've benchmarked the Radeon RX 9070 XT and GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB across 52 games to see what gamers are actually getting for roughly an $800 budget overseas or around $1,200 in Australia. Rather than walk through all 52 games individually, we'll highlight some of the more interesting results before getting to the full performance summary and cost-per-frame analysis. Let's do it...
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D | 
| Motherboard | MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi [BIOS 7E49v1A4] Resizable BAR Enabled | 
| Memory | G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB DDR5-6000 CL30 [CL30-38-38-96] | 
| Graphics Card | Sapphire Radeon RX 9070 XT Pure MSI Ventus 2X RTX 5060 Ti 16GB | 
| ATX Case | MSI Prospect 700R | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 25H2 | 
| Display Driver | AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.8.1 GeForce Game Ready Driver 610.88 | 
Benchmarks
007 First Light
Starting with 007 First Light, we see the 9070 XT is 81% faster at 1440p using the Medium preset, with frame rates jumping from 67 fps on the RTX 5060 Ti to 121 fps on the Radeon GPU. That seems like quite a lot.
The 4K results are even worse for the GeForce GPU. Again using the Medium preset, the 9070 XT was 106% faster, taking performance from a measly 34 fps to a highly playable 70 fps.
Switching to the Ultra preset didn't help the RTX 5060 Ti all that much. The margins did come down, but even so, the 9070 XT was still 62% faster at 1440p and 78% faster at 4K. At native resolutions, the 5060 Ti is effectively limited to 1440p here, while 4K is a realistic option with the 9070 XT.
Spider-Man 2
Swinging into Spider-Man 2, the 9070 XT continues to flex on the 5060 Ti. At 1440p using the Very High preset, it averaged 130 fps compared with 81 fps on the 5060 Ti, a massive 60% performance advantage.
Even at 4K, the Radeon GPU remained rock-solid at 80 fps, making it 70% faster than the 5060 Ti, which managed just 47 fps.
Enabling the demanding Ray Tracing Ultimate mode brings frame rates down, but the hierarchy stays firmly in place. At 1440p, the 9070 XT delivered a playable 67 fps, making it 60% faster than the 5060 Ti's 42 fps. Then at 4K, the 9070 XT averaged 36 fps, giving it a 50% advantage over the 5060 Ti's cinematic 24 fps.
Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight
Moving over to Lego Batman, we see the bloodbath continue. At 1440p using the Medium preset, the 9070 XT pumps out 234 fps compared with 149 fps for the 5060 Ti, making the Radeon card a cool 57% faster. Bumping the resolution to 4K makes the Nvidia card's value proposition look even more embarrassing. The 9070 XT crushes it by an 88% margin, delivering a buttery-smooth 147 fps while the 5060 Ti trails far behind at just 78 fps.
Cranking the visuals up to the Epic preset gives the RTX 5060 Ti a slight breather in terms of the performance gap, but it still gets thoroughly outclassed. At 1440p, the Radeon GPU maintains a comfortable 40% lead, hitting 102 fps versus 73 fps for the GeForce GPU.
Pushing the resolution to 4K, the 9070 XT manages to scrape by with an almost 60 fps experience, making it 51% faster than the 5060 Ti's rather pathetic 39 fps. Ultimately, while 1440p is doable on both GPUs, anyone hoping for a decent native 4K experience here will be severely disappointed by the GeForce card.
Fortnite
Fortnite gives the RTX 5060 Ti its closest showing yet, at least in lightweight competitive settings. At 1440p using Performance Mode, the 9070 XT was just 14% faster, though that gap stretched to 30% at 4K.
However, once Unreal Engine 5's full graphical suite is unleashed using Epic Quality settings with ray tracing enabled, normal service resumes. At 1440p, the 9070 XT rendered 120 fps, making it 54% faster than the 5060 Ti's 78 fps. Then at 4K, AMD held a flat 50% lead at 66 fps versus 44 fps.
Forza Horizon 6
In Forza Horizon 6, the rasterized and ray-traced results tell an identical story of AMD dominance. Using the Extreme preset at 1440p, the 9070 XT was 65% faster, rendering 140 fps compared with the 5060 Ti's 85 fps.
Moving to 4K, the 9070 XT breezed past the 100 fps mark, while the 5060 Ti failed to maintain 60 fps, giving the Radeon GPU a 76% advantage.
Tossing ray tracing into the mix highlights the hardware gap even further. At 1440p, the 9070 XT remained 79% ahead with 75 fps versus 42 fps. At 4K, both GPUs struggled, but the 9070 XT's 43 fps was still 79% faster than the unplayable 24 fps produced by the RTX 5060 Ti. With some upscaling support, the Radeon GPU would at least be usable here.
Crimson Desert
Next up is Crimson Desert, where the 9070 XT maintains a commanding lead. Using the Medium preset at 1440p, the Radeon GPU averaged 103 fps compared with 67 fps for the 5060 Ti, a 54% performance advantage.
At 4K, the disparity widened considerably. The Radeon GPU cruised along at 66 fps for a 69% advantage, while the GeForce card stumbled into sub-40 fps territory at just 39 fps.
Enabling the Cinematic quality preset doesn't do Team Green any favors either. At 1440p, the 9070 XT remained 54% faster, rendering 86 fps against the 5060 Ti's 56 fps. Meanwhile, at 4K, the 9070 XT averaged a respectable 53 fps, beating the 5060 Ti's 32 fps by 66%. For a smooth visual showcase at maximum settings, the 5060 Ti clearly punches well below its inflated price point.
Ark: Survival Ascended
Unreal Engine 5 continues to take no prisoners, but the RTX 5060 Ti suffers a particularly grim fate here. At 1440p using the Medium preset, the 9070 XT delivered 70% greater performance, managing 51 fps while Nvidia's offering crawled along at just 30 fps.
Stepping up to 4K effectively turned the RTX 5060 Ti into a slideshow at 18 fps, whereas the Radeon GPU was 72% faster at 31 fps. That's not exactly lightning quick, but it is substantially better.
Things get downright comical with the Epic preset. At 1440p, the 9070 XT was 81% faster, and at 4K the gap widened to 83%, leaving the 5060 Ti choking at a miserable 12 fps average with single-digit 1% lows. Simply put, native rendering on the 5060 Ti is essentially unplayable across the board in this title. It's so bad, in fact, that most of these results wouldn't be made workable even with Ultra Performance DLSS thrown into the mix.
Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty
In Night City, traditionally a stronghold for Nvidia hardware, particularly with ray tracing enabled, the raw tier mismatch makes for some brutal viewing. At 1440p using the Ultra preset, the 9070 XT sat comfortably at 131 fps, giving it a massive 90% lead over the 5060 Ti's 69 fps. Stepping up to 4K widened the gap further to 103%, with the Radeon GPU maintaining a playable 63 fps average while the 5060 Ti stumbled along at just 31 fps.
Even with Ray Tracing Ultra engaged, the 5060 Ti simply lacks the horsepower to compete. At 1440p, the 9070 XT was nearly twice as fast, with a 96% performance advantage.
Native 4K proved punishing for both, but the 9070 XT's 26 fps still placed it 86% ahead of the 5060 Ti's slideshow-like 14 fps average.
Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl
Venturing into the Zone at native resolution yields another heavy round of defeats for the GeForce GPU. At 1440p using the Medium preset, the 9070 XT clocked in at 122 fps, 54% faster than the 5060 Ti's 79 fps, with the Radeon GPU's 1% lows even surpassing the GeForce card's average frame rate. At 4K, the Radeon GPU delivered a 63% uplift, managing 70 fps while the 5060 Ti fell flat at 43 fps.
Dialing the visuals up to Epic tightens things slightly, but the hierarchy remains unchanged. At 1440p, the 9070 XT stayed 52% ahead with 70 fps versus 46 fps.
At 4K, neither GPU is delivering a high-refresh experience, but the 9070 XT's 40 fps still outpaced the 5060 Ti's 26 fps by 54%.
Pragmata
Rounding out this portion of the testing with Pragmata, the Radeon GPU continues its dominant sweep. At 1440p using the Max Quality settings, the 9070 XT rendered 138 fps, outpacing the 5060 Ti's 89 fps by 55%. Moving to 4K pushed that lead to 63%, with AMD hitting a smooth 78 fps while Nvidia struggled to break 50 fps at 48 fps.
Enabling ray tracing barely slowed down the 9070 XT. At 1440p with full ray tracing, the Radeon GPU averaged 135 fps, enjoying a 63% advantage over the 5060 Ti's 83 fps.
Then at 4K, the 9070 XT averaged a solid 76 fps for a 69% margin over the 5060 Ti's 45 fps. With both GPUs selling for equivalent money, giving up more than 60% of your frame rate for the GeForce badge is a tough pill to swallow.
Arc Raiders
Finally, in Arc Raiders, we see some of the narrowest margins of the test suite, though the 9070 XT still wins in every configuration. Using Epic Quality with RT Static at 1440p, the Radeon GPU was 30% faster, extending that margin to 38% at 4K.
Stepping up to RT Epic at 1440p compressed the margin to its narrowest point at 24%. At 4K, the gap settled at 30%, with the 9070 XT reaching 133 fps while the 5060 Ti achieved 102 fps. Both cards provide high frame rates here, but you're still getting roughly a third more performance from the Radeon GPU for the same money.
Performance Summary: 52 Games
Looking at the massive 52-game average across mixed quality settings, the overall picture doesn't get any prettier for Nvidia. At 1440p, the Radeon RX 9070 XT pulls ahead by 62%, averaging 123 fps compared with the RTX 5060 Ti's 76 fps.
In fact, the Radeon card's 1% lows of 97 fps comfortably beat the GeForce card's average frame rate, highlighting just how wide the performance gulf really is.
Step up to 4K and the margin widens to 71% in AMD's favor. Here, the 9070 XT delivers a genuinely smooth 72 fps average, whereas the 5060 Ti is left struggling in the low 40s at just 42 fps, with its 1% lows dipping to 33 fps.
When essentially the same retail price gets you a card capable of smooth 4K gaming on one side and a GPU that's clearly better suited to 1440p on the other, the value equation for the 5060 Ti completely falls apart.
Cost Per Frame
Australian Dollars
To better illustrate the value equation, here's the cost-per-frame data based on current Australian retail pricing. Despite coming in $100 cheaper, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB still costs 48% more per frame based on our 1440p results and 57% more at 4K. That's crazy.
United States
But the situation is far worse in the United States, and we strongly suspect Australian pricing will catch up over the coming weeks, as retailers currently appear hesitant to restock RTX 5060 Ti cards at today's asking prices.
Over at Newegg, the 5060 Ti comes in 71% more expensive per frame based on our 1440p data and an insane 81% more expensive at 4K.
There's really not much more that needs to be said here.
The GeForce Tax Is Getting Ridiculous
It's hard to say when this madness will end, or even how much worse things might get. If we'd told you just a few months ago that the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB would soon cost as much as, or even more than, the Radeon RX 9070 XT, most of you probably would have laughed us out of the room. And we wouldn't blame you. It's hard to imagine, but here we are.
In part, these inflated prices are the result of the industry-wide memory shortage. The 9070 XT is now at least 23% above MSRP, though the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is a little over 80% above its MSRP. Both feature 16GB of VRAM, but the GeForce GPU uses GDDR7 memory whereas the 9070 XT still relies on GDDR6, so there are cost differences there.
Tying into this, Nvidia recently notified board partners that it was increasing prices for its GPU and memory bundles, which was quickly followed by significant price increases for GeForce graphics cards, as we've seen with the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. Exactly how much is the increase isn't publicly known. I have some off-the-record details, but it sounds as though they've added a bit extra on top, which would help explain how the 5060 Ti has ended up more than 80% above MSRP.
Nvidia is also able to get away with these extreme prices because of AI demand. That doesn't just mean data centers, which aren't buying GeForce gaming cards, but also users building systems for local AI workloads. Those buyers are helping soak up these hideously overpriced GeForce GPUs.
As I understand it, and please note that I am far from an expert on this AI stuff, there is significantly greater demand for the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB than the Radeon RX 9070 XT among users running AI workloads locally. As we've just seen, the RX 9070 XT is an extremely capable gaming GPU, and it actually offers more raw memory bandwidth than the RTX 5060 Ti despite using GDDR6 memory. Memory bandwidth can also be an important factor in AI workloads.
However, Nvidia remains the dominant choice for local AI builders. The disparity in demand largely comes down to software support, ecosystem maturity, and ease of use.
Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem remains one of the foundational software layers for modern AI development. New AI models, interfaces, fine-tuning tools, and GitHub projects are frequently developed, optimized, and tested on Nvidia hardware first. Some popular tools and inference frameworks also specifically target Nvidia GPUs.
The Radeon RX 9070 XT can be a compelling option for users willing to work within AMD's software ecosystem, particularly under Linux, where its raw performance and memory bandwidth can be put to good use. But for most local AI users, the RTX 5060 Ti remains the "safer bet" as it guarantees compatibility with upcoming AI tools, requires less troubleshooting, and dominates in image generation. For these reasons, Nvidia has been able to jack up pricing and keep selling GPUs, but in doing so fewer and fewer gamers are now going GeForce, not that Nvidia cares.
If you're building a gaming PC and want more than 8GB of VRAM, as it stands, Radeon is increasingly the only way to go. At these prices, paying the GeForce tax simply isn't worth it.

articles.title: Aderant builds intelligent ticket triage with Amazon Nova | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Aderant builds intelligent ticket triage with Amazon Nova
This guest post is co-written by Angela Mapes and Adam Walker of Aderant.
In this post, we share how Aderant, a global provider of business management software for the legal industry, built an intelligent ticket triage system using Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock. Aderant’s solution automates much of the context gathering, classification, routing, and knowledge enrichment required for support-ticket triage.
The Intelligent Ticket Analyzer supports Aderant’s 38-person SierraOps team, which operates Expert Sierra across 268 client environments globally. It reviews newly submitted, unassigned tickets during scheduled hourly processing cycles on business days. It gathers operational context from Jira, Confluence, Amazon Athena, and Microsoft SharePoint to recommend a team assignment and resolution starting point, and it automates approved routing and communication actions.
During the first 2.5 weeks of production, from June 30 through July 17, 2026, the analyzer reviewed 109 tickets and achieved approximately 96% routing accuracy. Based on the team’s measured pre-automation triage baseline, Aderant estimates that the system recovers 8–14 engineering hours per week at a total operating cost of less than $30 per month.
The deployment extends Aderant’s earlier AI journey from unified search and on-demand investigation with Amazon Quick to scheduled, autonomous operational workflows powered by Amazon Nova.
The challenge: Reduce operational toil without losing control
Aderant’s SierraOps team processes an average of 34–40 support tickets per week. Before automation, each ticket required 15–25 minutes of manual investigation before resolution work could begin. Engineers had to interpret the request, locate client-environment details, determine ownership, search documentation and ticket history, and then assign or redirect the work.
The cost was broader than triage time alone. Misrouted tickets could remain in the wrong queue until an engineer identified them, while less-experienced team members needed more time or senior-engineer guidance to find the right context and make routing decisions.
Aderant needed automated, repeatable investigative workflows so engineers could focus on complex troubleshooting, platform improvement, and proactive operations while preserving human review for lower-confidence decisions.
The solution: Autonomous ticket analysis with human safeguards using Amazon Nova
Aderant built the Intelligent Ticket Analyzer as a serverless workflow orchestrated by a single AWS Lambda function and triggered hourly on weekdays by Amazon EventBridge. For each unassigned ticket in the CloudOps queue, the solution follows five stages:
- Identify: Retrieve unassigned tickets from Jira.
- Enrich: Gather client metadata from Amazon Athena, relevant knowledge from Confluence and SharePoint, and comparable resolved tickets from Jira.
- Classify: Send the ticket and assembled context to Amazon Nova Lite through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API for structured classification and recommended next steps.
- Act: Post analysis and acknowledgments, reassign misrouted tickets, notify the appropriate Microsoft Teams channel, and apply predefined actions for support-resolvable scenarios.
- Observe and improve: Publish operational metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and route lower-confidence classifications to human review.
Routing and reassignment decisions can operate autonomously when confidence meets the configured threshold. Lower-confidence tickets are flagged for human review. The team monitors confidence, misroutes, and processing latency, reviews routing corrections weekly, and uses the findings to refine prompts and routing logic.
Why Amazon Nova
Aderant chose Amazon Nova Lite after evaluating multiple foundation models through Amazon Bedrock using real ticket data. Three factors drove the decision.
Operational specificity: In comparisons using the same ticket content, environment data, runbooks, and resolution history, the team found that Amazon Nova Lite extracted more specific resolution steps and correlated past issues more effectively than the other evaluated models.
Native AWS integration: Amazon Nova Lite integrates with the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, the AWS SDK, and the existing AWS environment, reducing the need for an additional external model provider or vendor contract.
Economics at ticket scale: The model’s cost profile made it practical to analyze routine tickets, not only high-priority cases. In the initial production period, total system cost remained under $30 per month and Bedrock inference cost remained under $1 per month.
Architecture
The following diagram shows the architecture of the Intelligent Ticket Analyzer. The data flow moves sequentially from left to right through seven stages, all deployed through a single AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) and AWS CloudFormation template.
Amazon EventBridge triggers AWS Lambda. The function retrieves credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, queries environment metadata through Amazon Athena, and calls Jira, Confluence, and Microsoft Graph APIs for ticket and knowledge context. Amazon Bedrock returns structured classification output from Amazon Nova Lite. Amazon DynamoDB supports cross-ticket pattern tracking, while Jira, Microsoft Teams, and Confluence receive the resulting actions and updates. Amazon CloudWatch provides operational monitoring.
Data boundary: The analyzer uses internal operational ticket data, operational metadata, and internal knowledge sources. It does not access, process, or store client matter data or client application business data.
Early operational impact
The first 2.5 weeks of production provided an early view of both accuracy and efficiency. Routing accuracy was measured by comparing the analyzer’s assignment with the team that ultimately resolved each ticket. Time savings were based on a four-week pre-deployment baseline of 15–25 minutes of manual triage per ticket.
| Metric | Early production result | 
| Production measurement period | June 30–July 17, 2026 | 
| Tickets analyzed | 109 | 
| Routing accuracy | Approximately 96% (4 misroutes) | 
| Average ticket volume | 34–40 per week | 
| Measured manual triage baseline | 15–25 minutes per ticket | 
| Estimated engineering time recovered | 8–14 hours per week | 
| Estimated monthly time recovered | 32–56 hours | 
| Total system cost | Under $30 per month | 
| Amazon Bedrock inference cost | Under $1 per month | 
The recovered capacity is redirected toward complex troubleshooting, infrastructure improvements, and proactive work requiring human judgment. These findings represent an early production period and should be read as initial operational results rather than a long-term performance benchmark.
Three production examples
Correcting a misrouted request 
         A ticket describing a 404 error on an Azure DevOps site arrived in the CloudOps AWS queue. The analyzer classified it as a CloudOps Azure issue, updated the team field, and notified the requester of the reroute.
Accelerating resolution readiness 
         For an after-hours remote-access configuration request, the analyzer combined client-environment data with a relevant Confluence article and posted the procedure as an internal comment. The engineer completed the task in under 30 minutes the next morning without additional research.
Extending expertise to newer engineers 
         For a deployment request requiring PowerShell scripts and service verification, the analyzer provided commands, expected outputs, troubleshooting guidance, and related references. The engineer resolved the request the same day without escalating to a senior engineer.
Turning recurring issues into reusable knowledge
The analyzer also detects recurring issue patterns across clients running the same software version. When the configured threshold is reached, the workflow records the pattern, updates a dedicated Confluence tracking page, monitors resolved tickets for confirmed fixes, and links future matching tickets to the documented resolution.
This creates a continuous knowledge loop: identify a recurring pattern, document it, capture the confirmed resolution, and make that resolution available to future tickets. The capability reduces repeated discovery work and helps operational knowledge become reusable across the team.
Accelerating onboarding and knowledge access
Before the analyzer, unfamiliar ticket types often required manual Confluence searches or guidance from senior engineers. The automated workflow now places client-environment context, matched knowledge articles, and recommended steps directly in the ticket before an engineer begins work.
This does not replace engineering judgment. It gives newer engineers a stronger starting point, helps them handle unfamiliar scenarios earlier in onboarding, and allows experienced engineers to spend more time on complex work.
Five weeks from concept to production
Aderant used progressive validation rather than moving directly to autonomous actions:
- Rules-based start: A Jira automation rule established the initial routing concept but could not incorporate AWS context, ticket history, or model reasoning.
- AI-assisted validation: The existing Amazon Quick CloudOps Helper agent demonstrated that operational data could support useful routing and resolution recommendations.
- Production build: The team implemented the workflow with AWS Lambda and Amazon Nova Lite. Kiro supported integration scaffolding, architecture validation, and test generation.
- Monitoring-only testing: The analyzer ran against live tickets for approximately two weeks while its classifications were compared with manual decisions and the prompts and routing logic were refined.
- Production launch: The solution went live June 30, 2026, five weeks after the initial concept.
Looking ahead
Deeper client-history analysis: Connect related tickets over time to provide a broader view of ongoing client work.
Improved knowledge matching: Evaluate Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for semantic matching when ticket and documentation terminology differ.
Layered AI support: Continue using the analyzer for scheduled triage while retaining the CloudOps Helper bot for deeper, on-demand investigation and follow-up questions.
Conclusion
Aderant’s Intelligent Ticket Analyzer shows how operations teams can move from AI-assisted search to governed automation. In its first 2.5 weeks of production, the system reviewed 109 tickets, achieved approximately 96% routing accuracy, and was estimated to recover 8–14 engineering hours each week while operating for less than $30 per month.
The central design choice was not to ask AI to replace engineers or independently solve every issue. Instead, Aderant applied Amazon Nova Lite to the repeatable investigative work that delayed resolution: assembling context, identifying relevant knowledge, detecting patterns, and routing work with a useful starting point. Human review remains part of the control model for lower-confidence decisions.
By combining autonomous triage, operational safeguards, and a reusable knowledge loop, Aderant created a scalable foundation for reducing operational toil and directing engineering capacity toward higher-value work.
Learn more about Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Nova.

articles.title: Efficient MoE Training for Biological Foundation Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
As language models grow, scaling dense architectures becomes increasingly expensive. In a dense transformer, every token passes through every layer, so adding capabilities increases computation for both training and inference.
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures take a different approach to scaling by using many subnetworks, or experts, while activating only a small subset for each token.
This tradeoff has made MoE architectures increasingly attractive to the large language model (LLM) community. They can scale model capacity more efficiently, but the benefits depend heavily on implementation. Fragmented expert computation can reduce GPU utilization. Routing adds communication overhead, and larger parameter footprints create memory and distributed-training challenges. NVIDIA Transformer Engine (TE) helps address these bottlenecks with optimized primitives for grouped expert computation, kernel fusion, and low-precision training. As biological foundation models grow in parameter count and sequence length, these primitives can improve GPU efficiency while expanding model capacity.
This tutorial shows how to put these techniques into practice with the NVIDIA BioNeMo MoE recipe and TE. You’ll see how GroupedLinear improves expert computation, MXFP8 reduces memory use, and the GroupedMLP kernel fuses quantization, SwiGLU, and routing-weight scaling. Together, these capabilities provide a practical reference for efficiently training MoE-based biological foundation models.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, you need:
- Familiarity with Python, PyTorch, and distributed training concepts
- An NVIDIA CUDA-enabled environment—you can use the linked Dockerfile or install the recipe requirements
- At least two GPUs for expert parallelism; NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs are required to use the fused MXFP8 GroupedMLP kernel
Challenge 1: Fragmented expert kernels
MoE models replace a single dense feed-forward block with multiple expert networks. A naive implementation, however, can trigger excessive kernel launches. For example, the Hugging Face baseline implementation iterates over all experts in a Python loop, with each expert triggering separate kernel launches.
for expert_idx, expert_layer in enumerate(self.experts):
    idx, top_x = torch.where(expert_mask[expert_idx])
    current_state = hidden_states[None, top_x].reshape(-1, hidden_dim)
    current_hidden = expert_layer(current_state) * routing_weights[top_x, idx, None]
    final_hidden_states.index_add_(0, top_x, current_hidden)
Grouped execution preserves the individual expert matrices but submits their work together. TE’s GroupedLinear applies multiple linear transformations in one call by gathering the expert weights and input tokens. Because each expert can receive a different number of tokens, GroupedLinear accepts per-expert token counts (split_sizes). It submits the local experts through the TE grouped GEMM path instead of launching one PyTorch Linear operation per expert, reducing launch and scheduling overhead.
Use GroupedLinear as follows. Each expert retains its own weight tensor (weight0, weight1, and so on), and the call accepts the per-expert token counts as an additional positional argument:
from transformer_engine.pytorch.ops import GroupedLinear
experts_gate_up = GroupedLinear(
    num_groups=num_local_experts,
    in_features=hidden_size,
    out_features=2 * intermediate_size,
    bias=False,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device="cuda",
)
gate_up_output = experts_gate_up(tokens, split_sizes)
Compared with the Python loop, this approach submits the gate-up projections as one grouped operation instead of multiple separate calls.
Hugging Face Transformers also provides grouped_mm. However, TE can fuse GroupedLinear with MXFP8 quantization, activation, routing-weight scaling, and intermediate data movement into a GroupedMLP kernel, as shown in the later sections.
Challenge 2: Large model size and activation memory
MoE architectures increase total parameter capacity, and genomics workloads often use long sequences, which puts pressure on activation memory during training. BF16 uses 16 bits to represent each model weight and activation.
The BioNeMo recipe uses TE to support FP8 and MXFP8 training, reducing memory use. Both formats represent weight and activation values with 8 bits instead of 16. The main difference between FP8 and MXFP8 is scaling granularity: MXFP8 assigns a scaling factor to each block of 32 consecutive values, helping preserve numerical range and accuracy. On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, MXFP8 is hardware-accelerated, enabling MXFP8 GEMMs to use specialized Tensor Core instructions. For details about MXFP8 and block scaling, see the Transformer Engine FP8 primer.
Challenge 3: Quantization overhead in low-precision training
Although most training computation uses 8-bit precision, the model retains its master weights in 16 bits. The training framework therefore adds quantization and dequantization steps to convert between formats. Quantization converts BF16 weights and activations to MXFP8 before the low-precision GEMM; dequantization converts the result back to the higher-precision format. A naive path performs these steps as separate operations, motivating the fused MLP path described next.
fp8_recipe = te_recipe.MXFP8BlockScaling()
model = TEMixtralMXFP8ForCausalLM(config, fp8_recipe=fp8_recipe, dispatcher=dispatcher)
The TE autocast API enables MXFP8 precision for the model’s forward and backward passes:
with te.autocast(enabled=True, recipe=self._fp8_recipe):
    for decoder_layer in self.layers:
        hidden_states = decoder_layer(hidden_states)
See the BioNeMo recipe for the complete code.
To use the fused MLP, import the Transformer Engine Sequential API to chain together gate_up, ScaledSwiGLU, and down. The API also folds dequantization into the fused path. ScaledSwiGLU combines the routing probabilities (“scales”) with the expert feed-forward network computations.
from transformer_engine.pytorch.ops import GroupedLinear, ScaledSwiGLU, Sequential
experts_ffn = Sequential(GroupedLinear(gate_up), ScaledSwiGLU(), GroupedLinear(down))
The TE Sequential API scans the operations and, when the pattern matches, replaces the GroupedLinear → ScaledSwiGLU → GroupedLinear sequence with a fused operation object: ForwardGroupedMLP_CuTeGEMMSwiGLU_MXFP8 for the forward pass and a matching fused backward operation. This reduces framework overhead, fuses the SwiGLU and probability-scaling work into the grouped MLP path, and avoids materializing some intermediate results.
Results
These are several of the optimizations in the BioNeMo recipe. In our training benchmark on eight NVIDIA B200 Tensor Core GPUs, the recipe delivered up to 2.21x the throughput of the Hugging Face baseline.
Run the recipe
Start with the two-GPU L0_sanity configuration to confirm that expert parallelism and the training environment work correctly:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 train_fsdp2_ep.py --config-name L0_sanity
After validation, scale to the Mixtral-8x7B configuration with expert parallelism (EP=8) and MXFP8 precision across eight GPUs:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train_fsdp2_ep.py --config-name L1_8x7B_ep checkpoint.ckpt_dir=/path/to/ckpt
Select BF16 or MXFP8 based on your GPU and memory requirements and set the data-parallel and expert-parallel sizes so their product equals the total GPU count. The recipe README includes launch, checkpoint, and benchmark commands.
Try the Mixtral Native Transformer Engine recipe in BioNeMo Recipes and learn more about the optimized MoE kernels in the NVIDIA Transformer Engine documentation.
Acknowledgments

articles.title: Cologne-based Metycle secures €131.7 million credit facility to scale secondary copper and aluminium supply | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Metycle, a Cologne-based supplier of secondary copper and aluminium, has secured a €131.7 million ($150 million) credit facility.
The credit facility was provided by Rivonia Road Capital, a California-headquartered private capital manager specialising in asset-backed lending. The credit facility comes after the company raised €14 million in Series A funding in February 2025. In December 2023, it announced the closure of its €4.7 million Seed funding round.
Daniel Zinn, co-founder and Managing Partner of Rivonia Road Capital, said, “We are proud to support Metycle’s next phase of growth. The company has built a differentiated platform that brings greater transparency, reliability and efficiency to the global recycled metals market, while helping meet growing demand for sustainable raw materials.
“We have been particularly impressed by the management team’s deep industry expertise, disciplined execution and clear vision for scaling the business.
Alongside Rivonia Road Capital, Metycle’s investors and financing partners include 2150, which led its Series A round, Project A, Partech, Market One Capital, Dutch Founders Fund, Crédit Agricole Leasing & Factoring, and SCCF.
Founded in 2022 by Rafael Suchan and Sebastian Brenner, Metycle is a vertically integrated secondary metals company that buys, upgrades and supplies copper, aluminium and other non-ferrous metals to industrial customers globally. The company says it has traded more than €103 million ($120 million) worth of secondary metals over the past 12 months, a growth of 150% versus the prior year, with a team present in 15 countries.
Its business is built on three pillars: a global trading operation that manages sourcing, contracts and risk; SmartSorting Hubs that use AI-enabled sorting, mechanical separation and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy to convert mixed scrap into feedstock matched to buyer specifications; and TrustTrack, a digital layer that links records on material origin, quality, processing and logistics to each batch and trade. Metycle’s first SmartSorting Hub is located in Maasmechelen, Belgium.
Metycle argues that demand for secondary metals is not the constraint holding back the market, but predictability is. It points to the central role of copper and aluminium in electrification, power grids, data centre infrastructure and manufacturing, arguing that reliable secondary supply can enable material security while primary mine supply takes years to develop.
Despite its significance, the secondary metals market remains fragmented, with inconsistent specifications and documentation that make transactions hard to standardise, verify, and finance at scale, a gap it is trying to address with a combination of trading, physical processing, and digital verification.
“Our opportunity is to make secondary supply behave more like an industrial raw material: specified, traceable, and reliably delivered. This facility gives us the capacity to finance substantially more material through that system and serve customers at a much greater scale,” said Suchan, co-founder and CEO, Metycle.
The company says the facility will enable it to finance larger physical metal transactions, move greater volumes of recycled feedstock, and expand its supply to industrial buyers and smelters worldwide. The credit facility also gives it a repeatable framework to speed up execution for suppliers while delivering larger and more consistent flows of specified secondary feedstock to its industrial customers.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (September 24, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (September 24, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, September 24, 2026.
The tussle at the Tata Group continues while AI surges ahead, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
Tata tussle puts spotlight on Hanno’s TVS deal as filings reveal 29-year lease, build-to-suit structure
Regulatory filings reveal an arrangement in which TVS Motor is both the lessor of the underlying land and the customer for the facility Hanno is developing on it, with rental income projected to begin in November 2026.
Google Cloud pushes Gemini deeper into India’s businesses
Google Cloud is expanding its agentic AI push in India through partnerships that demonstrate how AI is moving from assistance to action. At its first ‘Let’s Talk AI’ media tour stop in Bengaluru on Thursday, the company highlighted collaborations with boAt, Cropin and Pine Labs across consumer hardware, agriculture and commerce.
How this woman entrepreneur is building a sustainable accessories brand with plant leather
Green Hermitage, founded by Gayatri Varun and Anubhav Pratap Rai, makes sustainable luxury accessories using plant-based materials.
Funding news
Enterprise AI startup Ema raises $77M in Series B round led by Creaegis
Enterprise AI startup Ema founded by former Google and Coinbase executive Surojit Chatterjee has raised $77 million in a Series B round of funding led by Creaegis.
ONYA raises Rs 12.5 crore to expand lab-grown diamond retail footprint
Lab-grown diamond jewellery startup ONYA has raised Rs 12.5 crore in a pre-Series A funding round led by Divisa Family Office, with existing investor Zeropearl VC doubling down on its initial investment. The company had earlier raised Rs 5.5 crore in seed funding. The new capital will be used to expand ONYA’s retail footprint, strengthen digital customer acquisition, enhance online personalisation and deepen research and development in product design and manufacturing.
Founded by Gaurav Choudhary and Himani Yadav, ONYA has established eight flagship stores across Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad within 20 months of launch. The company said it has reached a monthly recurring revenue of Rs 3.5 crore and plans to expand through company-owned and franchise stores.
ByteAsk raises $1M led by Y Combinator
ByteAsk, an AI coding startup founded by IIT Delhi graduates Anirudha Kulkarni and Pratyush Saini, has raised $1 million in pre-seed funding from Y Combinator, Entrepreneur First and angel investors from global quantitative trading firms.
Founded in June 2026 and headquartered in San Francisco, the company operates across the US and India and is developing AI coding agents specifically for C and C++. ByteAsk is targeting developers working in defence, aerospace, robotics, high-frequency trading, finance, automotive and semiconductor industries, where reliability and performance are critical.
The company has also been selected for Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 batch. The founders previously built legal AI startup LawSutra AI, which was acquired by Manupatra within four months of its launch.
Nuvah raises Rs 4 Cr from angel investors
Nuvah, a technology-led footwear startup focused on comfort-engineered heels, has raised Rs 4 crore in a pre-seed angel round from investors including Amit Jain, Shantanu Deshpande and Ishendra Agarwal.
Founded in October 2025 by Avni Jain, an IIM Ahmedabad alumna, the company plans to use the capital for research and development, advancing its proprietary comfort technology and testing go-to-market strategies. Nuvah’s core technology, SteadyForm, is a proprietary footbed designed to respond dynamically to shifting pressure across the foot.
Other news
Pine Labs to deploy 10 lakh soundboxes across India
Digital payments company Pine Labs has announced a strategic investment to deploy 10 lakh soundboxes across India as it seeks to strengthen the country’s digital payments infrastructure. The company said the initiative comes as UPI and other digital payment methods increasingly move beyond small-ticket transactions into new markets and business segments.
Pine Labs aims to use the rollout to deepen UPI adoption while supporting merchants participating in India’s digital commerce growth. Its cloud-based soundboxes provide real-time audio confirmation of payment transactions and support remote device management, over-the-air software updates and centralised monitoring.
CEO B Amrish Rau said the company intends to reinvest in the payments ecosystem as new monetisation opportunities emerge. Pine Labs operates a commerce technology platform spanning payments, issuing, credit and fintech solutions.
Nykaa partners with L’Oreal VC arm to invest in Indian BPC startups
Nykaa and BOLD (Business Opportunities for L’Oréal Development), the corporate venture capital fund of L’Oréal, have announced a collaboration to jointly invest in high-growth Indian beauty and personal care brands.
Through the collaboration, BOLD and Nykaa will take minority stakes in emerging Indian beauty and wellness brands with strong consumer traction and distinctive propositions. Such investments will be purely financial and minority in nature, where founders retain full ownership control and continue to run their businesses independently, with their own teams, culture, and creative direction.
BOLD and Nykaa will act as long-term partners beyond capital to the brands they back, offering mentorship, guidance, and the opportunity to benefit from L’Oréal’s global beauty expertise, alongside Nykaa’s deep omnichannel retail network and consumer ecosystem understanding. The intent is to help ambitious Indian beauty founders scale faster and build enduring brands for India & the world.
Gupshup launches Agentic AI solution for real estate
Conversational AI platform Gupshup has launched an Agentic AI solution for the real estate sector, designed to support customers throughout the property buying journey. The solution combines agentic AI, structured workflows and integrations with property, inventory and CRM systems, enabling prospective buyers to discover properties, ask questions, share requirements and take actions through WhatsApp and voice.
The system can gather details such as budget, preferred location, property type and purchase timeline before qualifying leads and triggering the next sales step.
Customers can also download brochures, request callbacks, schedule appointments and connect with sales representatives. Developers can extend the platform to post-sales services including maintenance requests and document access. Gupshup said the solution is available globally and supports regional languages and dialects.
Imagine Learning opens Bengaluru technology and product centre
US-based education company Imagine Learning has opened a new centre in Bengaluru as part of its long-term investment in India and expansion of its global product and technology capabilities.
The centre will support hiring across software engineering, product, AI, data science, cloud and platform engineering, quality engineering and cybersecurity. India-based teams will work on products and platforms used by educators globally. The company said Bengaluru’s technology and AI ecosystem provides an opportunity to build an integrated product and technology organisation.
Imagine Learning develops K–12 curriculum and learning solutions and serves more than 18 million students, two million teachers and 38,000 schools in the US. Its Bengaluru operation will also contribute to the company’s Curriculum-Informed AI approach, which combines AI with curriculum content, academic standards and research-backed instructional practices.
Fuel Cycle opens Navi Mumbai GCC for AI and product development
US-based AI-powered consumer insights platform Fuel Cycle has opened a Global Capability Centre in Navi Mumbai, marking an expansion of its global technology and product operations. Located in Vashi, the centre will initially have capacity for 50 employees, with plans to scale over the coming quarters. The GCC will serve as a hub for engineering, artificial intelligence and product development and will work with Fuel Cycle teams in the US and other global markets.
The company said the centre will contribute to core product development while strengthening its engineering and data infrastructure. Hiring is expected across AI and machine learning, data engineering, product engineering, UX, research technology and cloud functions. Fuel Cycle said the expansion reflects its focus on using India’s technology and AI talent to build products for a global customer base.
Mythic AI launches Bengaluru centre to expand AI chip engineering
Semiconductor company Mythic AI has launched a Bengaluru Centre of Excellence as part of its India expansion, with plans to build an AI chip development team and expand its workforce. The company develops analog compute-in-memory technology designed for energy-efficient AI inference.
Its Vanguard platform combines analog and digital computing on a single chiplet and is targeted at applications including automotive ADAS, defence and edge AI. Mythic said its Bengaluru team will contribute across architecture, front-end design, physical design and design-for-test, while also advancing analog and digital chiplet integration.
The company plans to quadruple its India workforce by the first quarter of 2027 and eventually expand the team into product development, testing, systems engineering and intelligent sensing chips. The move deepens Mythic’s engagement with India’s semiconductor and AI ecosystem.
CHRIST University, Salesforce set up AI Innovation Lab
CHRIST (Deemed to be University) has partnered with Salesforce to establish the Salesforce AI Innovation Lab and Academia Centre of Excellence. The initiative will give students and faculty hands-on exposure to agentic AI solutions, enterprise workflows and Salesforce technologies including Agentforce, Data 360 and Tableau Next. Through Salesforce’s Trailhead platform, learners will also receive access to role-based training, learning pathways and professional credentials.
The university said the collaboration will strengthen interdisciplinary research, entrepreneurship and industry-oriented learning while supporting its AI Vision 2030. The partnership is aimed at bridging the gap between classroom education and enterprise technology requirements. CHRIST University has more than 40,000 students and nearly 5,000 faculty members across its campuses in India.
AutoMovers Group lines up Rs 500 crore investment plans
AutoMovers Group, a multi-brand automotive retail company, has announced a Rs 500 crore investment plan for the next three years, starting Q1 FY 2026-27. With more than Rs 200 crore already invested in CAPEX, the company is now planning the next phase of expansion, with a focus on strengthening its sales and service network, and expanding its manufacturing capacity. The plan comes as the company aims to support growing customer demand while building a larger and more efficient automotive network across key markets.
The Rs 500 crore investment will be spread across four key areas - Rs 150 crore will go towards CAPEX expansion, including new workshops, and authorised service outlets. Another Rs 150 crore will be used to increase the inventory of commercial and passenger vehicles, taking the total stock capacity to more than 2,000 vehicles. Of the remaining Rs 200 crore, Rs 100 crore will be kept as a reserve for working capital and future expansion, while the other Rs 100 crore will be used to expand the trailer manufacturing facility in Lucknow.
Offgrid Energy Labs signs MoU with Keele University of UK
India-origin deep-tech energy storage company Offgrid Energy Labs has signed an MoU with Keele University in the UK to deploy its ZincGel long-duration energy storage technology on the university campus. The pilot will be installed at Keele’s Low Carbon Energy Generation Park and will use batteries manufactured at Offgrid’s facility in Hampshire.
The project is expected to assess the technology’s ability to store around 1 MWh of surplus renewable energy each month while evaluating safety, depth of discharge and round-trip performance. ZincGel uses proprietary zinc-bromine chemistry and is designed for six- to 16-hour discharge durations. Unlike lithium-based systems, the technology uses zinc and bromine and is designed to be non-flammable. The project could pave the way for a larger multi-MWh deployment at Keele.
Cognizant, Cognition report AI-led gains at Odyssey Logistics
Cognizant and Cognition have announced production results from autonomous AI engineering work at logistics company Odyssey Logistics using Cognition’s Devin AI software engineer. A seven-member Cognizant team used Devin to convert legacy Microsoft Access and Visual Basic for Applications forms into cloud-native applications while generating tests, deployment pipelines and documentation.
The project recorded a roughly one-third increase in delivery throughput and a 37% net cost saving compared with the conventional approach, according to the companies. Cognizant said it has trained more than 3,000 associates on Devin and that its own engineering work has seen more than a 50% reduction in time to release-ready code.
The collaboration has also expanded into modernisation, quality engineering and cybersecurity offerings. Cognizant and Cognition plan to explore additional applications across software development and maintenance.
PayGlocal gets IFSCA approval for GIFT-IFSC payments subsidiary
Cross-border payments company PayGlocal has received in-principle approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority to establish a wholly owned subsidiary as a Payment Service Provider in GIFT-IFSC. The approval covers account issuance, including e-money accounts, cross-border money transfers and merchant acquisition.
PayGlocal had earlier received final RBI authorisation to operate as a Payment Aggregator for cross-border inward and outward transactions and has also registered as a Money Services Business with the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. The company said the GIFT City presence will provide a regulated base for developing payment capabilities aimed at international businesses while continuing to build technology and operations from India. PayGlocal enables merchants to accept payments across 130-plus currencies and 40-plus global and local payment methods.
Nawgati crosses 3.5 million users on fuel-tech platform
Fuel-tech and mobility infrastructure platform Nawgati has crossed 3.5 million users on its fuelling app, which provides real-time information on fuel station queues, availability and pricing. The company said its platform addresses congestion at fuel stations, particularly for commercial drivers who can lose significant working time while waiting. Nawgati was founded in 2019 after its founders observed CNG cab drivers spending up to an hour a day in fuel queues.
The company has since expanded from a consumer information platform into a full-stack fuel retail data business focused on reducing congestion and improving fuel availability. Its Aaveg platform uses deep learning and real-time analytics to support fuel station operations and fleet management. Nawgati said it is now expanding internationally, beginning with the UAE and Sri Lanka.
Jaro Education plans to increase AI programmes to 25-30% of portfolio
Jaro Education is expanding its executive education portfolio in artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, with plans to increase the share of such programmes from around 15% currently to 25-30% by FY27. The company said its expanded offering will target CXOs, senior leaders, business professionals, working executives and technical talent.
Planned programmes will cover AI leadership, business applications, domain-specific use cases and emerging technologies. Jaro already offers programmes with institutions including IIT Roorkee, IISc Bengaluru, IIM Mumbai, IIT Bombay and IIT Delhi.
The company said the expansion reflects increasing demand for professionals who can apply AI across business functions as organisations move from experimentation towards broader enterprise adoption. The programmes will emphasise practical, career-oriented learning and industry-aligned outcomes.
Eco Hotels upgrades to Hotelogix multi-property management system
Eco Hotels and Resorts has upgraded to Hotelogix’s enterprise-grade multi-property management system to centralise operations across its hotel portfolio. The BSE-listed company currently operates nine properties in India and plans to add 10 more in the near future.
Hotelogix said the deployment will provide consolidated visibility across properties, centralised reporting and improved control over group-wide operations. Eco Hotels previously used a limited system that lacked centralised oversight and integration with key third-party tools, including channel management platforms. The new system is expected to help the company standardise processes, monitor performance and manage new properties more efficiently. Hotelogix provides cloud-based hotel technology solutions and said its systems are used by more than 12,000 hotels across over 100 countries.
ASMS, Ampivo to expand digital agriculture platform across rural network
Avio Smart Market Stack and Ampivo Smart Technologies are deepening their collaboration to introduce Ampivo’s digital agriculture platform, Agri Kisan Setu, across identified villages in ASMS’ rural network. The application, available in seven languages, provides farmers and rural stakeholders with access to farm management tools, agricultural market information, price discovery, buyer and seller connectivity, government scheme information and specialised services such as drone-based solutions.
Ampivo is also developing capabilities for carbon credits and digital measurement, reporting and verification, alongside workflows to help farmers identify relevant government schemes and entitlements. The initial collaboration will focus on onboarding farmers across selected ASMS network villages. The companies will subsequently evaluate deeper integration involving digital advisory, service delivery and eligible sustainability and carbon-credit programmes.
Truecaller partners with LinkedIn for professional identity verification
Truecaller has announced a global partnership with LinkedIn to bring professional identity information into its caller identification experience. The integration will allow users to connect their LinkedIn profiles with Truecaller and, where available, display verified professional information alongside caller details.
The companies said the initiative is aimed at providing additional context when people receive calls from individuals they have not previously met, including recruiters, suppliers and business contacts. New users can also use Login with LinkedIn to simplify account creation. Connecting a LinkedIn profile and displaying professional information on Truecaller remain optional.
The integration is currently available to Truecaller users on Android worldwide, with an iPhone rollout planned subsequently. Truecaller said its platform has more than 500 million active users globally, making caller identity a significant part of its communication service.
iThrive appoints former client services head Saloni Kulkarni to board
Functional medicine company iThrive has appointed Saloni Kulkarni, its former head of Client Services, to its Board of Directors. Kulkarni joined iThrive in 2021 as a Functional Nutritionist after completing her bachelor’s degree in nutrition and subsequently took on additional responsibilities within the company.
She will continue contributing to iThrive’s strategic direction, with a focus on strengthening its functional nutrition practice and advancing the organisation’s work in nutrition and wellness.
Founder and CEO Mugdha Pradhan said Kulkarni’s career progression reflects the opportunities the company seeks to create for women professionals. iThrive said the appointment also marks a milestone for its leadership structure, with its board currently represented entirely by women. Kulkarni will continue working on the company’s strategic and functional nutrition initiatives.
Qlik, ICT Academy renew partnership to reach one million students
Data and analytics company Qlik and ICT Academy have renewed their memorandum of understanding to expand data literacy, analytics and AI education to one million additional students. The collaboration will establish and expand Centres of Excellence, help educators incorporate data and AI concepts into curricula, and deliver student learning programmes, Learnathons and applied problem-solving challenges. The partnership has so far reached more than 200,000 students and educators.
Qlik and ICT Academy said the next phase will expand the model nationally and support qualifications and certifications that demonstrate workforce-relevant capabilities. India is the largest footprint of Qlik’s Academic Program in Asia Pacific, with more than 1,100 universities, colleges and institutions participating. The programme also operates five Centres of Excellence across Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai.
Mygate launches community-based carpooling feature
Community management platform Mygate has introduced a carpooling feature that allows residents to discover and coordinate shared rides with neighbours travelling along similar routes. The feature enables users to create recurring rides, specify destinations and available seats and share pickup information. Mygate said the service is designed to provide a more familiar environment for ride-sharing than platforms that connect strangers.
The feature was initially piloted across 50 communities, where more than 4,000 users participated during a 15-day period. Mygate estimates that if 20% of its 5.7 million residents use the service, approximately 18.2 crore litres of fuel could potentially be saved annually. The company currently serves more than 5.7 million homes across over 27,000 gated communities and plans to expand the carpooling service across its platform.
LTTS, Cognite partner to develop industrial AI solutions
L&T Technology Services has partnered with industrial AI company Cognite to develop and deliver AI and data solutions for asset-intensive industries. As part of the collaboration, LTTS has established a Cognite Centre of Excellence and certified an initial group of more than 50 engineers.
The companies will co-develop solutions for sectors including oil and gas, chemicals, LNG, consumer goods, mining and industrial manufacturing. The partnership combines LTTS’ engineering and asset lifecycle expertise with Cognite’s industrial AI and data capabilities. The companies have already begun a project with a global top-10 oil and gas company to transform a manual mechanical-integrity process into a contextualised digital workflow. LTTS and Cognite said the collaboration will support applications including digital twins, predictive maintenance and operational intelligence across industrial enterprises.
Procol unveils agentic AI command centre for procurement
Agentic AI procurement platform Procol is set to showcase a role-based command centre at DPW Amsterdam 2026 that enables procurement teams to initiate complete workflows through plain-language requests.
Powered by its Clara AI orchestration layer, the platform can coordinate sourcing, budget checks and approvals across systems including SAP Ariba, Coupa and Oracle without requiring data migration. Procol said early enterprise deployments have recorded up to 15% lower operational processing costs, an 80% reduction in procurement cycle times and a 99% decline in manual platform touchpoints. The system can interpret requests, identify suppliers, verify budgets and issue requests for quotations. In one example cited by the company, quote-comparison turnaround was reduced from 6.4 days to one day.
NETSCOUT adds MCP connectivity to Omnis AI Insights
NETSCOUT Systems has announced Model Context Protocol connectivity for its Omnis AI Insights solution, allowing AI assistants and agents to access AI-ready Smart Data on demand. The company said its Smart Data is generated using its Adaptive Service Intelligence technology, which extracts operational context from network data before it reaches downstream AI systems. NETSCOUT said the approach can reduce the volume and complexity of raw telemetry processing while providing AI models with richer operational evidence. The new capability also supports integrations with platforms including Splunk, ELK Stack, Datadog, ServiceNow and Dynatrace, extending existing network infrastructure investments.

articles.title: CyberPowerPC lands rare RTX 50-series Founders Edition cards in discounted Walmart rigs — complete RTX 5090 PC costs $2,400 less than a standalone GPU
articles.text:
CyberPowerPC lands rare RTX 50-series Founders Edition cards in discounted Walmart rigs — complete RTX 5090 PC costs $2,400 less than a standalone GPU
Now's your chance to get an RTX 50-series Founders Edition at a sane price.
Nvidia Founders Edition GPUs are often harder to come by compared to cards from AIB partners, and they’re typically sold on specific retail channels only. However, it seems that CyberPowerPC got its hands on these graphics cards, and you can now get them inside pre-built gaming PCs sold by the company on Walmart. These PCs are also on sale as part of the Nvidia GeForce Week from September 21 through 27 on the retail platform. Aside from coming with these coveted GPUs from Nvidia, these pre-built gaming PCs are also on a huge discount, giving gamers savings of $580 to over $1,300. Unfortunately, these units are only available in limited quantities, so we’re unsure how long stock will last.
Nvidia has recently sold Founders Edition GPUs in a pop-up retail store at QuakeCon 2026 while also having them available at the PAX West gaming convention in Seattle, Washington, earlier this month. The company calls these retail pop-up stores “Verified Priority Access IRL,” meaning only real people can buy the cards, which are sold at MSRP. The VPA program started with the launch of the RTX 4090 FE, but the company brought it back with the arrival of the RTX 5090 and RTX 5080 to help prevent scalping.
The aggressive discounts on these pre-builts suggest that CyberPowerPC acquired these Founders Edition GPUs at MSRP. The RTX 5070 FE PC with an Intel i7-14700KF, which had an SRP of $2,139.99, now only costs $1,549.00, offering savings of $590.99, while the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D version is priced at $1,599.00 — a $580.99 discount from its $2,179.99 regular price.
The RTX 5080 FE pre-builts offer bigger savings: the AMD Ryzen 7 version is now only $2,299.00, saving you $680.99 from its $2,979.99 SRP, while the Intel Core Ultra 9 option has its prices to $2,399.00 from $3,149.99 through its $750.99 discount. Finally, the RTX 5090 FE pre-built gaming PC has a regular price of $5,649.99 but is on sale at just $4,299.00, giving you $1,350.99 in savings.
These prices will let you get your hands on some of the best gaming GPUs on the market right now without breaking your wallet. According to the Tom’s Hardware GPU Price Tracker, the cheapest RTX 5090 is the Asus TUF Gaming RTX 5090, and it’s already priced higher on Amazon at $6,699.00, making this entire pre-built cheaper than that standalone GPU. While the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 GPUs in the list are cheaper than these CyberPowerPC units, you’re still getting a complete system with a modern processor and a PSU, plus RAM and an SSD, which are some of the most expensive components you can find today. You also don’t have to worry about other specifications — even though the listing does not mention the brands and models of the other components included in the gaming PCs, they’re still decently specced with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD (2TB for the RTX 5090 version). You’ll have to act quickly, though, as they seem to be selling out fast.
