articles.title: ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Review A New AMD EPYC 8005 Sorano Motherboard
articles.text:
A couple of months back AMD launched their EPYC 8005 “Sorano” lineup of processors, which brought AMD’s Zen 5 architecture to its mid-tier SP6 platform. With up to 84 CPU cores and 96 lanes of PCIe Gen5, Sorano is a balanced EPYC offering with all of the Zen 5 architecture’s features, just in a smaller serving. And as a replacement for AMD’s earlier EPYC 8004 “Siena” processors, Sorano is especially remarkable, as it replaces the former’s Zen 4c cores with full-fat Zen 5 cores, allowing Sorano to hit far greater performance levels.
While Sorano is fully backward compatible with existing SP6 motherboards after a BIOS update, a few board manufacturers have opted to launch new boards specifically to align with the newer SP6 EPYC processor, and ASRock Rack is among them. For Sorano, the company has released the plainly named SORANOD8-2L2T, a basic server and workstation motherboard that brings all of Sorano’s key features to bear.
| ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Key Specs |  | 
| Processor Family | AMD EPYC 8004/8005 | 
| Socket | SP6 | 
| Memory | 8x DDR5 RDIMM Slots (2DPC*) Max Speed: DDR5-5200 | 
| PCIe Slots | 4x PCIe x16 (Gen5 x16 Electrical) 1x PCIe x8 (Gen5 x8 Electrical) | 
| Storage | 2x M.2 22110/2280 (Gen5 x4) 2x MCIO x8 (Gen5 x8/SATA 6Gbps x8) | 
| Ethernet | 2x 10GbE (Intel X710-AT2) 2x 1GbE (Intel I210) | 
| Rear USB | 2x 5Gbps USB-A | 
| Front USB | 2x 5Gbps USB-A | 
| Video | VGA (DB15) | 
| BMC | ASPEED AST2600 | 
| Form Factor | “ATX-like” (12-inch x 10-inch) | 
The SORANOD8-2L2T is essentially an upgraded version of ASRock Rack’s earlier SIENAD8-2L2T, with a slightly larger board and minor I/O changes. In addition to exposing all of Sorano’s I/O for server use, the other notable aspect of the SORANOD8-2L2T is its networking capabilities. The “2L2T” in the name refers to the two pairs of network adapters built into the motherboard. It includes a pair of 10GbE adapters and a pair of 1GbE adapters, giving the motherboard strong network capabilities out of the box. As a result, the SORANOD8-2L2T is a simple yet highly flexible motherboard for server or workstation deployments.
ASRock Rack SORANOD8-2L2T Hardware Overview
ASRock Rack has a well-earned reputation for simple and rock-solid server motherboard designs, and the SORANOD8-2L2T lives up to that pedigree. Other than networking controllers, there is very little extra hardware on the motherboard. This is a board designed to run a CPU, run it well, and expose all of that I/O so that the server builder can do with it as they please.
In terms of size, the SORANOD8-2L2T is what ASRock Rack classifies as an “ATX-like” motherboard. With dimensions of 12-inches x 10-inches, the board is ever so slightly too wide to meet the ATX specification. Few cases should have an issue with this, especially as the even larger EEB form factor is routinely used in this space. But it is notable since it can present an issue in cases that accept a regulation ATX motherboard – and no larger.
As always with server boards, a good chunk of the SORANOD8-2L2T’s space is dominated by the CPU socket and RDIMM slots. While the SP6 socket is smaller than the mighty SP5 (with over 1000 fewer pins), it is by no means a small socket. And 8 RDIMM slots take up a good amount of space on their own.
Those 8 RDIMM slots are designed to be eye-catching, and for a good reason: SP6 is natively a 6-channel platform. So we would usually expect to see either 6 or 12 RDIMM slots on a motherboard, for 1DPC or 2DPC operation respectively. But for all of their SP6 motherboards, ASRock Rack has taken things in an interesting direction by installing 8 RDIMM slots, effectively making this a 2DPC-ish motherboard.
The RDIMM slot coloring, in turn, is meant to signify which channel each slot belongs to. The blue slots are all the first RDIMMs for their respective channels, and are the slots that should be filled first. Meanwhile the black RDIMM slots are the second RDIMM slots on two of SP6’s six channels, and as such need to be the last slots filled. Two-tone DIMM slots are nothing new, of course, but ASRock Rack’s unusual organization means that there will never be any doubt about which color is for the first RDIMM versus the second RDIMM.
As for the purpose behind 8 slots, it is meant to balance the memory capacity of the board versus how much size the RDIMM slots take up. A traditional 7 PCIe slot layout does not afford enough space for 12 DIMMs, but it does for 8. And thus this is the direction ASRock has gone, squeezing in an extra two RDIMM slots in order to increase the amount of memory the board can address to 2TB.
The trade-off, however, is that this means the SORANOD8-2L2T is meant to function like a 2DPC motherboard through and through, and that means taking the memory frequency penalty. While a 1DPC board can clock as high as DDR5-6400, the SORANOD8-2L2T tops out at DDR5-5200 in exchange for its extra memory capacity.
Memory matters aside, looking around the CPU socket and DIMM slots we find the usual collection of chokes and MOSFETs that make up the board’s VRM system. The MOSFETs are under some very basic heatsinks here. As SP6 chips top out at 225 Watts (and presumably no one is going to be throwing liquid nitrogen at them), the power delivery system does not need to be too exotic. By the same token, however, server boards are designed around significant airflow, so the heatsinks do not need to be massive to be fit for purpose.
Speaking of power, we find a trio of ATX12V connectors spread out over the board, and these are where the SORANOD8-2L2T draws its power from. Curiously, ASRock Rack has built two of them as vertical connectors, and a third as a right-angled connector. All three are necessary for the board’s operation, so they are functionally equivalent. Presumably, the right-angled connector is meant to better fit server vendors’ needs, though we have seen plenty of server boards without such an angled connector.
Being that this is a server board first and foremost, ASRock Rack also eschews a full 24-pin ATX connector. In its place is a simple 4-pin micro-fit connector that only provides signaling.
Since you do not get a standard ATX power header, you plug the 24-pin ATX power supply connector into the included adapter, and into the 4-pin connector on the motherboard. We tend to prefer full-size ATX connectors to this solution on larger boards, though in the case of the SORANOD8-2L2T, the edges of the board are already pretty packed.
Moving on, let us talk about I/O and storage expansion, as the SORANOD8-2L2T provides a lot of it.
First and foremost, ASRock Rack has equipped the board with 5 PCIe slots. Four of these are full PCIe Gen5 x16 slots, while the final is an open-ended PCIe Gen5 x8 slot. This accounts for 72 of SP6’s 96 PCI Gen5 slots right here, and provides a great deal of flexibility with PCIe expansion cards. All of the x16 slots are double-spaced, though using the x8 slot will cut into the space for the top slot.
The top slot is a particularly special slot here since, alongside PCIe (and CXL) connectivity, it can also be switched over to providing 16 SATA 6Gbs connections. This does require a special riser card – ASRock Rack recommends their own 1U2G-RB1U2SL-G4 – but in effect it allows switching the PCIe lanes over to SATA connections.
For more fixed storage needs, the SORANOD8-2L2T also provides for a pair of M.2 Gen5 x4 slots. Both of these slots are designed to accept either M.2 22110 or M.2 2280 SSDs, with movable standoffs used to adjust the slot.
As is usually the case for ASRock Rack motherboards, the company also provides for a pair of thumbscrews to secure the SSD slots. We cannot say enough nice things about how much we appreciate thumbscrews here.
For the final set of storage options, towards the top corner of the motherboard, ASRock Rack has placed a pair of MCIO x8 connectors. These connectors normally carry 8 lanes of PCIe Gen5 each (accounting for the final 16 lanes provided by the CPU), which in turn is normally split up among two EDSFF SSDs each. However, in a feature that is new to the SORANOD8-2L2T and sets it apart from its Siena predecessor, these MCIO slots can also be configured to carry SATA signaling instead. This converts each MCIO connector into an eight-port SATA 6Gbps host, allowing for up to (another) 16 SATA drives, ideal for high-density storage servers.
As for external I/O, the SORANOD8-2L2T goes heavy on Ethernet ports, and light on everything else.
On the rear I/O panel for the motherboard, we find no less than 5 different RJ45 ports. These cover a pair of 10GbE ports, a pair of 1GbE ports, and finally an IPMI management port.
Farthest to the left is the IPMI management port, which is attached to the ASPEED AST2600 BMC. The AST2600 continues to this day to be the most prevalent BMC we see in boards that cross our labs.
To the right of that, the stacked RJ45 ports are 1Gb Ethernet ports. These are hanging off of a pair of Intel I210 Ethernet controllers.
Meanwhile, farther to the right and spread out over two rows are the 10GbE ports. These are powered by an Intel X710-AT2 controller, which provides for full 10Gbps bandwidth in each port along with the ability to negotiate to 5Gbps, 2.5Gbps, 1Gbps, and lower speeds.
All of the network controllers, along with the BMC, are located under a heat sink at the edge of the board, behind the PCIe slots. None of these components is particularly hot, but the 10GbE controller in particular is just hot enough to require some extra cooling, which the low-profile heatsink supplies.
Finally, farthest to the right is an old-school DB15 VGA port, which is part of the BMC and provides video output from the management controller. Given that the SORANOD8-2L2T is a brand-new motherboard, it is a bit odd to see a VGA port in 2026, but even with the AST2600 supporting DisplayPort for digital displays, VGA still sees significant use in data centers.
For all of those Ethernet jacks, what you will not find on the SORANOD8-2L2T is much in the way of USB ports. The rear of the motherboard has only two USB ports, both 5Gbps USB-A ports.
For the front panel connector, there is a single 20-pin USB connector to provide another pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports.
For a server installation, this is fine, as it is rare for more than a couple of USB ports to ever be in use. It also means that although ASRock Rack pitches the SORANOD8-2L2T as both a server and a workstation motherboard, you would look to fill more USB connectivity via PCIe for the workstation role. This is very clearly a server motherboard first and foremost.
The number of fan headers further drives this point home. Towards the front edge of the motherboard, there are six 6-pin fan headers, with the 6-pin variant being something of an ASRock Rack specialty.
Next, let us get to the block diagram.

articles.title: AI-Powered Campaign Targets Hundreds of Online Retailers
articles.text:
A threat actor is using autonomous AI agents in an ongoing campaign targeting hundreds of online retailers, cybersecurity outfit Gambit reports.
Active since July, the campaign relies on three AI harnesses to automate the attack chain, including vulnerability research, exploitation, and orchestration.
“Between 10 and 15 September alone, 105 attack projects were launched, and at least 27 companies were compromised to varying degrees,” Gambit says.
The hackers stole information from over 600,000 unexpired credit cards from two of the compromised companies and injected skimmer scripts into five online stores.
Additionally, they gained some access to a Fortune 500 hospitality company and to three US firms, including an airline, a private industrial supplies distributor, and an online fashion retailer.
“The campaign goes back further, and has impacted at least tens of other companies since July 2026. Where access was achieved, it usually took less than a day, and in many cases just a few hours,” Gambit notes.
Open source AI tools for automation
Mounted by a Chinese-speaking, financially motivated threat actor, the campaign used the open source AI penetration testing tool Strix for vulnerability hunting. Between August 23 and 31, the attackers ran it 146 times in ‘deep mode’ against 138 hosts, through OpenRouter on GLM 5.2 and on DeepSeek v4 Pro.
The generated reports were then handed to the autonomous penetration testing engine Cairn, which was used to launch 105 attack projects between September 10 and 15 on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Gambit retrieved 48 of the attack reports, as the others were deleted.
“Each attack path was chosen by the harness in real time through extensive probing and exploitation attempts, resulting in dynamic and mostly different TTPs across victims,” Gambit notes.
For the third stage of the attack, the threat actor used the open source autonomous AI agent Hermes, which has persistent memory, self-written skills, a searchable session archive, and a web console, and supports scheduled jobs.
The adversary loaded a Chinese system persona and 121 skills, including 78 attack skills. Using Anthropic’s opus-4.6, Hermes handled orchestration, intrusions, tactical guidance, and direct hacking activities.
Gambit identified “1,951 prompts typed by the human across 260 sessions – only a few prompts per target. The human prompts are short instructions in Chinese, usually launching an attack, tasking the agent with a general next step, or what to do next after achieving access.”
600,000 credit cards stolen at marginal cost
The threat actor used a website traffic ranking service to select targets, focusing on shops running custom code. A human operator pasted 301 results into the console, but also handpicked at least two targets for which they already had an administrator password.
According to Gambit, at least 600,000 credit card records were stolen from two victim companies, including over 488,000 cards from the US.
The cybersecurity firm also identified a Hermes agent skill designed to delete the stolen card data from the victim’s Magento database. Additionally, the agent deleted a bicycle retailer’s backup tables after being instructed to erase staging tables created within the database.
As part of the campaign, the threat actor also focused on injecting skimmer scripts into online shops’ checkout pages. Gambit initially confirmed 19 victims. Working with security researcher Varys, it discovered over 100 additional infected websites.
The skimmer was typically appended to a JavaScript file present on the website, but the threat actors also deployed it as a script tag, inside the site’s Google tag block, in an AWS S3 bucket, in database content fields, in a Kubernetes initContainer, and in the cached page model of the checkout page.
“At a US wine retailer, the application redeploy restored the clean checkout bundle, so the operator left a cron job in the JBoss log directory that checked the file size every two minutes and appended the skimmer again whenever it was reverted,” Gambit notes.
What matters most about the campaign, the cybersecurity firm notes, is that the operator incurred marginal cost through the use of open source tooling. Based on the retrieved data, Gambit estimates a mean cost of $25.46 over 101 completed scans.
“This is a very concerning incident which demonstrates what the future of cyberattacks will more commonly look like. When the major AI players announced their agents had carried out breaches in testing scenarios, this caused serious concern, but given that these activities were not deliberately malicious, the incidents were contained,” Talion Cyber Security threat intelligence analyst Daniel Wilcock said.
“Here we are seeing something very different. AI was deliberately used to maliciously target organizations under the pretense of running a pen test. This wasn’t social engineering; it was a full-scale attack, where agents were prompted to probe for weaknesses, which they did persistently, and wipe clean any evidence of the assault,” Wilcock added.

articles.title: Dispositivo de manejo asistido de Comma.ai, bajo investigación: habría provocado cinco accidentes de tránsito
articles.text:
El regulador de seguridad automotriz de Estados Unidos abrió una investigación federal contra Comma.ai después de cinco choques que dejaron tres muertos y once heridos, todos vinculados a su sistema de manejo asistido con inteligencia artificial instalado como accesorio en autos ya existentes.
La Oficina de Investigación de Defectos (ODI, por sus siglas en inglés) dependiente de la Administración Nacional de Seguridad del Tráfico en las Carreteras (NHTSA, por su sigla en inglés, el organismo que regula la seguridad de los vehículos en el país), abrió el expediente el 21 de septiembre.
PUBLICIDAD
El foco está puesto en los casos en los que los autos equipados con los dispositivos de Comma.ai no detectaron o no respondieron a vehículos detenidos o que circulaban a baja velocidad en el mismo carril.
En cuatro de los cinco choques hubo heridos, algunos de gravedad. Dos de los siniestros fueron fatales y se cobraron tres vidas en total, según TechCrunch con base en los materiales de la investigación.
La investigación de la ODI se encuentra en una etapa preliminar, previa a cualquier determinación sobre si hubo una falla de diseño o un llamado a revisión. El organismo deberá establecer qué combinación de hardware y software estaba activa en cada uno de los cinco choques reportados.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo fue uno de los siniestros relacionados con la investigación
Uno de los choques fatales ocurrió en febrero de 2026 en el condado de Ascension Parish, Louisiana, Estados Unidos. Una Toyota RAV4 2022 que corría bajo FrogPilot, una versión modificada por terceros del software de Comma.ai, impactó contra un patrullero detenido de la policía de Gonzales (ciudad de Louisiana).
El vehículo policial estaba sin ocupantes, ubicado en el carril izquierdo con las luces de emergencia encendidas.
Dos pasajeros que viajaban en los asientos traseros de la Toyota murieron en el impacto, según los detalles publicados por la policía estatal de Louisiana, que coinciden con el reporte incluido en la base de datos de la NHTSA.
PUBLICIDAD
Comma.ai, fundada en 2015 por George Hotz, vende un dispositivo que se instala en autos de más de 325 modelos distintos y corre openpilot, un software de código abierto que controla el control de crucero adaptativo y el centrado automático de carril. La empresa compara sus funciones con las de Autopilot de Tesla.
El problema de las versiones modificadas del software de Comma.ai
La ODI señaló que algunos de los choques, incluido al menos uno de los fatales, podrían haber involucrado versiones modificadas del software oficial de Comma.ai. Esa distinción abre una pregunta regulatoria inédita para la industria del manejo asistido.
El propio sitio de Comma.ai advierte que el rendimiento de su control de crucero adaptativo puede verse afectado por “vehículos en el mismo carril que no están en movimiento” y que el sistema “está diseñado con límites” en maniobras de frenado abrupto.
PUBLICIDAD
La empresa también exige que los conductores estén siempre en condiciones de retomar el control manual del vehículo, ya sea pisando alguno de los pedales o presionando el botón de cancelación. El dispositivo incluye, además, un sistema de monitoreo por cámara que detecta si el conductor está distraído o somnoliento.
Comma.ai no respondió a los pedidos de comentario sobre la investigación. Hotz, que se alejó de la operación diaria de la empresa en 2022 pero sigue siendo uno de sus principales dueños, tampoco contestó las consultas, según TechCrunch.
El fundador Comma.ai ya tenía antecedentes con la NHTSA
Hotz ya había tenido un cruce previo con la NHTSA. En 2016, cuando el organismo pidió información sobre un dispositivo que la compañía planeaba lanzar, Hotz canceló ese producto y decidió publicar el software de manejo asistido como código abierto en lugar de venderlo como un sistema cerrado.
PUBLICIDAD
Esa decisión amplió la cantidad de desarrolladores que pudieron modificar el software con el paso de los años, pero complicó el trabajo de los investigadores, que ahora deben distinguir entre la versión oficial de Comma.ai y las variantes creadas por la comunidad, como FrogPilot.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Could AI threaten humanity? 8 Africans weigh the risks
articles.text:
Will AI kill us all?
It sounds like the plot of a science fiction movie, but in 2026, the question is being taken seriously by some of the people building the technology. As AI systems become more capable of reasoning and carrying out tasks with less human input, concerns are growing about what happens when humans can no longer fully control them.
Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, recently resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies are racing towards self-improving systems and “gambling with our lives.” OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki also warned that no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.
But this debate is not only about what happens in Silicon Valley. Africans are already using AI in their businesses and everyday lives, while local innovators are building with it and investors are putting money into the industry.
So we asked eight people across five groups —everyday users, educators, innovators, policy experts, and investors—one question: do you think AI could eventually become a threat to humanity, potentially even to the point of killing us all?
“Which AI is going to kill us exactly?” Sarah Pra, Ghana
Sarah Pra, a restaurant owner in Kumasi, Ghana, has heard the warnings and seen people talking about AI taking over and eventually killing humans. But the idea did not seem particularly convincing to her.
“Which AI is going to kill us exactly? Is it ChatGPT or Meta AI?” she asked, rhetorically.
She had seen the conversation on the short-form video-sharing platform, TikTok, but she was not buying it.
“How is the AI going to kill us, honestly?” she said. “They are all shouting that AI is going to kill us, but I have not seen where they showed me exactly how it is going to do it.”
For now, Pra’s experience with AI looks nothing like a science fiction apocalypse.
When she wants to learn how to cook something she has never made before, she used to turn to Google. Now she asks Meta AI or ChatGPT. She uses ChatGPT to help make flyers for her restaurant and turns to the tools for personal questions too.
“You don’t want to see my WhatsApp Meta AI or my ChatGPT history,” she said.
There is a contradiction at the heart of Pra’s relationship with AI: she does not trust it completely, but she has already made it part of her daily life.
“ChatGPT can lie,” she said. “I always take what I want from whatever it tells me and leave the rest.”
She has caught it giving her wrong information before, including advice about a food she wanted to cook. And while she has not worked out exactly what she would never share with an AI system, she knows there are limits.
“It is not human in any way,” she said. “So, not everything.”
For Pra, the threat is what people might choose to do with it.
She has seen AI used to create fake nude images of women and to spread false information about people. She worries about people using the technology to harm, but she sees that as a problem with its users rather than proof that AI itself is becoming dangerous.
“If anyone is using it to build anything bad, the owners of the AI should know what to do,” she said.
And if AI becomes substantially more capable? Pra would welcome more capable AI if it helped people do things more easily and quickly.
“If it can get better to help us do things easily and quickly, I will not mind,” she said.
“Artificial Intelligence was created to help the Natural Intelligence”, Elijah, Nigeria
Elijah Akuma, a master’s student at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, a public university in Enugu state, eastern Nigeria, is not convinced that AI will kill humanity either.
To him, the technology is still fundamentally a human creation and therefore limited by the people who build and use it.
“AI was made by man; every good product has its deficiencies too,” he said. “But to the point of AI killing us all is unrealistic.”
Akuma is a writer, researcher and teacher, and AI has become part of how he works. He uses it to test ideas, criticise his drafts and suggest ways to improve his work.
Before AI, he said, he would spend more time at the ideation stage, trying to work out which direction to take. Now he can put an idea into an AI tool, ask it to challenge him, and decide for himself what is useful.
“I always have my ideas and plans figured out, but AI helps me polish it, criticise it, and make suggestions on what could be done to enhance it,” he said.
He does not see that as handing over his thinking to a machine.
“AI doesn’t think for me,” he said. “It makes suggestions, and I consider them and pick which is relevant to what I’m working on.”
For him, the relationship is closer to collaboration. “We are more like a team,” he said.
But Akuma worries that not everyone is using AI that way.
Students, he said, are increasingly turning to AI for almost everything, and some are no longer engaging deeply with problems themselves.
A 2026 study by researchers Patience Ebekeyi Bakre and Fa’iza Tukur-Bello, published by Springer in Discover Education, surveyed 535 students across eight Nigerian tertiary institutions and found that they used AI tools including ChatGPT, Grammarly and Gemini for academic work such as coding, writing essays, finding materials and summarising information.
“The most worrisome of them all is that students now depend so much on it that it is difficult for them to think any longer,” he said. “They literally depend on it for everything without engaging their ingenuity.”
That, rather than a machine independently deciding to destroy humanity, is the future that concerns him most.
“Artificial Intelligence was created to help the Natural Intelligence,” he said. “I worry that the overdependence on AI will make their thinking degenerate into a pitiable state.”
He is also wary of trusting AI with decisions that require human judgment or experience. He would not use it to diagnose or prescribe treatment, seek marital advice, or write his research papers.
For his research, there is a reason he prefers to speak directly to people.
“I’d rather get my responses directly from people affected by what I am writing about,” he said.
For Elijah, authenticity is something AI cannot provide. He knows the technology can be useful. He also expects it to become more capable. But he believes the more powerful it becomes, the more important it will be to decide where its boundaries should lie.
“The horror comes in when it is designed to uproot the principles and values that guide human existence,” he said.
“The important question is: Do you understand the answer?”, Akpan, Nigeria
If Akuma worries that students are becoming too dependent on AI, Aniedi Akpan sees the same concern from inside the education system.
Akpan is the Head of Careers and Team Lead, Relationship Management at 16 Plus Schools, a private co-educational school in Lagos that offers secondary and sixth-form education. He thinks AI could eventually become a threat to humanity, although he is cautious about presenting that as inevitable.
He is more concerned about what humans do with increasingly powerful systems: deploying them without sufficient safeguards or using them to amplify existing problems such as warfare, misinformation, cybercrime, surveillance and inequality.
In education, however, AI is already changing the way students learn.
“A student can now ask a question, receive an explanation at an appropriate level, explore alternative approaches to a problem, practise a skill and receive immediate feedback,” Akpan said.
For students who may not always have access to one-to-one support, he said, this can be powerful. But the availability of instant answers is also changing what students need to learn.
“The important question is becoming less ‘Can you find the answer?’ and more ‘Do you understand the answer, and can you determine whether it is correct?’” he said.
Akpan worries about what happens when students allow AI to do the difficult parts of learning for them.
“If a student routinely asks AI to write the essay, solve the equation, or formulate the argument without first attempting it, the student may complete the task while missing the learning,” he said.
He does not think AI will inevitably make people less intelligent. A calculator did not make mathematics disappear, and the internet did not eliminate the need to think, he said. The difference is how the technology is used.
His biggest concern is dependency. He worries about a generation becoming so accustomed to having AI think, write, remember, and decide for them that they gradually lose confidence in their own ability to struggle through difficult problems.
“I am less worried about students using AI than I am about students using it without understanding what it is doing,” he said.
AI can be confidently wrong, reproduce biases, and produce convincing information without genuine understanding. Akpan wants students to grow up neither fearing AI nor treating it as an unquestionable authority.
“They should be comfortable using it, but equally comfortable challenging it,” he said.
“Humans should hold the reins”
ThankGod Obiechina is not particularly worried that AI will wipe out humanity. The business growth strategist at Wehostname.com, a Nigerian web hosting company, thinks there are more immediate threats to human survival, including the possibility of another world war.
“I believe AI can threaten humanity, but not to the point of killing us all,” he said.
The idea of AI causing human extinction, he believes, has been amplified by science fiction and popular imagination.
“If we start talking about human extinction, there are other issues we should be concerned with, and one of them is World War III,” he said.
But like Akuma, Obiechina has a different concern about where AI could take humanity. He worries that people may become so dependent on AI that they gradually lose the ability to think independently and interact with one another.
“The next generation would completely resolve to rely absolutely on Artificial intelligence, thereby stripping themselves of the ability of reason, logic and interaction,” he said.
That fear is already influencing the way Obiechina uses AI. He relies on it to make his work more efficient, accurate and timely, but he does not completely hand over decisions to it.
“I trust the AI tools I use, but I don’t completely rely on them,” he said.
There are certain decisions he would not leave to a machine at all, particularly those involving human relationships, spirituality, and instinct.
“There’s a human touch to everything I do with AI,” he said, “because I believe AI can never replace humans.”
He is not opposed to AI becoming more powerful. In fact, he expects it to evolve as humans do. He just wants humans to remain in charge of that evolution.
“We are evolving; I would be happy if AI evolves too,” he said. “However, I would be more glad if humans hold the reins of that evolution.”
“We don’t need an extinction scenario to take AI risk seriously,” Adetona, founder, Decide
AI becoming very good at doing the work humans currently depend on for a living may be a more immediate danger than AI deciding to kill humanity, said Abiodun Adetona, an AI developer and founder of Decide AI, which helps users analyse spreadsheets and business data using natural-language prompts. He thinks talk of AI wiping out humanity can sometimes distract from risks that are already much easier to imagine.
“I think the idea that AI will kill all of us gets into fear-mongering,” he said. “But there are legitimate risks.”
One of those risks is what happens when increasingly capable AI gives ordinary people access to capabilities that once required years of expertise.
Bad actors, he said, could use AI to penetrate fragile systems. But the consequences could also be economic.
“I also worry about labour displacement,” he said. “If millions of people are displaced from their jobs without alternatives, the political and economic consequences could be serious.”
For Adetona, that is enough reason to take the technology’s risks seriously.
“We don’t need an extinction scenario to take AI risk seriously,” he said.
That concern is particularly relevant as AI systems become capable of performing more tasks that once required human workers. Adetona is himself building AI systems, so he does not see the answer as stopping development. Instead, he believes capability needs to be matched with control.
“As our agents become more capable, we have to be deliberate about what they can access, what actions they can take and what requires approval,” he said.
The principle is simple: an AI system being technically capable of doing something does not automatically mean it should be allowed to do it.
“The more consequential the action, the stronger the controls around it should be,” he said.
Adetona also does not think the industry should slow down simply because the technology carries risks.
“We shouldn’t stop building because there are risks,” he said. “But moving fast doesn’t mean being careless.”
“Responsible stewardship will determine our future,” Roman, founder, Daraja AI
Kelvin Roman is building AI at a time when the technology’s capabilities are advancing faster than many people expected. As founder of Daraja AI, which builds AI tools and infrastructure for African languages and contexts, Roman is helping build the technology he is assessing for risk. Roman does not dismiss the possibility that AI could cause serious harm.
“AI, like many transformative technologies before it, carries risks if not developed and used responsibly,” he said.
But he does not believe the technology itself determines what happens next.
“The real risk comes from how humans design, deploy, and govern these systems,” he said.
That responsibility shapes how Daraja AI develops its systems, with safety checks, testing protocols, and transparent oversight built into the process. Daraja AI also places limits on what Babel, its AI system, can be used for. Roman said the company does not allow it to generate harmful content, violate privacy, or support illegal activities.
“Public safety always comes first,” he said.
Roman also thinks some of the public conversation about AI risk focuses too heavily on science-fiction scenarios, while more immediate problems include AI systems reinforcing biases, spreading misinformation, or making critical errors at scale. These risks do not require an AI system to become independently hostile to humanity; they can happen while the technology is still being designed, deployed, and controlled by people.
He sees rapid progress as an opportunity, particularly for countries like those in Africa, where AI could help improve healthcare access, education, and business efficiency.
“I wouldn’t say we are moving fast or slow,” he said. “We are moving at the speed of AI.”
For Roman, the answer to the risks created by that speed is not to abandon the technology, but to make sure safeguards evolve alongside it.
“Our focus should be on building robust safeguards and ethical guidelines around AI,” he said. “Ultimately, responsible stewardship — not the technology itself — will determine our future.”
“AI is a force multiplier,” Bankong, investment associate, Oui Capital
For Pius Bankong, an investment associate at Oui Capital, an Africa-focused venture capital firm that invests in early-stage technology companies, AI is worth investing in because of the economic possibilities it could unlock.
“AI is a force multiplier,” he said. “It has the potential to add to global GDP through productivity, enable economic activity that was previously limited or locked, and unlock new economic possibilities that could have positive social effects.”
Those possibilities extend beyond software. Bankong also sees opportunities in hardware and robotics, but says investors have to account for the risks that come with developing and deploying the technology. AI’s potential to create and destroy is not unique to the technology, he said. He compares it with nuclear energy, another technology whose impact depends on how it is used.
“There is a considerable argument that AI could threaten humanity,” he said. “But whether it does or not depends on corporate governance, policies, organisations being intentional about the technology and the power that it wields.”
For Bankong, that becomes particularly important as companies compete to develop AI and investors look for returns.
“In capitalism, the first objective is to maximise profits and returns,” he said. But there are checks and balances through policy, legislation, safeguards, corporate governance and long-term thinking.
“What’s the use of maximizing profits only then for certain hazards to erase them?” he said.
He believes investors have a role in that process, although they are not solely responsible for how AI companies operate. Management has primary responsibility, while investors can provide oversight and guidance through their involvement with companies.
The responsibility, he said, is shared across management, investors, policymakers, and others in the ecosystem. And if he believed there was a significant chance that advanced AI could cause catastrophic harm, that would change his investment decision.
“Of course,” he said. “Why would you invest in something that is catastrophic? Short-term stellar returns are pointless if eventually a catastrophe wipes them out.”
“It’s a chicken-and-egg thing,” Adeniyi, AI policy expert and researcher
Kayode Adeniyi, an AI policy expert and researcher, sees both real risks and exaggerated fears in the conversation about AI and human extinction. He believes some of the fear surrounding AI may be amplified because fear itself can be useful, but that does not mean the underlying risks are imaginary.
“It’s a chicken-and-egg thing,” said Adeniyi, who is pursuing a PhD at Imperial College London on using machine learning to develop sensors for monitoring global water risk.
“There’s a part of AI news that you hear about AI is incredibly very dangerous. We need to take it very serious. We need to be cautious about the development. That is marketing.”
But there is another side, he said, where the threats are real. One concern is what happens when AI systems become capable of combining and applying knowledge at a scale no individual human can match. “It’s just like combining the brains of millions of people together,” he said. “So what a single individual cannot achieve, when you have multiple brains together, they should be able to do times a hundred, or times one thousand.”
That possibility, he said, creates risks on different timescales, some of which are already visible. Misinformation and disinformation can be generated and distributed rapidly, while people can use AI to create convincing fake images and videos that could influence how others understand events or make decisions. Other risks are more difficult to see.
Adeniyi works in AI safety, including the problem researchers call AI alignment—the challenge of making sure increasingly capable AI systems behave in ways consistent with human values and intentions.
He offered a hypothetical example. If a sufficiently capable AI were asked to find the best way to solve climate change, it could identify humans as a major source of environmental damage. A system that did not properly understand or share human values could, in theory, arrive at a solution that humans would consider unacceptable.
“The best solution for an AI that is not aligned to human values, or doesn’t have the real emotions that we have, is to kill all of us,” he said.
That scenario is not inevitable, Adeniyi stressed. An AI system does not simply wake up with its own intentions and decide to destroy humanity.
But he believes the possibility becomes more serious as systems become more capable — particularly if humans fail to understand how to make them reliably follow human intentions.
“We need to take the alignment research right,” he said, referring to efforts to understand and control the behaviour of advanced AI systems.
Adeniyi believes African governments also need to do more to prepare for the risks of increasingly capable AI. “Most governments on the continent are not really doing enough,” he said. While countries focus on adopting AI, developing infrastructure and encouraging people to build with the technology, he said, AI safety and evaluation have received less attention. African countries will also continue to use AI systems developed elsewhere, making it important to evaluate them before they are deployed in sensitive sectors.
For African governments, Adeniyi believes preparation should therefore go beyond regulation. The continent needs people who understand how to build AI safely, evaluate its behaviour and test systems for vulnerabilities.
“Talent development is very key,” he said.
Africa may not have the resources to compete immediately with the largest technology companies in building enormous AI models. But Adeniyi believes it can develop expertise in AI safety, research, engineering, and evaluation — areas that will become increasingly important as the technology advances.
“The best thing we can do for ourselves,” he said, “is to develop the right talent.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Rockstar pone a la venta una caja de 'GTA VI' por 400 euros. Tiene toda la morralla del mundo excepto el videojuego
articles.text:
Rockstar parece que está ejecutando un experimento. El próximo 19 de noviembre se pondrá a la venta 'GTA VI' que es, posiblemente, el juego más esperado de la década. Se estima que va a ser el producto de entretenimiento más caro de la historia y algo que sigue picando es que no va a venir en formato físico. Tendrá una caja con un código por 80 euros, la edición sin recortar por 100 euros sólo en digital y... listo.
Sin embargo, que no haya una edición física de 'GTA VI' no implica que no se pueda lanzar de todo en ese formato. Hace unos días anunciaron la banda sonora original en vinilo (por alguna razón, el vinilo sí mola), y ahora nos presentan 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State - Vice City Collection'. Según la compañía, y esto es literal, es un paquete "prémium con todos los artículos esenciales para la diversión".
Todos los elementos para la diversión por 400 euros y, si quieres divertirte con el juego, toca pagar aparte.
La caja de 400 euros del 'GTA VI'
Aquí hay dos términos que es importante que controlemos. Por un lado, Leónida, que es como la versión ficticia de Florida al igual que Vice City es la versión de Miami en el universo 'GTA'. Por otro lado, Macca el caimán, la mascota de una serie de televisión local.
Esto es importante porque gran parte del merchan que viene en la caja corresponde tanto a Leónica como a Maccan. ¿Qué merchan? Este:
- Figura de Macca, el caimán.
- Gafas de sol Oakley Frogskins.
- Riñonera de los cayos de Leónida.
- Gorra ajustable New Era 9FORTY.
- Espejo magnético de Macca, el caimán.
- Vaso de chupito de Chunkee, el manatí.
- Cuchara de cocktail coleccionable de Vice City.
- Llavero cuchilla de Vice City.
- Pines esmaltados de los cayos de Leónida en una lata metálica.
- Pegatinas de los cayos de Leónida en una bolsita.
- Póster de doble cara de suvenir con el mapa de Leónida.
El precio de esta "Collector's Box Prémium" es de 399,99 euros y, como bien indica en una nota, "el juego 'Grand Theft Auto VI' se vende por separado". Además, el envío se paga aparte.
Es cierto que los pines están guay (aunque sólo el de Rockstar o el del 'VI' son icónicos, el resto tienen el diseño feo de cualquier establecimiento de baratijas turísticas en cualquier ciudad, el póster no es ni del juego y cosas como el vaso de chupito o la cuchara de cóctel... pues bueno, ahí están para sazonar el compendio de 'cosas' que han metido en la caja.
Las gafas y la gorra son de marca, eso sí.
Al final, como decía, parece que Rockstar se ha propuesto ver hasta dónde llega el usuario. El malestar por la no existencia de una versión física (y lo que ello conlleva) de 'GTA VI' sigue latente, pero a la vez están anunciando multitud de objetos físicos que complementan la experiencia en el caso de la banda sonora y, en el mejor de los casos, complementan un hueco en una estantería en el caso de la caja.
Como no puede ser de otro modo, en redes los usuarios se han tomado como recochineo el anuncio de la caja de 400 eurazos, pero bueno, quedan menos de dos meses para el lanzamiento del juego y, por mucho malestar que haya por algunos aspectos de negocio, es evidente que hay ganas porque el juego pinta muy, pero que muy bien.
Las decisiones de marketing pues ya son otro cantar.

articles.title: Après les avoir installées de force sur votre PC, Microsoft abandonne ces 3 applications
articles.text:
En octobre 2025, Microsoft annonçait en grande pompe l’arrivée de trois nouvelles applications compagnons pour les utilisateurs de Microsoft 365. « Conçues pour rationaliser les flux de travail quotidien », ces trois applications devaient également aider « les utilisateurs à rester concentrés, à réduire les changements de contexte et à effectuer des tâches plus rapidement ».
Moins d’un an plus tard, les résultats escomptés par Microsoft ne sont visiblement pas au rendez-vous. La firme de Redmond vient en effet d’officialiser leur abandon.
Des fonctions déjà présentes dans d’autres applis
À l’époque, Microsoft avait jugé bonne l’idée d’installer ces trois applications (Contact, Calendrier et Fichiers) par défaut chez les utilisateurs Microsoft 365. Ces applications compagnons squattaient donc la barre des tâches de Windows 11 pour vous permettre d’accéder en un clic à des informations essentielles pour vos tâches quotidiennes.
Leur utilité ne semble malheureusement pas avoir convaincu beaucoup de monde. C’est sans doute ce qui a poussé Microsoft à les abandonner. L’entreprise vient d’annoncer qu’elles cesseront totalement de fonctionner à compter du 16 décembre 2026. Elle a d’ailleurs déjà interrompu les mises à jour et les correctifs de sécurité à destination de ces applications, et à même bloqué leur installation automatique via les mises à jour Microsoft 365.
La fin précipitée de ces applications n’a rien de très étonnant. Car les fonctionnalités qu’elles proposaient faisaient doublon avec d’autres fonctions déjà présentes dans les différents outils de Microsoft. Le Calendrier et les Contacts sont déjà intégrés à Outlook et Microsoft Teams, et les Fichiers sont accessibles via la recherche Windows, l’Explorateur de fichiers, Sharepoint, OneDrive et même directement dans les applis Office. Sans oublier l’assistant intelligent Copilot qui peut être interrogé pour retrouver rapidement des fichiers, des personnes ou des rendez-vous.
Des applis installées de force, mais à supprimer manuellement
Si Microsoft n’a pas eu de mal à imposer l’installation de ses applications compagnons sur le PC des utilisateurs Microsoft 365, l’entreprise semble avoir un peu plus de mal pour ce qui est de leur désinstallation. Comble de l’ironie, ces trois applications, bien que rendues inutilisables, resteront installées sur votre machine. Microsoft n’a prévu aucune mise à jour permettant de les faire disparaître. C’est à vous que reviendra la charge de leur désinstallation.
Une opération, somme toute simple, que vous devrez réaliser manuellement, mais dont vous auriez pu vous passer. Vous devrez en effet vous rendre dans les Paramètres > Applications > Applications installées afin de rechercher les applications Microsoft 365 Compagnons pour enfin les Désinstaller.

articles.title: Qled vs Oled : ne vous faites pas avoir par cette simple lettre qui change tout !
articles.text:
Qled vs Oled : ne vous faites pas avoir par cette simple lettre qui change tout !
Le sigle Qled semble toucher à sa fin, mais beaucoup de gens pensent encore que le Qled et l'Oled se valent ou se ressemblent alors qu'il n'en est rien. On fait le point sur ces deux technologies phares de nos téléviseurs.
Il semblerait que Samsung puisse abandonner le QLED prochainement, après des années de marketing concernant cette technologie. Ils ne vont toutefois pas disparaître tout de suite et mieux vaut quand même faire un petit récap sur cette technologie, surtout si vous pensiez que le Qled était une technologie cousine de l'Oled ? C'est FAUX !
Malgré des noms étrangement similaires entretenus par le marketing des grandes marques, ces deux technologies n'ont strictement rien à voir. Avant d'acheter votre téléviseur, voici la réalité qui se cache derrière les étiquettes.
C'est l'une des confusions les plus fréquentes en magasin. Vous voyez un téléviseur "QLED" et un autre "OLED". Une seule lettre change, et pourtant, c'est le jour et la nuit en termes de technologie d'image.
Le marketing est parfois trompeur : la ressemblance entre les acronymes n'est peut-être qu'une coïncidence, mais les performances, elles, ne sont pas du tout les mêmes. Voici comment ne plus tomber dans le panneau.
Le Qled : du LCD maquillé ?
Ne vous y trompez pas : le Qled (porté principalement par Samsung, Hisense et TCL) n'est pas une technologie révolutionnaire qui remplace l'Oled.
En réalité, le Qled est une évolution de la technologie LCD, celle-là même qui équipe nos écrans depuis les années 2000. C'est une dalle LCD classique avec un panneau de leds à l'arrière pour la lumière, à laquelle on a ajouté un filtre à "points quantiques" (Quantum Dots) pour booster les couleurs. La qualité d'image est donc un peu meilleure, et surtout la technologie reste abordable. Attention toutefois, cela reste du LCD, avec ses défauts historiques : des contrastes limités, du blooming, et une luminosité plus limitée que les téléviseurs Mini Led.
L'Oled : la vraie rupture technologique
L'Oled, lui, joue dans une autre ligue. Développée par LG pour le W-Oled, et Samsung pour le QD-Oled (et adoptée par Philips, Sony, Panasonic...), cette technologie n'utilise pas de rétroéclairage global. Chaque pixel produit sa propre lumière et peut s'éteindre complètement. Cela donne des noirs "parfaits" (contraste infini), zéro effet de halo (blooming) autour des objets lumineux, et des angles de vision excellents. C'est la technologie reine pour les cinéphiles qui regardent des films dans le noir. Ses défauts étaient liés au burn-in (potentiel marquage de la dalle), mais le phénomène temps à disparaître sur les modèles récents, et la luminosité de l'Oled plafonnait par rapport au Mini-Led, mais les dalles de 2025 ont fait d'énormes progrès.
Le verdict : lequel choisir ?
C'est essentiellement votre budget qui vous orientra vers telle ou telle technologie. Optez pour le Qled si vous avez un budget serré (on trouve de bons modèles dès 450-600 €), voire son évolution Mini-Led pour une luminosité plus importante et une meilleure gestion du blooming, en tout cas chez Hisense et TCL.
Et choisissez l'Oled si vous cherchez la meilleure qualité d'image possible pour le cinéma et les jeux vidéo, et que vous avez un budget un peu plus conséquent (comptez environ 1000 € pour une référence comme le LG C5 en promo). Il existe certes des Oled d'entrée de gamme à moins de 800 € comme la gamme B de chez LG, et si on conserve les contrastes de la dalle, leur luminosité est malheureusement très limitée.
Ce qu'il faut retenir : Si vous voyez un prix barré alléchant sur un TV "QLED", vérifiez bien ses caractéristiques et lisez nos tests ! Vous n'achetez pas de l'Oled, mais un écran LCD avec tout ce que cela implique. Pour le "vrai" noir profond et les meilleures couleurs, c'est vers le O qu'il faut se tourner, et non pas vers le Q.

articles.title: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
articles.text:
Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
A breakthrough nanolaser could let future computer chips communicate with light, potentially doubling down on speed while cutting energy use in half.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- Scientists have created an ultra-small nanolaser that could eventually allow microchips to transmit information with light instead of electricity, potentially making computers faster while cutting energy use roughly in half. Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.
- Share:
The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.
In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.
"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.
Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.
Using Light Inside Computer Chips
Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.
Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.
Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.
The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.
Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers
The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.
At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.
When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.
The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.
Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use
The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.
Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.
In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.
Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Technical University of Denmark. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Meng Xiong, Yi Yu, Yury Berdnikov, Simon Klinck Borregaard, Adrian Holm Dubré, Elizaveta Semenova, Kresten Yvind, Jesper Mørk. A nanolaser with extreme dielectric confinement. Science Advances, 2025; 11 (51) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adx3865

Oi está com a conta quase zerada e sem condições de pagar ex-funcionários
Cerca de mil ex-trabalhadores aguardam pagamentos de verbas rescisórias. Valores somam R$ 72 milhões.
A Oi informou à Justiça que ficou com apenas R$ 10 mil em caixa em setembro e não tem condições financeiras de cumprir o acordo para pagar as verbas rescisórias dos quase mil trabalhadores demitidos. Os valores devidos são estimados em R$ 72 milhões.
A situação ocorre após a Justiça do Rio de Janeiro decretar novamente a sua falência. Segundo informações do site Convergência Digital, os salários dos funcionários que permanecem contratados estão em dia, mas não há previsão para o pagamento das rescisões.
A Oi não apresentou uma data, mas propôs à Justiça que os ex-funcionários recebam por rateios conforme a disponibilidade de caixa. Caso o dinheiro não seja suficiente para quitar as verbas, o saldo seria incluído nos rateios seguintes, até o pagamento integral.
Dos R$ 72 milhões estimados, R$ 30,4 milhões correspondem às verbas rescisórias ordinárias, como saldo de salário, aviso prévio e férias proporcionais. Outros R$ 41,6 milhões são referentes à multa do FGTS. Quase R$ 12 milhões deveriam ser pagos em setembro como primeira parcela das verbas e multa do fundo.
O acordo homologado antes da falência estabelecia condições diferentes. A multa de 40% do FGTS seria quitada integralmente entre 30 e 120 dias após o desligamento, conforme a faixa salarial. As demais verbas seriam divididas em seis parcelas para funcionários com salário bruto de até R$ 5 mil e em dez parcelas para os demais, com a primeira vencendo 30 dias após a demissão.
O acerto também previa a manutenção do plano médico e hospitalar por 90 dias após a rescisão, incluindo dependentes cadastrados. A companhia ainda se comprometeu a não descontar o saldo do tíquete refeição ou alimentação creditado no mês do desligamento.
Segundo a Oi, enquanto não ocorrer a venda da Oi Soluções, divisão corporativa da operadora focada no mercado B2B (empresas e grandes clientes do governo), as obrigações precisam ser ajustadas ao fluxo de caixa disponível.
A companhia argumenta que a medida é necessária para manter provisoriamente os negócios e a prestação de serviços essenciais. O processo de alienação de ativos, porém, enfrenta outros obstáculos. Uma decisão recente da Justiça estabeleceu novas condições envolvendo bens da companhia, em mais um desdobramento do processo de falência.
A administração judicial reconheceu a relevância do pagamento das verbas trabalhistas e afirmou que, quando o acordo foi celebrado, havia perspectiva de que os valores pudessem ser pagos nos termos estabelecidos. Com a decretação da falência, porém, os pagamentos passaram a ficar sujeitos às regras do processo.
A decisão sobre a proposta apresentada pela Oi caberá à juíza Simone Gastesi Chevrand, da 7ª Vara Empresarial do Rio de Janeiro.
Este texto originalmente dizia que a Oi tinha apenas R$ 0,01 em caixa. No entanto, descobriu-se posteriormente que a rubrica na prestação de contas equivaleria a R$ 10 mil. A matéria foi corrigida.
